borrowed time intimate indie folk

▼

Aug 16, 2026. Conversational and close-mic, built from small domestic details rather than a clean goodbye.

[Verse 1]
you had this way of talking about your daughter
like the rest of the world went quiet when you did
her first words, her bad dreams, what she ate for breakfast
i never told you how much i loved listening
not to the stories but to your voice going soft
the version of you that didn't know i was watching

[Verse 2]
i used to lie awake while you slept next to me
you'd snore a little and i'd just... stay there
noticing how your breath caught then steadied
wondering how something so ordinary
could make me feel like i was already grieving
like i knew i was holding borrowed time

[Pre-Chorus]
dark brows, serious mouth
the type i never learn to stop choosing
you looked at me once like you were trying to solve something
and i mistook that for being seen

[Chorus]
i left before you could
not because i stopped loving you
but because i'd already hollowed myself out
trying to be enough for someone mid-exit
the last time we talked it didn't feel like the end
it just felt like a tuesday
and now i know that's how it always goes

[Bridge]
she's five now
i found out the way strangers do
you used to tell me everything
now i learn it from a screen
and even missing you like this
i know we're not finding our way back
some things just stay where you left them

[Outro]
you were never going to fix what i was using you for
and i think i always knew that
even when your breath slowed next to me
even when i wanted to stay

maybe pile country indie · 120 BPM

▼

Aug 13, 2026. Country indie, 120 BPM, D or G major. Warm female alto, intimate then fuller. Acoustic guitar-driven with building drums, tambourine, piano bridge, string swells, atmospheric echoes.

[Intro, soft fingerpicked acoustic guitar, 4 bars, light shaker]

[Verse 1, soft conversational close-mic]
I text you things I'd never say when the sun is up
Watching if you'd take the bait or leave me hanging tough
My heart's a deep end kind of love, not everyone can swim
But I keep throwing ropes to boys who won't jump in

[Chorus, lift into chest voice]
I like the chase more than the catch, ain't that a shame
(echo: shame... shame...)
Want the fever not the fire, want the dream without the flame
You're prettier from far away where I can fill the gaps
So I'll keep you in my maybe pile and never look back
(echo: back... back...)

[Verse 2, more confident, hint of bitterness]
You stood beside me in the sun, I waited for the rush
But you were just a man in yellow, nothing but a crush
The fantasy's the best part, the real thing falls flat
I built a castle in the clouds and you can't live in that

[Chorus]
I like the chase more than the catch, ain't that a shame
(echo: shame...)
Want the fever not the fire, want the dream without the flame
You're prettier from far away where I can fill the gaps
So I'll keep you in my maybe pile and never look back

[Bridge, solo piano, vulnerable]
Maybe it's safer wanting what won't stay
I get the ache without the breaking when you walk away
If you got closer I might have to let you in
And that's a game I never learned to win
(echo: win... win...)

[Final Chorus, full band]
I like the chase more than the catch, ain't that the truth
(echo: truth...)
Want the longing not the losing, want the proof without the proof
You're prettier from far away where I control the scene
So I'll keep loving who you aren't and what we'll never be
(echo: never be... never be...)

[Outro, acoustic guitar and piano fade]
(whispered) ...never be

violence to become gentle soft indie pop · 72 BPM

▼

Aug 13, 2026. Soft indie pop, 72 BPM, C or G major. Soft breathy female vocal, fingerpicked guitar, muted piano, subtle synth pads, soft kick/snare brush, airy bedroom-pop reverb. Never belting.

[Intro, soft guitar picking, airy, 4 bars]

[Verse 1, whispered]
I learned to hold my tongue before I learned to speak
Swallowed every scream until my voice came out soft and sweet
You see a girl who's patient, who forgives and who forgets
But you don't see the war I wage between my chest and head

[Pre-Chorus]
I broke myself in pieces just to smooth out all the edges
Burned the angry girl alive and scattered all her ashes

[Chorus, restrained ache]
No one will ever know the violence it took
(echo: it took...)
To become this gentle, to unhook from every hook
I built this calm from chaos, made peace out of the pain
And no one sees the thunder underneath the quiet rain
(echo: rain...)

[Verse 2, tender, tired]
They call me understanding like it came to me for free
Like I didn't claw my way out of the girl I used to be
You think I'm soft by nature, born with kindness in my bones
But mercy was a language that I taught myself alone

[Pre-Chorus]
I held the knife, I chose to set it down instead
Wore forgiveness like a coat when I was cold inside my head

[Chorus]
No one will ever know the violence it took
To become this gentle, to unhook from every hook
I built this calm from chaos, made peace out of the pain
And no one sees the thunder underneath the quiet rain

[Bridge, almost spoken]
And maybe that's the loneliest part
Carrying a war no one saw me start
I wanted to be sharp, I wanted to be mean
But I chose to be the quiet in between
(echo: in between...)

[Final Chorus, soft but present]
No one will ever know the violence it took
To become this gentle, to let go of every hook
I built this calm from chaos, made peace out of the war
And I'm still standing soft... even when I wanted more
(echo: wanted more...)

[Outro, voice and guitar fade]
(whispered) ...even when I wanted more

soft archive

the journal.

notes, observations, the things you'd otherwise lose.

Aug 16, 2026 · Sun
i distract myself by obsessing over people i can't have because it feels safer than loving someone who could stay and watching them disappoint me anyway. unavailable people arrive with the ending already built in; i get the longing without ever having to find out whether ordinary love would choose me. later, seeing that his daughter had turned five made the distance concrete. i used to hear every small story about her. now i find out the way strangers do. wrote “borrowed time” from that.
Aug 14, 2026 · Fri
maddie called the import flow "100% broken" during the demo and told me not to touch the code. it was working — the crawl was quiet for the first few minutes, and my mac was the thing crashing. stayed calm, proved it, then spent the whole night making the criticism impossible to repeat: three production runs, every issue fixed, $93 in credits, tested PR submitted at 3:13am. she merged yesterday’s draft instead. the part worth remembering is not that i proved myself. it’s how quickly proving myself became another all-nighter. competence is mine; i do not have to keep buying proof of it with sleep.
Aug 14, 2026 · Fri
kazie finished the plans for the second-floor house extension on mapa street: three bedrooms, a living area, restroom, and six-metre balcony. it is no longer just a renovation number in a savings tracker; it has floor plans, steel columns, stairs, windows, and my name under owner. found a few things to tighten before permits — the stair and plumbing sheets, electrical load schedule, balcony rail height, and whether one restroom is enough — but the shape of the future house exists now.
Aug 13, 2026 · Thu
played pickleball with natnat, asked him to coach us. standing next to him there were no butterflies at all — just some guy in a yellow shirt explaining my backhand. the wanting only came back once he was far away again. maybe the distance is part of what i like. wanting someone unavailable can feel safer because i get the ache without the risk of being fully seen. wrote two songs out of it — "maybe pile" and "violence to become gentle."

Jul 8, 2026 · Tue
jazer. dandan's father. the one before rhyle.

gaslighter from the start. love bombed me the first few weeks. never mentioned he had a wife and son. when his wife contacted me, he said it was his brother's wife. he doesn't have a brother.

proposed to me knowing it would never go through. asked my mom for ₱20k for the wedding. useless.

ran off with him after the pandemic. didn't realize he was with his wife during lockdown. then we had dandan.

while i was pregnant, while we were living together, he would leave for hours to call his wife and kids. came back like nothing happened. my mom supported us financially for 6 months because he refused to work, kept saying he was looking for jobs but no one ever contacted him.

my brother changed the way he treated me because i kept choosing jazer.

the whole time we were together — flirting with other girls, meeting them, sleeping with them.

almost 6 years no contact now but he still bugs me on instagram nonstop.

after me: 1 long-term gf (2 kids), 1 one night stand (1 kid), and a rumor he impregnated a 15 year old.

he was the first one who broke me.
Jul 8, 2026 · Tue
rhyle christian. the guy after jazer. met around july 2022 after he saw me in calatrava. he was married dec 2021 but his wife died july 2022 from cancer. had a premature daughter, exact replica of him — dark thick brows, slightly downturned eyes.

we started talking october 2022. first date at boulevard, san carlos. he was a basketball player, played for ucpb in manila, known in san carlos basketball circles. quiet person, deep voice, sounded sweet and sad. i fell for his sadness because i related to it.

december 24, 2022 — i asked what we were. he said bf/gf. that made me happy.

he kept calling me his peace. his pahinga.

but he was nonchalant. wouldn't reply for days. only talked when he wanted to come over. i had such bad anxiety waiting for him. made him my world. my time revolved around when he'd come back.

he was good with dandan. they'd play, i took photos/videos. we'd go to beaches, cook together (he loved home cooked meals), watch movies or basketball youtube or those short corny dramas he loves.

his red car with white stripes. headlights i could see from afar — the ones i waited for every night. hours on short trips uphill. eyes crinkling when he laughs. goofy jokes, waiting for me to laugh. the teasing.

wila (dandan's yaya) didn't like him. my friends didn't like him. i was lost to the world for years.

songwriting playbook

the craft.

techniques for writing songs that stick. learned from taylor swift, applied to your lyrics.

dynamics & structure

Drop Technique

Chorus starts sparser and lower energy than the verse, builds tension, then hits a moment of silence before exploding into a high-energy post-chorus. Creates anticipation. Example: "I Knew You Were Trouble"

S.I.A. (Section Impact Accentuator)

Pull parts or all instrumentation out to spotlight a hook, usually at the end of a chorus. Everything cuts out so the hook lands harder. Example: "Love Story", "Lover"

vocal & lyrical techniques

Vocal Register Contrast

Shift between low and high registers based on what the lyrics need. Low register for negative/sad lyrics, high register for passion/desire. The register matches the emotion. Example: "Cardigan"

Production Mirrors Lyrics

Tiny sounds that make the lyric land. "High heels on cobblestones" sound in Cardigan, pen click in "Blank Space" before "and I'll write your name"

Duets with Countering Lyrics

Two voices singing different sides of the story simultaneously. He sings "you never gave a warning sign" while she sings "i gave so many signs" — listeners hear both perspectives at once. Example: "Exile"

Changing Chorus Lyrics

Most pop songs repeat the exact same chorus. Change the words each time to move the story forward. Over half of Taylor's hits do this. Creates narrative momentum.

signature moments

"Swiftisms"

Signature vocal embellishments — laughs, quips, spoken words, clever hooks spotlighted by silence. "Like, ever" and the laugh in "We Are Never Getting Back Together." These became iconic but she phased them out after Reputation to avoid predictability.

Nonsense Lyrics with Purpose

The "whoa" in "Cruel Summer" isn't random — it rhymes with the hook AND sounds like "woe" which fits the negative emotion. Even filler words serve a purpose.

karen's song structure

Verse 1 (8 lines, AABB)
Chorus (4 lines + 2 echo lines)
Verse 2 (8 lines, AABB)
Chorus (4 lines + 2 echo lines)
Bridge (4 lines + 2 powerful lines)
Final Chorus (with variation)
Outro (2-4 lines, soft landing)

Style options: soft acoustic folk OR indie folk chamber pop à la Folklore, OR Hozier-inspired soulful folk rock with blues/gospel undertones (80-85 bpm), OR OPM rock ballad like December Avenue meets Moira Dela Torre, OR alternative pop rock (Olivia Rodrigo meets Florence + The Machine)

vocabulary notes

Elevated vocabulary for lyrics: reckless desire, oblivious to the war, gravity of your gaze, fortress built from sand, paralyzed, undertow, surrender this charade, cascade, paradigm, dissolve, sanctuary, remnants, phantom, silhouette, constellation, unraveling, fractured, illuminate, remnants of what we were

Balance poetic with conversational. Mix complex metaphors with accessible everyday phrasing so the storyline stays easy to grasp.

Søren Kierkegaard

Copenhagen, 5 May 1813 – 11 November 1855 · the father of existentialism, and the man who broke off the only engagement of his life on purpose, then spent fourteen years and roughly thirty books writing around the hole it left

aug 17, 2026▼

childhood & early life

Start with the father, because Kierkegaard did. Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard was born into bonded poverty in Sæding, on the west Jutland heath, and put out to tend sheep as a small boy. Somewhere out there, cold and starving and about eight years old, he raised his fists and cursed God. Then his life got inexplicably good. He was released from bondage, sent to Copenhagen, made a fortune in wool and textiles, retired rich at forty, and spent the rest of his long life convinced that every good thing that had happened to him was the down payment on a punishment not yet delivered.

His second wife, Ane Sørensdatter Lund, had been a servant in his house. He married her within a year of his first wife's death and four months into her pregnancy. She was a distant cousin, she is described by everyone who mentions her as warm and plain and uneducated, and here is the strangest fact in the whole story: in something like seven thousand pages of journals, her famous son never once mentions her. Not on the day she died. Not afterwards. His mother is a hole in the record.

Søren was the seventh and last child, born when his father was fifty-six and his mother forty-four. He was small, thin, hunched slightly to one side, with an oversized head and a talent for language that frightened adults. His father did not send him outside to play; he walked him up and down the drawing room and made him describe imaginary streets in such detail that the boy could smell them. That was his childhood. A rich, elderly, guilt-poisoned man performing the world for a child indoors.

Then the deaths started. Two siblings gone before Søren was nine. His mother and three more siblings inside a span of under three years, all before his twenty-first birthday. Of seven children, five were dead. And the father did the arithmetic out loud: this was the curse coming due, and none of his children would live past thirty-three, the age of Christ. Søren believed it. He believed it so thoroughly that when he passed thirty-four he was genuinely disoriented, and had the parish register checked to make sure of his own birth date.

He drifted through the university for ten years, ran up debts, drank, dressed well, became known around Copenhagen as a wit, and wrote in his journal at twenty-two the sentence that is really the seed of everything he did later: what I really need is to be clear about what I shall do, to find a truth which is truth for me, to find the idea for which I am willing to live and to die. Not a truth. Truth for me. That small preposition is the entire beginning of existentialism.

In 1838 his father, dying, told his sons something. Nobody knows what. Kierkegaard called it the great earthquake, the terrible upheaval, which suddenly forced on me a new and infallible interpretation of all phenomena. Probably the curse on the heath; possibly the pregnancy. Whatever it was, he came out of that room a different person, sat his theology exams within months, and began to write.

what he did & why he's remembered

In roughly twelve years he wrote a shelf of books that invented most of what we now call existentialism and a fair amount of modern psychology, and he did it almost entirely under fake names. Victor Eremita, Johannes de Silentio, Constantin Constantius, Johannes Climacus, Anti-Climacus, Vigilius Haufniensis. They argue with each other. They review each other's books in the newspaper. He would publish an aesthetic book under one pseudonym and a devotional book under his own name on the same day, in the same shop, and let you work out which one you reached for.

This was not vanity. He called it indirect communication, and the logic is sharp: if the thing you want to say is that a person must choose their own life, then telling them what to choose destroys the message in the act of delivering it. So he built a hall of mirrors and made the reader do the work. You cannot skim Kierkegaard and come away with his position, because he refuses to have one in public.

The central obsession is the individual against the crowd. He hated the word public. He thought the nineteenth century had invented a machine for turning people into an audience, and that a person who lives as part of an audience has quietly stopped existing. In The Sickness Unto Death he defined despair not as sadness but as a mismatch with yourself, and made the terrifying observation that the most common form of despair is the kind that does not know it is despair, that goes to work, pays its bills and is well liked. In The Concept of Anxiety he described anxiety as the dizziness of freedom — not fear of any particular thing, but vertigo at the discovery that you could do anything at all, and nothing external is going to stop you.

He is the reason Sartre, Camus, Heidegger and Jaspers had a vocabulary. He is also, quietly, the reason a lot of therapists have one. Freud read Kierkegaard's translator. Auden carried him around. And he did all of it in Danish, in a small city, ignored or mocked, financed by his dead father's wool money.

family life

He never had one of his own. What he had was an inheritance, in both senses.

The literal one was large enough that he never worked a day, and he spent it deliberately, calculating that it would run out around the time he did. He was right almost to the month. The last of the money was gone when he collapsed.

The other inheritance was the melancholy, which he never described as an illness and never tried to cure. He called it a companion. There is a line in the Diapsalmata, quoted in full below, where he introduces it like a person he is dating: my melancholy is the most faithful sweetheart I have had — no wonder that I return the love. That is not a man asking for help. That is a man who has decided the thing eating him is the thing that makes him interesting, and has arranged a truce.

The only surviving sibling was his older brother Peter Christian, who became a bishop — that is, a senior officer in the exact institution Søren spent his last year destroying in print. Peter buried him, and later resigned his own see, and later still was declared incapable of managing his affairs. The family curse did not need to be supernatural. It ran perfectly well on ordinary machinery.

romantic life

One woman. Fourteen months. He built a career on the wreckage.

He met Regine Olsen in 1837, when she was fifteen and he was twenty-four, and circled her for three years. On 8 September 1840 he walked into her family's house while she was at the piano, and by all accounts made an absolute mess of the declaration. Two days later they were engaged. She was eighteen. He was twenty-seven and, by his own later account, in despair the very next morning.

The reasons he gave shift depending on which journal year you read. His melancholy, which he could not lift and would not hand to her. Something he called the thorn in the flesh, which may have been physical, may have been sexual, may have been guilt about the father. A conviction that he had been marked for an unusual task and had no business dragging a bright, ordinary, happy girl into it. And underneath all of it something simpler that he admits in a much later entry: with more faith, he would have married her.

On 11 August 1841 he mailed the ring back with a letter. She refused it. She came to the house, she begged, she said she would live in a cupboard if she had to. So he chose the cruellest possible method and executed it flawlessly: he pretended he had never loved her. He played the shallow, frivolous, faithless man around Copenhagen for two months, made sure she saw it, made sure the whole city saw it, and let everyone he knew think he was a scoundrel — because a girl can recover from being jilted by a scoundrel, and cannot recover from being renounced by a man who loves her and is leaving anyway. On 11 October she released him. He went home, cried, and took the boat to Berlin.

Read the first Abraham variation below. It is the opening of Fear and Trembling, written two years after this, and it is not really about Abraham. Abraham on the mountain grabs Isaac, throws him to the ground and says believest thou I am thy father? An idol-worshipper am I — and then whispers to himself, better is it that he believes me inhuman than that he should lose his faith in thee. That is Kierkegaard explaining himself to Regine in a language he was fairly sure she would never learn to read. And the little paragraph that follows it, about the mother blackening her breast to wean a child, is the same idea in domestic miniature: you make yourself repulsive so the leaving will hurt less, and the person you are protecting never finds out that your face was tender the whole time.

Then the ending, which is worse than the breakup. In 1843 she nodded to him outside Vor Frue Church and he read it as forgiveness and went home elated. In 1847 she married Johan Frederik Schlegel, a decent man she had known before him. On 17 March 1855, on the day she sailed for the Danish West Indies where her husband had been made governor, she picked Kierkegaard out of the crowd on the quay, came over, and said quietly: God bless you — I hope the best for you. He could not produce a single word. He raised his hat. That was the last time they were ever in the same place.

He died seven months later. His will left everything he had to her, on the grounds that to me an engagement was and is just as binding as a marriage, and that therefore my estate is her due exactly as if I had been married to her. Schlegel declined it, and took only the letters. Regine outlived him by forty-nine years, spoke of him without bitterness, and told an interviewer in old age that she had loved two men. She died in 1904, an old woman in Copenhagen, and is buried a short walk from him.

life until death

Two disasters shaped the second half, and he walked into both on purpose.

The first was The Corsair, a satirical Copenhagen weekly that had been praising him. In 1846 he baited it publicly, essentially daring it to attack him, on the principle that a man who allows himself to be flattered by a scandal sheet is compromised. It obliged. For months it ran caricatures of his trousers, his uneven shoulders, his thin legs, his habit of walking the streets talking to strangers. And it worked completely: schoolboys shouted Either/Or at him in the street, he could no longer take the daily walks that were how he composed his books, and he wrote in his journal, what is it to be roasted alive at a slow fire, or to be broken on the wheel, or, as they do in warm climates, to be smeared with honey and put at the mercy of the insects — what is that in comparison with this torture: to be grinned to death?

Grinned to death. Nobody has ever described public ridicule better, and it is worth noticing that he understood in 1846 exactly what a comment section does to a person.

The second was the church. He had come to believe the Danish State Church was a machine for making Christianity comfortable, and that a salaried clergyman preaching the crucifixion in a warm room was a contradiction with legs. But Bishop Mynster had been his father's pastor and he would not attack an old man, so he wrote the letter and left it in his desk. For nine months after Mynster died he still did not publish it, in case it looked like ambition or spite.

Then he published. The pamphlet series The Moment is one of the most sustained pieces of controlled fury in European letters — nine issues in nine months, funded out of his own dwindling capital, hammering the same nail: stop calling this Christianity. His most-quoted advice from that year is not a call to convert but the opposite. Do not go to church, he told his readers, and you will at least have one fewer sin on your account, namely the sin of trying to fool God.

On 2 October 1855 he collapsed in the street with the tenth issue written and unpublished. He was carried to Frederiks Hospital, paralysed in the legs, and lived about six weeks. He was cheerful. He talked. His friend Emil Boesen asked whether he was bitter about anyone, and he said no, he had loved them all. He refused communion from the hospital chaplain — not from loss of faith, but because the man was an official of the state, and he would take the sacrament from a layman or not at all. He did not take it. He said of the attack on the church: the bomb explodes, and the conflagration will follow. He died on 11 November, forty-two years old, with the money gone.

His funeral turned into a small scandal — the church buried him as one of its own, and his nephew stood up in the graveyard to object that the man had spent his last year saying he was not. He had written years earlier that he wished his gravestone to say only that individual. It does not. Instead it carries a stanza of an eighteenth-century hymn he had chosen: Just a little while, then I have won. Then the whole struggle entirely disappears. Then I may rest in halls of roses, and unceasingly, unceasingly speak with my Jesus.

his works

Everything below is from L. M. Hollander's Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard (University of Texas Bulletin no. 2326, 1923), the first substantial English Kierkegaard, long in the public domain and available as Project Gutenberg ebook 60333. Journal fragments are Hollander's renderings from his introduction. The Diapsalmata are aphorisms opening the first volume of Either/Or (1843), written in the voice of a nameless young aesthete; the Fear and Trembling pieces are signed Johannes de Silentio — John of Silence.

1. What is a poet. The single most famous paragraph he ever wrote, and the best description of the transaction between a person in pain and the people who enjoy their work.

What is a poet? An unhappy man who conceals profound anguish in his heart, but whose lips are so fashioned that when sighs and groans pass over them they sound like beautiful music. His fate resembles that of the unhappy men who were slowly roasted by a gentle fire in the tyrant Phalaris' bull — their shrieks could not reach his ear to terrify him, to him they sounded like sweet music. And people flock about the poet and say to him: do sing again; which means, would that new sufferings tormented your soul, and: would that your lips stayed fashioned as before, for your cries would only terrify us, but your music is delightful. And the critics join them, saying: well done, thus must it be according to the laws of æsthetics. Why, to be sure, a critic resembles a poet as one pea another, the only difference being that he has no anguish in his heart and no music on his lips. Behold, therefore would I rather be a swineherd on Amager, and be understood by the swine, than a poet, and misunderstood by men.

2. On his melancholy. Four lines. He gives it a relationship status.

In addition to my numerous other acquaintances I have still one more intimate friend — my melancholy. In the midst of pleasure, in the midst of work, he beckons to me, calls me aside, even though I remain present bodily. My melancholy is the most faithful sweetheart I have had — no wonder that I return the love!

3. On busyness. Written in 1843. Print it out and put it above a desk.

Of all ridiculous things the most ridiculous seems to me, to be busy — to be a man who is brisk about his food and his work. Therefore, whenever I see a fly settling, in the decisive moment, on the nose of such a person of affairs; or if he is spattered with mud from a carriage which drives past him in still greater haste; or the drawbridge opens up before him; or a tile falls down and knocks him dead, then I laugh heartily. And who, indeed, could help laughing? What, I wonder, do these busy folks get done? Are they not to be classed with the woman who in her confusion about the house being on fire carried out the fire-tongs? What things of greater account, do you suppose, will they rescue from life's great conflagration?

4. On his own century. His complaint is not that people are wicked. It is that they are too small to manage it.

Let others complain that the times are wicked. I complain that they are paltry; for they are without passion. The thoughts of men are thin and frail like lace, and they themselves are feeble like girl lace-makers. The thoughts of their hearts are too puny to be sinful. For a worm it might conceivably be regarded a sin to harbor thoughts such as theirs, not for a man who is formed in the image of God. Their lusts are staid and sluggish, their passions sleepy; they do their duty, these sordid minds, but permit themselves, as did the Jews, to trim the coins just the least little bit, thinking that if our Lord keep tab of them ever so carefully one might yet safely venture to fool him a bit. Fye upon them! It is therefore my soul ever returns to the Old Testament and to Shakespeare. There at least one feels that one is dealing with men and women; there one hates and loves, there one murders one's enemy and curses his issue through all generations — there one sins.

5. When he learned to laugh. A whole worldview in one paragraph, and the joke gets darker the longer the list goes.

Just as, according to the legend, Parmeniscus in the Trophonian cave lost his ability to laugh, but recovered it again on the island of Delos at the sight of a shapeless block which was exhibited as the image of the goddess Leto: likewise did it happen to me. When I was very young I forgot in the Trophonian cave how to laugh; but when I grew older and opened my eyes and contemplated the real world, I had to laugh, and have not ceased laughing, ever since. I beheld that the meaning of life was to make a living; its goal, to become Chief Justice; that the delights of love consisted in marrying a woman with ample means; that it was the blessedness of friendship to help one another in financial difficulties; that wisdom was what most people supposed it to be; that it showed enthusiasm to make a speech, and courage, to risk being fined 10 dollars; that it was cordiality to say "may it agree with you" after a repast; that it showed piety to partake of the communion once a year. I saw that and laughed.

6. The dream of the seventh heaven. He is offered anything in the world.

A strange thing happened to me in my dream. I was rapt into the Seventh Heaven. There sat all the gods assembled. As a special dispensation I was granted the favor to have one wish. "Do you wish for youth," said Mercury, "or for beauty, or power, or a long life; or do you wish for the most beautiful woman, or any other of the many fine things we have in our treasure trove? Choose, but only one thing!" For a moment I was at a loss. Then I addressed the gods in this wise: "Most honorable contemporaries, I choose one thing — that I may always have the laughs on my side." Not one god made answer, but all began to laugh. From this I concluded that my wish had been granted and thought that the gods knew how to express themselves with good taste; for it would surely have been inappropriate to answer gravely: your wish has been granted.

7. Fear and Trembling, the Preparation. A man who cannot stop thinking about one Bible story. Then he imagines it four different ways, because he cannot make it come out right. This is the frame:

There lived a man who, when a child, had heard the beautiful Bible story of how God tempted Abraham and how he stood the test, how he maintained his faith and, against his expectations, received his son back again. As this man grew older he read this same story with ever greater admiration; for now life had separated what had been united in the reverent simplicity of the child. And the older he grew, the more frequently his thoughts reverted to that story. His enthusiasm waxed stronger and stronger, and yet the story grew less and less clear to him. Finally he forgot everything else in thinking about it, and his soul contained but one wish, which was, to behold Abraham: and but one longing, which was, to have been witness to that event… But his wish was, to have been with Abraham on the three days' journey, when he rode with sorrow before him and with Isaac at his side… For the mind of this man was busy, not with the delicate conceits of the imagination, but rather with his shuddering thought.

8. Variation I — the one that is about Regine. Abraham makes his son believe he is a monster, so the boy will not lose faith in God. Then, immediately after, in a completely different register, four lines about weaning a baby. He does that after every variation. The pairing is the argument.

It was in the early morning, Abraham arose betimes and had his asses saddled. He departed from his tent, and Isaac with him; but Sarah looked out of the window after them until they were out of sight. Silently they rode for three days… He stood still, he laid his hand on Isaac's head to bless him, and Isaac bowed down to receive his blessing. And Abraham's aspect was fatherly, his glance was mild, his speech admonishing. But Isaac understood him not, his soul would not rise to him; he embraced Abraham's knees, he besought him at his feet, he begged for his young life, for his beautiful hopes, he recalled the joy in Abraham's house when he was born, he reminded him of the sorrow and the loneliness that would be after him. Then did Abraham raise up the youth and lead him by his hand, and his words were full of consolation and admonishment. But Isaac understood him not. He ascended Mount Moriah, but Isaac understood him not.

Then Abraham averted his face for a moment; but when Isaac looked again, his father's countenance was changed, his glance wild, his aspect terrible, he seized Isaac and threw him to the ground and said: "Thou foolish lad, believest thou I am thy father? An idol-worshipper am I. Believest thou it is God's command? Nay, but my pleasure." Then Isaac trembled and cried out in his fear: "God in heaven, have pity on me, God of Abraham, show mercy to me, I have no father on earth, be thou then my father!" But Abraham said softly to himself: "Father in heaven, I thank thee. Better is it that he believes me inhuman than that he should lose his faith in thee."

When the child is to be weaned, his mother blackens her breast; for it were a pity if her breast should look sweet to him when he is not to have it. Then the child believes that her breast has changed; but his mother is ever the same, her glance is full of love and as tender as ever. Happy he who needed not worse means to wean his child!

He wrote that in 1843, eighteen months after making Regine believe he was a shallow man who had never loved her. Happy he who needed not worse means. He is not defending it. He is filing a confession in a place where it will be read for two hundred years by everyone except the one person it was addressed to.

9. Variations II, III and IV. Same morning, four times. Each one is a different way the sacrifice could ruin someone, and none of them is faith.

II. …Without a word he put the fagots in order and bound Isaac, and without a word he unsheathed his knife. Then he beheld the ram God had chosen, and sacrificed him, and wended his way home… From that day on Abraham grew old. He could not forget that God had required this of him. Isaac flourished as before; but Abraham's eye was darkened, he saw happiness no more.

When the child has grown and is to be weaned, his mother will in maidenly fashion conceal her breast. Then the child has a mother no longer. Happy the child who lost not his mother in any other sense!

III. …There he cast himself down on his face and prayed to God to forgive him his sin in that he had been about to sacrifice his son Isaac, and in that the father had forgotten his duty toward his son. And yet oftener he rode on his lonely way, but he found no rest. He could not grasp that it was a sin that he had wanted to sacrifice to God his most precious possession, him for whom he would most gladly have died many times. But, if it was a sin, if he had not loved Isaac thus, then could he not grasp the possibility that he could be forgiven: for what sin more terrible?

When the child is to be weaned, the mother is not without sorrow that she and her child are to be separated more and more, that the child who had first lain under her heart, and afterwards at any rate rested at her breast, is to be so near to her no more. So they sorrow together for that brief while.

IV. …And Abraham prepared everything for the sacrifice, calmly and mildly; but when his father turned aside in order to unsheathe his knife, Isaac saw that Abraham's left hand was knit in despair and that a trembling shook his frame — but Abraham drew forth the knife.

Then they returned home again, and Sarah hastened to meet them; but Isaac had lost his faith. No one in all the world ever said a word about this, nor did Isaac speak to any man concerning what he had seen, and Abraham suspected not that any one had seen it.

The fourth is the quietest and the worst. Nothing visible happens. The father's hand shakes for half a second, the son sees it, and something between them is over forever, and neither of them ever mentions it. Kierkegaard's whole psychology is in that paragraph: the decisive events of a life are unwitnessed, unspoken, and usually about half a second long.

10. The Panegyric on Abraham, opening. The nearest thing to a statement of what he thought was at stake — and notice that the case for meaning is made entirely as a description of what its absence would look like.

If a consciousness of the eternal were not implanted in man; if the basis of all that exists were but a confusedly fermenting element which, convulsed by obscure passions, produced all, both the great and the insignificant; if under everything there lay a bottomless void never to be filled — what else were life but despair? If it were thus, and if there were no sacred bonds between man and man; if one generation arose after another, as in the forest the leaves of one season succeed the leaves of another, or like the songs of birds which are taken up one after another; if the generations of man passed through the world like a ship passing through the sea and the wind over the desert — a fruitless and a vain thing; if eternal oblivion were ever greedily watching for its prey and there existed no power strong enough to wrest it from its clutches — how empty were life then, and how dismal!

11. From the same, on greatness. Read the last clause of each pair. He keeps raising the price.

No, no one shall be forgotten who was great in this world. But each hero was great in his own way, and each one was eminent in proportion to the great things he loved. For he who loved himself became great through himself, and he who loved others became great through his devotion, but he who loved God became greater than all of these. Everyone of them shall be remembered, but each one became great in proportion to his trust. One became great by hoping for the possible; another, by hoping for the eternal; but he who hoped for the impossible, he became greater than all of these.… For he who strove with the world became great by overcoming himself; but he who strove with God, he became the greatest of them all… and there was he who conquered God by his weakness.… But Abraham was greater than all of these — great through the strength whose power is weakness, great through the wisdom whose secret is folly, great through the hope whose expression is madness, great through the love which is hatred of one's self.

12. On the poet as the hero's better self. Written by a man who spent his life writing under other people's names, about people braver than him.

The poet is the genius of memory, and does nothing but recall what has been done, can do nothing but admire what has been done. He adds nothing of his own, but he is jealous of what has been entrusted to him… If thus, faithful to his love, he battles day and night against the guile of oblivion which wishes to lure the hero from him, then has he accomplished his task, then is he gathered to his hero who loves him as faithfully; for the poet is as it were the hero's better self, unsubstantial, to be sure, like a mere memory, but also transfigured as is a memory.

13. Journal fragments, in Hollander's rendering.

"What I really need is to be clear about what I shall do, to find a truth which is truth for me, to find the idea for which I am willing to live and to die."  — age 22, in a notebook, before he had written anything

"The great earthquake, the terrible upheaval, which suddenly forced on me a new and infallible interpretation of all phenomena."  — on whatever his father told him

"He died, not away from me, but for me, so that there might yet, perchance, become something of me."  — on his father's death

"Genius does not whine, but like a thunderstorm goes straight counter to the wind."

"My becoming an author is due chiefly to her, my melancholy, and my money."

"What is it to be roasted alive at a slow fire, or to be broken on the wheel or, as they do in warm climates, to be smeared with honey and put at the mercy of the insects — what is that in comparison with this torture: to be grinned to death!"

"The bomb explodes, and the conflagration will follow."  — on his deathbed, aged 42

The thing to take from him is not the Christianity, which you can leave on the shelf. It is the method. He believed that the decisive facts of a life are private, unprovable, and never available to a crowd; that most people are in despair without the word for it; and that the moment you can genuinely choose is also the moment you feel sick. And he worked all of that out from one engagement he ended himself, on purpose, for reasons he could never get to sound reasonable, at twenty-eight.

Sources: all quoted text from L. M. Hollander, trans., Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard, University of Texas Bulletin no. 2326, 8 July 1923, public domain, Project Gutenberg ebook 60333 — the Diapsalmata, the Preparation and Panegyric from Fear and Trembling, and the journal fragments quoted in Hollander's introduction. Biographical detail cross-checked against the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Kierkegaard, the Søren Kierkegaard Research Centre at the University of Copenhagen, and the Wikipedia entries for Søren Kierkegaard and Regine Olsen. The gravestone stanza is from Hans Adolph Brorson's hymn Halleluja, jeg har min Jesum funden.

Gudrún Gjúkadóttir

Norse legend · sung across northern Europe from perhaps the 5th century, written down in Iceland c.1270 · the woman at the centre of the Völsung cycle — three husbands, every one of her brothers and children dead, and a grief so total that when they laid her husband's body in front of her she could not produce a single tear

aug 16, 2026▼

childhood & early life

She is not a historical person, and that matters less than you would think. Behind her stands a real catastrophe — the Burgundian kingdom on the Rhine was annihilated by Hunnic mercenaries around the year 437, and its king, Gundahar, died with his people. Attila died in 453 on his wedding night beside a Germanic bride named Ildico, of a haemorrhage, and northern Europe spent the next eight hundred years quietly deciding that she had killed him. Out of those two facts came a body of song that travelled from the Rhine to Iceland and grew, in the retelling, into the story of one woman.

In the Icelandic version she is Gudrún, daughter of King Gjúki and Queen Grimhild, sister to Gunnar and Högni. She grows up in the hall of the Gjúkungs, well loved, well dressed and well guarded, and the first thing we are ever shown her doing is waking up frightened and being told not to worry about it. The Völsunga Saga gives us her girlhood in one scene: she tells her women she can find no joy of heart, and when they ask why, she describes a dream. She had caught a beautiful golden hawk and it sat on her wrist, and nothing in the world was dearer to her than that bird, and she would rather have lost every possession she had than lose it.

Nobody in her own household can read it, so she rides out to Brynhild, the wisest woman in the north, to have it interpreted. Brynhild — who is at that moment already in love with the man the hawk represents, and who knows perfectly well what the dream means — tells her the truth in the flattest possible way. There will be a great king; you will have him; you will lose him; you will marry again, badly; and there will be killing. Gudrún's answer is four words long and it is the last uncomplicated thing she ever says: grief and woe to know that such things shall be.

So the character is introduced already knowing her own ending. Everything after that is a woman walking into a future she has been shown in advance and cannot get out of, which is what a Norse poet meant by fate: not that you are ignorant, but that knowing changes nothing.

what she did & why she's remembered

Sigurd came to her father's hall having killed the dragon Fáfnir and taken its hoard, and he was the most famous man alive. Her mother Grimhild wanted him in the family, and Grimhild's method — this is important, because she does it twice — was a drink. Sigurd was given a cup that erased Brynhild from his memory, and he married Gudrún instead, and by all accounts they were happy. He gave her a piece of the dragon's heart to eat and she became, the saga says, grimmer than before and wiser. Then he helped Gunnar win Brynhild by riding through the ring of fire in Gunnar's shape, which is the lie that eventually kills everybody.

It comes apart over something almost petty. Gudrún and Brynhild go down to the river to wash their hair, and Brynhild wades upstream so that Gudrún's water will not touch her, because she has the greater husband. They argue. Gudrún, pushed too far, produces the ring — the one Sigurd took from Brynhild inside the flames and gave to his wife — and says the sentence that ends the world: Grani would not abide the fire under Gunnar the King. It was Sigurd. It was always Sigurd. Brynhild had been married to a man who won her by proxy and she had not known.

Brynhild demands Sigurd's death and gets it. Gunnar and Högni are bound by oath not to harm him, so they feed their youngest brother Guttorm wolf-meat and snake-broth until he is mad enough to do it, and he stabs Sigurd in his bed, beside his sleeping wife. The Short Lay of Sigurd says Gudrún woke soaked in her husband's blood, and her son Hamdir throws that image back at her decades later, in the version of the line quoted below, as if to say: this is where all of it started, and you were in the bed.

What Gudrún is remembered for is what came next, and it is not the vengeance, though the vengeance is spectacular. It is the way she grieves. The First Lay of Gudrún is one of the strangest poems in medieval Europe, because almost nothing happens in it. Sigurd's body is in the hall. Gudrún sits beside it and does not cry, and does not speak, and does not wring her hands, and the women of the court realise she is going to die of it. So they take turns telling her their own griefs, each one worse than the last, trying to unlock her. It does not work. Read it below; it is the oldest and most accurate description of shock I know of in any literature, written by an anonymous poet a thousand years ago who had clearly watched someone go through it.

What finally breaks her is not sympathy and not competition in suffering. Her sister Gullrönd tells the wise old foster-mother to stop talking, walks over, pulls the sheet off Sigurd's corpse and turns his face towards Gudrún's knees. Look on thy loved one, lay lips to his lips. And Gudrún looks once — once — and sees his hair matted with blood and his chest cut open, and falls back and weeps so hard that the geese in the yard start screaming.

Someone in the Viking age understood that grief which has been held in does not respond to being asked about. It responds to being shown the thing.

family life

Her family kills her husband to protect their own reputation. Then her mother drugs her so she will stop being inconvenient about it.

This is the single coldest passage in the whole cycle and it is quoted in full below. Gudrún has fled to Denmark and spent seven years there embroidering — literally sewing pictures of battles and ships into cloth, which is what women in these poems do with what they cannot say. Grimhild hears where she is and comes for her, because a widowed royal daughter is a diplomatic asset going to waste. And Grimhild brings the horn. Not wine: a compound with runes carved and reddened on the horn's face, containing sea-cold water, blood, burnt acorns, soot, entrails, boiled swine's liver. A memory-killing drink brewed by her own mother, so that a state marriage to Atli can proceed without the awkwardness of a daughter who is still in mourning.

And it half works. Then waned my memory when that was within me, of my lord 'mid the hall by the iron laid low. She still refuses. Grimhild offers lands, gold, the hall of Lodver, an army of Hunnish embroiderers. Gudrún tells her, correctly and in advance, that this marriage will end with Gunnar stung to death and Högni's heart cut out. Grimhild starts crying, because she knows her daughter is right, and pushes the marriage through anyway.

Children: with Sigurd, a daughter, Svanhild. With Atli, two sons, Erp and Eitil. With Jonak, three more, Hamdir, Sörli and a second Erp. She outlives every one of them, and she kills two of them herself. There is no version of this story where anybody protects her, and there is no version where she is innocent.

romantic life

Three marriages. One she chose and loved, two she was handed into like furniture.

Sigurd is the only one she wanted, and even that was engineered by her mother with a memory potion, which the poems never bother to resolve — whether he loved her freely or only because Brynhild had been chemically removed from him is left standing there, unexamined, for a thousand years. What she says about him afterwards is not romantic in any modern sense. It is all comparison and scale: he was to my brothers as the green leek is over the low grass, as a high-limbed hart over hurrying deer, as red gold over grey silver. She measures him. It is how a proud woman says he was better than all of you without saying it.

Atli — Attila — she names as a horror before the wedding and is proved right. He invites her brothers to his court, murders them for the dragon's gold, and has Högni's heart cut out of him alive. And Gudrún, who was drugged out of her first grief, is fully awake for the second one.

The third is Jonak, and there is nothing to say about him, which is the point. Her own summary is four lines: then I went a-bed — ah, better in the old days, this was the third time! — to a king of the people. A king of the people. Not even a name. She got there because she walked into the sea to drown herself after killing Atli and the water refused to take her; the waves carried her across the fjord to his land instead. She married the man the current dropped her in front of.

One line survives from her marriage bed with Sigurd, remembered at the very end of her life, and it is the only tender thing in the entire cycle: they had promised each other that he would come to her from Hel and she to him from the earth. She is an old woman shouting at a dead man to saddle his black horse and hurry up. He does not come. Nothing in Norse poetry ever comes when called.

life until death

Here the story stops being about sorrow and becomes something else entirely.

Atli kills her brothers. Gudrún meets him at the door of his own hall coming back from the murder, holding out a gilded cup, and says: Come, then, and take it, king glad in thine hall, from Gudrún's hands, for the hell-farers groan not. He drinks. She serves the feast herself, going down the benches, pouring, handing round the delicacies, the perfect hostess, and the poet calls her the sweet-faced delight of the shield-folk in the same breath as the dreadful woman, which is exactly right. Then she tells him what he has been eating.

She had cut the throats of Erp and Eitil, her own sons by him, and cooked their hearts in honey. The passage is below. What is unbearable about it is not the horror, it is the second half, where she takes the time to describe to him in detail the ordinary life he has lost — the boys will never again be called to your knee, never sit in the middle of the seat handing out gold, never trim a horse's mane or ride out. She makes him grieve properly, item by item, which is the one thing she was never allowed to do for Sigurd. Then she gave the household's gold away, poured blood into the bed, let the dogs loose and set the hall on fire with everyone inside it.

She walks into the sea afterwards and it will not have her. The poem's word for what she feels at that moment is directed at the Norns: she went to the shore with the Norns sorely wroth, meaning she was furious with fate itself, and fate declined to let her out.

Old age with Jonak, and one more disaster. Her daughter by Sigurd, Svanhild — the child she loved best, whose hair she describes as sunlight in the hall — is married to the Gothic king Jörmunrekk, falsely accused of adultery with his son on the advice of a counsellor named Bikki, and trampled to death under horses. And Gudrún does the last thing she has left to do, which is send her remaining sons out to die.

She shames them into it. She tells them they are nothing like Gunnar and Högni. Hamdir answers her with the coldest line any son gives a mother in Norse verse — little didst thou praise Högni's doings when Sigurd woke from out of sleep, and then, if you had not butchered your own sons we would have had allies for this. He knows he is being sent to die and he goes. And the poet gives us one word that turns the whole scene: laughing went Gudrún to the bower of good gear. Laughing, as she fetched her boys their armour. Grief that has gone that far around comes back looking like joy.

They reach Jörmunrekk's hall and cut off his hands and feet before the Goths stone them to death. And Gudrún sits down in the forecourt, alone, and delivers the lament that closes the entire Völsung cycle: three fires, three hearths, three husbands, and only Sigurd ever mattered. She calls for a pyre to be built higher than any queen has ever had, and asks the fire to thaw her heart, which she describes as hard and heavy with sorrow. The poem ends with the anonymous poet saying, in effect: may everyone who hears this find their own troubles lighter afterwards.

That is what she was for. A thousand years of people put their worst nights next to hers to make them survivable.

her works

Gudrún wrote nothing; she is a voice in anonymous poems sung for centuries before anyone in Iceland set them down in the Codex Regius around 1270. But the Edda gives her more first-person speech than any other woman in early Germanic literature, and three whole poems are titled with her name. The verse below is William Morris and Eiríkr Magnússon's translation (Völsunga Saga, 1888) except where marked, where it is Henry Adams Bellows (The Poetic Edda, American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1923). Both long out of copyright. The short lines are the original half-line metre, not modern free verse.

1. Her dream, from the Völsunga Saga. Before any of it happens. Prose, Morris.

"I dreamed that I had a fair hawk on my wrist, whose feathers were of gold… I dreamed that naught was so dear to me as this hawk, and all my wealth had I given rather than him."

…"Grief and woe to know that such things shall be!"

2. The First Lay of Gudrún, complete opening. Sigurd is dead in the hall. This is what shock actually looks like, recorded around the tenth century.

Gudrun of old days
Drew near to dying
As she sat in sorrow
Over Sigurd;
Yet she sighed not
Nor smote hand on hand,
Nor wailed she aught
As other women.

Then went earls to her,
Full of all wisdom,
Fain help to deal
To her dreadful heart:
Hushed was Gudrun
Of wail, or greeting,
But with a heavy woe
Was her heart a-breaking.

3. The competition of griefs. The court women take turns. Giaflaug goes first, then Herborg, Queen of Hunland, who has the worst story anyone present has ever heard. Watch the refrain after each attempt.

Then spake Giaflaug,
Giuki's sister:
"Lo upon earth
I live most loveless
Who of five mates
Must see the ending,
Of daughters twain
And three sisters,
Of brethren eight,
And abide behind lonely."

Naught gat Gudrun
Of wail and greeting,
So heavy was she
For her dead husband,
So dreadful-hearted
For the King laid dead there.

Then spake Herborg,
Queen of Hunland —
"Crueller tale
Have I to tell of,
Of my seven sons
Down in the Southlands,
And the eighth man, my mate,
Felled in the death-mead.

"Father and mother,
And four brothers,
On the wide sea
The winds and death played with;
The billows beat
On the bulwark boards.

"Alone must I sing o'er them,
Alone must I array them,
Alone must my hands deal with
Their departing;
And all this was
In one season's wearing,
And none was left
For love or solace."

Naught gat Gudrun
Of wail or greeting,
So heavy was she
For her dead husband,
So dreadful-hearted
For the King laid dead there.

Two women have now offered up their entire annihilated families and it has made no difference at all. Sympathy is not a key that fits this lock.

4. Gullrönd pulls back the sheet. The most physical moment in Norse poetry and the only thing that works.

Then spake Gullrond,
Giuki's daughter —
"O foster-mother,
Wise as thou mayst be,
Naught canst thou better
The young wife's bale."
And she bade uncover
The dead King's corpse.

She swept the sheet
Away from Sigurd,
And turned his cheek
Towards his wife's knees —
"Look on thy loved one,
Lay lips to his lips,
E'en as thou wert clinging
To thy king alive yet!"

Once looked Gudrun —
One look only,
And saw her lord's locks
Lying all bloody,
The great man's eyes
Glazed and deadly,
And his heart's bulwark
Broken by sword-edge.

Back then sank Gudrun,
Back on the bolster,
Loosed was her head array,
Red did her cheeks grow,
And the rain-drops ran
Down over her knees.

Then wept Gudrun,
Giuki's daughter,
So that the tears flowed
Through the pillow;
As the geese withal
That were in the homefield,
The fair fowls the may owned,
Fell a-screaming.

The geese. A grief so loud that the birds outside join in. Nobody has improved on that image in a thousand years.

5. What she says once she can speak. Praise, then a curse laid directly on her own brother.

"Such was my Sigurd
Among the sons of Giuki,
As is the king leek
O'er the low grass waxing,
Or a bright stone
Strung on band,
Or a pearl of price
On a prince's brow.

"Once was I counted
By the king's warriors
Higher than any
Of Herjan's mays;
Now am I as little
As the leaf may be,
Amid wind-swept wood
Now when dead he lieth.

"I miss from my seat,
I miss from my bed,
My darling of sweet speech…

"So may your lands
Lie waste on all sides,
As ye have broken
Your bounden oaths!
Ne'er shalt thou, Gunnar,
The gold have joy of;
The dear-bought rings
Shall drag thee to death,
Whereon thou swarest
Oath unto Sigurd."

6. The Second, or Ancient, Lay of Gudrún — the opening. Years later, in Atli's house, she tells the whole thing to a stranger. First-person, start to finish. Note the flat, itemised way she narrates the worst day of her life.

A may of all mays
My mother reared me
Bright in bower;
Well loved I my brethren,
Until that Giuki
With gold arrayed me,
With gold arrayed me,
And gave me to Sigurd.

Such was my Sigurd,
Among the sons of Giuki
As is the green leek
O'er the low grass waxen,
Or a hart high-limbed
Over hurrying deer,
Or glede-red gold
Over grey silver.

Till me they begrudged,
Those my brethren,
The fate to have him,
Who was first of all men;
Nor might they sleep,
Nor sit a-dooming,
Ere they let slay
My well-loved Sigurd.

Grani ran to the Thing,
There was clatter to hear,
But never came Sigurd
Himself thereunto;
All the saddle-girt beasts
With blood were besprinkled,
As faint with the way
Neath the slayers they went.

Then greeting I went
With Grani to talk,
And with tear-furrowed cheeks
I bade him tell all;
But drooping laid Grani,
His head in the grass,
For the steed well wotted
Of his master's slaying.

The horse comes back without him and puts its head in the grass. She interrogates a horse because there is nobody else in the household she can trust to tell her the truth, and the horse is the only one that answers honestly.

7. Högni tells her where the body is. Her own brother, describing the scene to her in detail, and her answer to him.

Then Gunnar hung head,
But Hogni told
Of the cruel slaying
Of my Sigurd:
"On the water's far side
Lies, smitten to death,
The bane of Guttorm
To the wolves given over.

"Go, look on Sigurd,
On the ways that go southward,
There shalt thou hear
The ernes high screaming,
The ravens a-croaking
As their meat they crave for;
Thou shalt hear the wolves howling
Over thine husband."

"How hast thou, Hogni,
The heart to tell me,
Me of joy made empty,
Of such misery?
Thy wretched heart
May the ravens tear
Wide over the world,
With no men mayst thou wend."

One thing Hogni
Had for answer,
Fallen from his high heart,
Full of all trouble:
"More greeting yet,
O Gudrun, for thee,
If my heart the ravens
Should rend asunder!"

She curses him and he says, quietly: it would only give you more to cry about. He is right, and he knows what is coming for him. Years later she watches his heart cut out and it does not help.

8. The night beside the body, in her own words.

No sigh I made,
No smote hands together,
Nor did I wail
As other women
When I sat over
My Sigurd slain.

Night methought it,
And the moonless dark,
When I sat in sorrow
Over Sigurd;
Better than all things
I deemed it would be
If they would let me
Cast my life by,
Or burn me up
As they burn the birch-wood.

9. Seven years of embroidery. What she did instead of speaking. She sewed the wars of her family into cloth.

From the fell I wandered
Five days together,
Until the high hall
Of Half lay before me;
Seven seasons there
I sat with Thora,
The daughter of Hacon,
Up in Denmark.

My heart to gladden
With gold she wrought
Southland halls
And swans of the Dane-folk;
There had we painted
The chiefs a-playing;
Fair our hands wrought
Folk of the kings.

Red shields we did,
Doughty knights of the Huns,
Hosts spear-dight, hosts helm-dight,
All a high king's fellows;
And the ships of Sigmund
From the land swift sailing;
Heads gilt over
And prows fair graven.

10. Grimhild's drink. Her mother comes to fetch her and brings a memory-killing potion. The recipe is given in full, which is the poet's way of making sure you understand this was deliberate.

Then brought me Grimhild
A beaker to drink of,
Cold and bitter,
Wrong's memory to quench;
Made great was that drink
With the might of the earth,
With the death-cold sea
And the blood that Son holdeth.

On that horn's face were there
All the kin of letters
Cut aright and reddened,
How should I rede them rightly?

The ling-fish long
Of the land of Hadding,
Wheat-ears unshorn,
And wild things' inwards.

In that mead were mingled
Many ills together,
Blood of all the wood,
And brown-burnt acorns;
The black dew of the hearth,
And god-doomed dead beasts' inwards
And the swine's liver sodden,
For wrongs late done that deadens.

Then waned my memory
When that was within me,
Of my lord 'mid the hall
By the iron laid low.

11. She refuses, and predicts exactly what will happen. The bargaining scene between mother and daughter, and the daughter is right about everything.

Gudrún:
"Never will I
Wend to a husband,
Or wed the brother
Of Queen Brynhild;
Naught it beseems me
With the son of Budli
Kin to bring forth,
Or to live and be merry."

Grimhild:
"Nay, the high chiefs
Reward not with hatred…
To thy heart shall it be
As if both these had life,
Sigurd and Sigmund,
When thou hast borne sons."

Gudrún:
"Naught may I, Grimhild,
Seek after gladness,
Nor deem aught hopeful
Of any high warrior,
Since wolf and raven
Were friends together,
The greedy, the cruel,
O'er great Sigurd's heart-blood.

"Nay, nay, bid me not
With thy words long abiding
To take unto me
That balefullest kin;
This king shall bid Gunnar
Be stung to his bane,
And shall cut the heart
From out of Hogni."

[Grimhild offers lands: Wineberg, Valberg. Gudrún gives in.]

"Then him must I take
From among kingly men,
'Gainst my heart's desire,
From the hands of my kinsfolk;
But no joy I look
To have from that lord:
Scarce may my brother's bane
Be a shield to my sons."

Grimhild weeps during this scene, the poem says, because she already knows her daughter's prophecy is accurate. She does it anyway. That is the whole logic of the dynastic marriage in four lines: everyone can see the ending, nobody stops.

12. The Song of Atli — the feast. Her brothers are dead. She greets her husband at the door with a cup. Then she serves dinner.

Out then went Gudrun,
'Gainst Atli returning,
With a cup gilded over,
To greet the land's ruler;
"Come, then, and take it,
King glad in thine hall,
From Gudrun's hands,
For the hell-farers groan not!"

Then hastened the sweet-faced
Delight of the shield-folk,
Bright in the fair hall,
Wine to bear to them:
The dreadful woman
Gave dainties withal
To the lords pale with fate,
Laid strange word upon Atli:

"The hearts of thy sons
Hast thou eaten, sword-dealer,
All bloody with death
And drenched with honey:
In most heavy mood
Brood o'er venison of men!
Drink rich draughts therewith,
Down the high benches send it!

"Never callest thou now
From henceforth to thy knee
Fair Erp or fair Eitil,
Bright-faced with the drink;
Never seest thou them now
Amidmost the seat,
Scattering the gold,
Or shafting of spears;
Manes trimming duly,
Or driving steeds forth!"

Din arose from the benches,
Dread song of men was there,
Noise 'mid the fair hangings,
As all Hun's children wept;
All saving Gudrun,
Who never gat greeting,
For her brethren bear-hardy
For her sweet sons and bright.

Everyone in the room is crying except her. Exactly as it was in the hall with Sigurd's body, only this time she is the cause. The poet puts the same phrase on her twice, forty years apart in her life, and lets you draw the line yourself.

13. The burning.

To the bed with sword-point
Blood gave she to drink
With a hand fain of death,
And she let the dogs loose:
Then in from the hall-door —
— Up waked the house-carls —
Hot brands she cast,
Gat revenge for her brethren.

To the flame gave she all
Who therein might be found;
Fell adown the old timbers,
Reeked all treasure-houses;
There the shield-mays were burnt,
Their lives' span brought to naught;
In the fierce fire sank down
All the stead of the Budlungs.

Wide told of is this —
Ne'er sithence in the world,
Thus fared bride clad in byrny
For her brothers' avenging;
For behold, this fair woman
To three kings of the people,
Hath brought very death
Or ever she died!

14. Gudrún's Inciting — Bellows's translation, stanzas 2 to 8. She sends her last sons out to be killed, and Hamdir tells her exactly what she is.

2. "Why sit ye idle, | why sleep out your lives,
Why grieve ye not | in gladness to speak?
Since Jormunrek | your sister young
Beneath the hoofs | of horses hath trodden…

3. "Not like are ye | to Gunnar of yore,
Nor have ye hearts | such as Hogni's was;
Vengeance for her | ye soon would have
If brave ye were | as my brothers of old…"

4. Then Hamther spake, | the high of heart:
"Little the deed | of Hogni didst love,
When Sigurth they wakened | from his sleep;
Thy bed-covers white | were red with blood
Of thy husband, drenched | with gore from his heart.

5. "Bloody revenge | didst have for thy brothers,
Evil and sore, | when thy sons didst slay;
Else yet might we all | on Jormunrek
Together our sister's | slaying avenge…"

7. Laughing did Guthrun | go to her chamber,
The helms of the kings | from the cupboards she took,
And mail-coats broad, | to her sons she bore them;
On their horses' backs | the heroes leaped.

8. Then Hamther spake, | the high of heart:
"Homeward no more | his mother to see
Comes the spear-god, | fallen mid Gothic folk;
One death-draught thou | for us all shalt drink,
For Svanhild then | and thy sons as well."

15. The last lament. The end of the Völsung cycle. An old woman sitting in an empty forecourt, counting. Morris's translation.

Greeted Gudrun,
Giuki's daughter;
Sorrowing she went
In the forecourt to sit,
That she might tell,
With cheeks tear-furrowed,
Her weary wail
In many a wise.

"Three fires I knew,
Three hearths I knew,
To three husbands' houses
Have I been carried;
And better than all
Had been Sigurd alone,
He whom my brethren
Brought to his bane.

"Such sore grief as that
Methought never should be,
Yet more indeed
Was left for my torment
Then, when the great ones
Gave me to Atli…

"To the sea-strand I went
With the Norns sorely wroth,
For I would thrust from me
The storm of their torment;
But the high billows
Would not drown, but bore me
Forth, till I stepped a-land
Longer to live.

"Then I went a-bed —
— Ah, better in the old days,
This was the third time! —
To a king of the people…

"But around Swanhild
Bond-maidens sat,
Her, that of all mine
Most to my heart was;
Such was my Swanhild,
In my hall's midmost,
As is the sunbeam
Fair to behold.

"In gold I arrayed her,
And goodly raiment,
Or ever I gave her
To the folk of the Goths.
That was the hardest
Of my heavy woes,
When the bright hair, —
O the bright hair of Swanhild! —
In the mire was trodden
By the treading of horses.

"This was the sorest,
When my love, my Sigurd,
Reft of glory
In his bed gat ending:
But this the grimmest
When glittering worms
Tore their way
Through the heart of Gunnar.

"But this the keenest
When they cut to the quick
Of the hardy heart
Of the unfeared Hogni.
Of much of bale I mind me,
Of many griefs I mind me;
Why should I sit abiding
Yet more bale and more?

"Thy coal-black horse,
O Sigurd, bridle,
The swift on the highway!
O let him speed hither!
Here sitteth no longer
Son or daughter,
More good gifts
To give to Gudrun!

"Mindst thou not, Sigurd,
Of the speech betwixt us,
When on one bed
We both sat together,
O my great king —
That thou wouldst come to me
E'en from the hall of Hell,
I to thee from the fair earth?

"Pile high, O earls,
The oaken pile,
Let it be the highest
That ever queen had!
Let the fire burn swift,
My breast with woe laden,
And thaw all my heart,
Hard, heavy with sorrow!"

Now may all earls
Be bettered in mind,
May the grief of all maidens
Ever be minished,
For this tale of sorrow
So told to its ending.

She asks the fire to thaw her heart. Not to burn it, not to destroy her — to melt something that froze at the beginning of the story, in the hall, when she sat over Sigurd and could not cry. The whole cycle is a woman waiting sixty years for one thing to come unstuck, and the only thing hot enough is her own pyre.

One footnote worth having: there is a second, entirely different Gudrún in Icelandic literature — Gudrún Ósvífrsdóttir of Laxdæla saga, a real-world woman of tenth-century Iceland with four husbands and a famously withheld confession. They are not the same person and the sagas do not connect them. But it is telling that the two most quoted women in Old Norse are both called Gudrún and both defined by something they would not say out loud.

Sources, all public domain: verse and prose from The Story of the Volsungs, translated by William Morris and Eiríkr Magnússon (1888), Project Gutenberg ebook 1152, including its appendix of Eddaic poems (the First Lay of Gudrún as chapter XXXI, the Second or Ancient Lay of Gudrún, the Song of Atli, the Whetting of Gudrún and the Lay of Hamdir). Item 14 is Henry Adams Bellows's The Poetic Edda (American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1923), Guðrúnarhvöt, from the parallel Old Norse and English text at voluspa.org. Historical background on the Burgundians, Attila and Ildico cross-checked against the Wikipedia entries for Gudrun, Gunther, Attila, Ermanaric and the Völsunga saga.

Elizabeth I

Queen of England · 7 September 1533 – 24 March 1603 · declared a bastard at two, imprisoned in the Tower at twenty, queen at twenty-five, and then spent forty-four years refusing to hand control of her life to anyone — a woman who learned before she was three that the people closest to you can sign the order

aug 15, 2026▼

childhood & early life

She was born at Greenwich on 7 September 1533 and she was a disappointment on arrival. Her father had broken with Rome, ruined his own reputation and set his kingdom on fire to marry her mother, and the entire point of the exercise was a son. The birth announcements had already been written out. A clerk had to squeeze an extra letter into the word prince.

She was two years and eight months old when Anne Boleyn was arrested, tried, convicted on evidence that convinced almost nobody, and beheaded on Tower Green. Eleven days later Henry married Jane Seymour. Within weeks Parliament passed an act declaring Elizabeth illegitimate. She went from princess to Lady Elizabeth, and her governess had to write to Thomas Cromwell to ask for clothes, because the child had outgrown everything she owned and nobody in the kingdom was sure whose job it was to buy her a dress now.

She almost never spoke about her mother. Not in forty-four years of reign, not in the surviving letters, not in the speeches. She kept a ring — a mother-of-pearl locket ring, found on her hand at her death — that opens to two enamel portraits, one of herself and one of a woman most historians take to be Anne. That is the whole record. A woman who talked and wrote constantly, who could improvise Latin invective on her feet, and who put the one thing she could not say into a piece of jewellery that only opened if you knew how.

What she did instead was study. Roger Ascham, one of the best scholars in England, taught her Greek and Latin and said flatly that her mind had no womanly weakness in it and that she read more Greek in a day than some churchmen did Latin in a week. She ended up fluent in French and Italian, competent in Spanish, and able to conduct diplomacy in Latin without notes. At eleven she translated Marguerite de Navarre's Le Miroir de l'âme pécheresse from French into English as a New Year's gift for her stepmother Katherine Parr, and embroidered the binding herself in silver thread. It survives. An eleven-year-old girl with no legal status hand-stitching a book cover for the only adult woman who had ever been consistently kind to her.

Then, at fourteen, the thing that probably set the shape of the rest of her life. Katherine Parr, widowed by Henry, married Thomas Seymour, and Elizabeth lived in their house. Seymour began coming into her bedchamber in the mornings in his nightgown, tickling her, slapping her backside, pulling at the bedcurtains. On one occasion in the garden Katherine held Elizabeth still while Seymour cut her black gown into a hundred pieces. Katherine eventually sent her away. When Seymour was arrested for treason the following year, investigators went at Elizabeth hard, hoping to prove she had agreed to marry him without the Council's consent, which would have been enough to kill her. She was fifteen. She admitted nothing, corrected the record where it suited her, and demanded a public proclamation clearing her name. Her interrogator wrote to London in something close to despair that she had a very good wit and nothing was to be got out of her except by great policy.

She was fifteen and she had already worked out that saying nothing is a form of power, that an older man's attention can be a trap dressed as a compliment, and that the state will interrogate a teenage girl about her own body and call it treason law. Everything she became is visible in that year.

what she did & why she's remembered

Her brother Edward died at fifteen. Her sister Mary took the throne, restored Catholicism, and burned nearly three hundred people. In January 1554 Thomas Wyatt raised a rebellion against Mary's Spanish marriage, and Elizabeth — who almost certainly knew nothing useful about it — was the obvious Protestant alternative and therefore the obvious person to destroy.

On 17 March 1554 they came to take her to the Tower. She asked to write to her sister first, and then she wrote the slowest letter in English history. She filled the page, then struck diagonal lines across the empty space at the bottom so nobody could forge an addition, and by the time she finished the tide on the Thames had turned and the barge could not shoot the arches of London Bridge. She bought herself one day. That letter is below, and it is the work of a twenty-year-old arguing for her own life in real time.

She went into the Tower the next morning, Palm Sunday, through the water gate, in the rain, and by one account sat down on the wet steps and refused to move. Her mother had gone in through a gate like that and had not come out. She was held two months, then moved to Woodstock under house arrest for the best part of a year with guards on the doors, where she scratched two poems into the fabric of the building because it was the only publishing she had access to. One of them, cut into a window with a diamond, is three lines long and is the most Elizabethan sentence ever written: much suspected by me, nothing proved can be. Not "I am innocent." Just: you cannot prove it.

Mary died in November 1558 and Elizabeth was twenty-five and queen, and she inherited a country that was bankrupt, at war with France, split in half over religion, and universally assumed to need a man in charge of it within the year. John Knox had just published a pamphlet arguing that female rule was monstrous and against nature. That was the intellectual weather.

What she did with it: a religious settlement deliberately vague enough that most people could live inside it, on the principle that she was not interested in policing what anyone privately believed as long as they turned up. She restored the currency, which her father had debased and which was strangling trade.
