She kept England out of full-scale continental war for most of thirty years by treating her own marriage as a permanently dangled asset — negotiating with Spain, with Sweden, with two French princes, with an Austrian archduke, extracting the diplomatic value of each courtship and closing none of them. It was, quite deliberately, a foreign policy made out of a woman's refusal to answer a question.

And she talked. This is the part that gets underrated. She wrote her own speeches, revised them afterwards, and used rhetoric as an actual instrument of government at a time when a queen speaking in her own voice to a room full of men was itself the argument. In 1566, when Parliament tried to make funding conditional on her naming a successor, she told them to their faces that it was monstrous that the feet should direct the head. In 1597 the Polish ambassador delivered a public complaint in Latin instead of the expected compliment, and she stood up and demolished him extempore, in Latin, in front of the whole court, then turned to her councillors and said she had been forced to scour up her old Latin that had long been rusting. In 1588, with an invasion fleet in the Channel, she rode out to Tilbury and gave the speech everyone still quotes, and the reason it works is that she names the objection out loud before anyone else can — I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman — and then walks straight through it.

The Armada was scattered in 1588. The reign lasted forty-four years and produced Shakespeare, Marlowe, Spenser, Byrd, Drake and the East India Company charter. It also produced brutal wars in Ireland, the beginnings of the English slave trade under Hawkins, executions of Catholic priests, and an intelligence service under Walsingham that ran torture and entrapment as routine policy. She was not a nice ruler. She was an extraordinarily effective one who survived a job that had killed most of the people who held it.

family life

Her father executed her mother and disinherited her. Her stepmother Jane Seymour died. Her stepmother Anne of Cleves was divorced and became, oddly, a friend. Her stepmother Catherine Howard was beheaded when Elizabeth was eight, on charges that rhymed exactly with her mother's. Her stepmother Katherine Parr loved her, educated her, and then sent her out of the house over a man. Her half-brother Edward was fond of her and died. Her half-sister Mary imprisoned her and considered killing her.

That is the family. Six mother-figures in thirteen years, two of them killed by the same man, and the surviving lesson available to a bright child is not people leave, it is something colder: people are removed, and the person who removes them may love you.

She built a replacement. Kat Ashley, her governess from childhood, stayed with her for decades and was twice imprisoned over her. Blanche Parry served her for fifty-six years, from the cradle to her own blind old age. Her cousin Katherine Carey and her daughters filled the privy chamber. William Cecil advised her for forty years, and when he was dying she is said to have sat by his bed and fed him with a spoon. These were the relationships she could choose, and she kept them for life. The ones she was given, she buried.

She had no children and she knew what that meant, and she said the thing out loud to Parliament in 1563 with a bluntness nobody expected: that though after her death they might have many stepmothers, they would never have a more natural mother than she intended to be to them all. Which is a queen doing statecraft, and also a woman who had personally survived four stepmothers making a promise with her own childhood inside it.

romantic life

There was one man she probably loved, and the timing of what happened to him is the reason she never married anybody.

Robert Dudley had known her since they were children; they had both been prisoners in the Tower in the same year. She made him Master of the Horse within days of her accession, which put him physically beside her every day. By 1560 the court was openly saying they were lovers and that he meant to marry her. Then on 8 September 1560 his wife Amy Robsart was found dead at the bottom of a short flight of stairs at Cumnor Place with a broken neck, on a day she had emptied the house of servants. The inquest said accident. Nobody believed it. And that was the end of it, because Elizabeth understood immediately that marrying him now would mean ruling for the rest of her life as a woman who had married a man whose wife conveniently fell down some stairs. She kept him at court for twenty-eight more years and never married him.

When he secretly married Lettice Knollys in 1578 she was incandescent and banished Lettice from her presence essentially forever. When he died in September 1588, a few weeks after the Armada, she shut herself in her rooms until Cecil had the door broken open. Among her possessions at her own death, fifteen years later, was a small box by her bed. Inside was his last letter, and on it, in her handwriting: his last letter.

The other real one was late and strange. François, Duke of Anjou, came courting in 1579 when she was forty-six and he was twenty-four, and by every account she genuinely liked him; she called him her Frog and wore a frog-shaped earring. It was the closest she ever came to going through with it, and the country revolted at the idea of a French Catholic king — one pamphleteer who said so had his right hand cut off, and reportedly lifted his hat with the left and shouted God save the Queen. She let it die. When he left England in 1582 she wrote "On Monsieur's Departure", the most naked thing she ever put on paper, and then kept it in her private papers where nobody would see it until she was dead. Read it below and notice the exact mechanism she is describing: not "I lost him", but I am forbidden to show what I feel, and the performance has eaten the person.

She turned the refusal into an institution. She told Parliament in 1559, at twenty-five, that a marble stone declaring she had reigned and died a virgin would be sufficient for her, and she said she had chosen this life herself and that no danger, no ambition and no offer had ever moved her from it. Cynically, it was the only way to keep sole authority in a legal system where a husband would have outranked her. Personally, it is also a woman who watched two wives of her father die on a scaffold and one stepmother die in childbed, and then declined the institution entirely. Both readings are true and she would have refused to confirm either.

The last one was not romance so much as a car crash. Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, Leicester's stepson, thirty-three years younger, beautiful and reckless and utterly incapable of the deference the arrangement required. He turned his back on her in council and she boxed his ears and he half-drew his sword on the Queen of England. He failed catastrophically in Ireland, abandoned his post, and burst unannounced into her bedchamber at Nonsuch in 1599 before she was dressed — no wig, no white lead, a sixty-six-year-old woman with thin grey hair. She was pleasant to him in the moment and finished him afterwards. He raised a farcical rebellion in 1601 and she signed the warrant, and he was beheaded in the Tower. She was sixty-seven and she never really recovered from it.

life until death

The hardest thing she ever did was Mary, Queen of Scots. Her cousin arrived in England in 1568 fleeing her own nobles and Elizabeth kept her under guard for nineteen years, because Mary alive was a permanent invitation to every Catholic plot in Europe and Mary executed was the precedent that anointed queens can be killed by their subjects — which was precisely the thing Elizabeth needed the world to believe was impossible. Walsingham finally trapped Mary in the Babington plot with intercepted letters. Elizabeth stalled for months, hinted broadly to Mary's keeper that a quiet private murder would be more convenient, was refused, and eventually signed. Then, when the execution was carried out, she raged, wept, claimed she had never meant it to be delivered, and threw her secretary William Davison into the Tower for sending the warrant she had signed. Her council thought it was theatre. It was probably both: real horror at what she had done and a deliberate laying-off of the blame, which is not the same as innocence and she knew it.

The last fifteen years were harder than the legend admits. Bad harvests through the 1590s, real hunger, plague, an unwinnable war in Ireland eating the treasury, and monopolies sold to courtiers that had made the price of ordinary goods a scandal. In 1601 the Commons came at her over it and she did something almost no monarch does: she conceded, revoked the patents, and then gave them the speech afterwards that came to be called the Golden Speech. It is quoted in full below and it is worth reading slowly, because it is a very old, very tired woman with sixteen months to live, telling a room of men that the crown is heavier than it looks and that the only part of it she valued was being loved. She also had them all brought up to kiss her hand before they went home. She knew exactly what she was doing and she meant it too.

By then the coronation ring had grown into the flesh of her finger and had to be sawn off — the ring she had held up to her councillors in 1559 and called her wedding ring to England. Everyone who saw it thought it was an omen. She kept dancing, kept riding, and told an ambassador that her sight was not what it was but she could still see a man's character.

She died at Richmond in the early hours of 24 March 1603, sixty-nine years old, after refusing for days to go to bed. She lay on cushions on the floor with a finger in her mouth, not speaking, refusing physicians, refusing food. The one thing everybody reports is the refusing. She had spent her entire life declining to be moved by other people's urgency, and she died the same way. When they finally asked her to name James of Scotland as her heir she was past speech and is said to have made a sign with her hand. Which is either a clear answer or nothing at all, depending on what you needed it to be, and she was consistent to the last breath.

She is buried in Westminster Abbey. James later moved her, and she now shares a single tomb with Mary, the sister who imprisoned her, under an inscription about partners in throne and grave, sleeping in the hope of resurrection. Nobody asked either of them.

her works

Everything below is hers — poems, letters and speeches she wrote or dictated herself, all long out of copyright. The speech texts survive in several versions taken down by listeners and later printers; the most widely reproduced ones are used here. Spelling is modernised where the source modernises it, and the one letter kept in original spelling is marked as such.

1. Written with a diamond on her window at Woodstock, c.1555. House arrest, age twenty-one. Three lines. Foxe and Holinshed both record them. Note what she does not claim.

Much suspected by me,
Nothing proved can be,
Quoth Elizabeth prisoner.

2. Verses at Woodstock, written in charcoal on a shutter, signed 1555. The longer version of the same year, and much angrier. The last line is a curse disguised as a prayer.

Oh, Fortune! how thy restless wavering state
Hath fraught with cares my troubled witt!
Witnes this present prisonn, whither fate
Could beare me, and the joys I quitt.
Thou causedest the guiltie to be losed
From bandes, wherein are innocents inclosed:
Causing the guiltles to be straite reserved,
And freeing those that death had well deserved.
But by her envie can be nothing wroughte,
So God send to my foes all they have thoughte.

— signed A. D. MDLV. Elizabethe, Prisonner.

3. The Tide Letter, 17 March 1554. Written to her sister Mary as the guards waited to take her to the Tower, deliberately slowly, until the tide turned. Original spelling, from the manuscript at the National Archives. It is the sound of someone reasoning for her life without once sounding frightened.

If any ever did try this olde sayinge that a kinges worde was more than a nother mans othe I most humbly beseche your Majestie to verefie it in me and to remember your last promis and my last demaunde that I be not condemned without answer and due profe wiche it semes that now I am…

…wiche I pray god I may dye the shamefullyst dethe that ever any died afore I may mene any suche thynge; and to this present hower I protest afor God (Who shall judge my trueth, whatsoever malice shall devis) that I neither practiced, conciled nor consented to any thinge that might be prejudicial to your parson any way…

Therefor ons again kneling with humblenes of my hart, bicause I am not suffer'd to bow the knees of my body I humbly crave to speke with your higthnis wiche I wolde not be so bold to desire if I knewe not my selfe most clere as I knowe my selfe most tru… and to this my truth I wil stande in to my dethe.

I humbly crave but only one worde of answer from your selfe.

Your hignes most faithful subject that hathe bine from the beginninge, and wylbe to my ende. Elizabeth.

Mary never answered. She went to the Tower the next morning.

4. Answer to the Commons on her marriage, 10 February 1559. Twenty-five years old, three months on the throne, and a delegation of grown men has come to ask her to hurry up and get a husband. She thanks them, refuses them, warns them never to try picking the man, and closes with one of the great last lines in English.

And to the first part I may say unto you that from my years of understanding since I first had consideration of myself to be born a servitor of almighty God, I happily chose this kind of life in which I yet live, which I assure you for my own part hath hitherto best contented myself and I trust hath been most acceptable to God. From the which, if either ambition of high estate offered to me in marriage… or if the eschewing of the danger of my enemies or the avoiding of the peril of death, whose messenger or rather continual watchman, the prince's indignation, was not a little time daily before my eyes… if any of these, I say, could have drawn or dissuaded me from this kind of life, I had not now remained in this estate wherein you see me.

For the other part, the manner of your petition I do well like of and take in good part, because that it is simple and containeth no limitation of place or person. If it had been otherwise, I must needs have misliked it very much and thought it in you a very great presumption, being unfitting and altogether unmeet for you to require them that may command or those to appoint whose parts are to desire, or such to bind and limit whose duties are to obey, or to take upon you to draw my love to your likings or frame my will to your fantasies; for a guerdon constrained and a gift freely given can never agree together.

…And in the end this shall be for me sufficient, that a marble stone shall declare that a Queen, having reigned such a time, lived and died a virgin.

5. Response to a parliamentary delegation, 1566. Seven years later they are still at it, and this time she loses her temper, and it is magnificent. She opens by demanding they audit her, and then she reminds them what she has personally survived.

Was I not born in the realm? Were my parents born in any foreign country? Is not my kingdom here? Whom have I oppressed? Whom have I enriched to other's harm? What turmoil have I made in this commonwealth that I should be suspected to have no regard to the same? How have I governed since my reign? I will be tried by envy itself. I need not to use many words, for my deeds do try me.

…A strange order of petitioners that will make a request and cannot be otherwise assured but by the prince's word, and yet will not believe it when it is spoken.

…A strange thing that the foot should direct the head in so weighty a cause. I am sure there was not one of them that ever was a second person, as I have been and have tasted of the practices against my sister… There were occasions in me at that time, I stood in danger of my life, my sister was so incensed against me.

…As for my own part I care not for death, for all men are mortal; and though I be a woman yet I have as good a courage answerable to my place as ever my father had. I am your anointed Queen. I will never be by violence constrained to do anything. I thank God I am indeed endowed with such qualities that if I were turned out of the realm in my petticoat I were able to live in any place in Christendom.

6. "The Doubt of Future Foes", c.1568–71. A reigning monarch writing a poem about a specific living enemy — Mary, Queen of Scots, the "daughter of debate" — and circulating it. It is a threat in verse, and the last two lines are not metaphorical. Modernised text.

The doubt of future foes exiles my present joy,
And wit me warns to shun such snares as threaten mine annoy;
For falsehood now doth flow, and subjects' faith doth ebb,
Which should not be if reason ruled or wisdom weaved the web.
But clouds of joys untried do cloak aspiring minds,
Which turn to rain of late repent by changed course of winds.
The top of hope supposed the root upreared shall be,
And fruitless all their grafted guile, as shortly ye shall see.
The dazzled eyes with pride, which great ambition blinds,
Shall be unsealed by worthy wights whose foresight falsehood finds.
The daughter of debate that discord aye doth sow
Shall reap no gain where former rule still peace hath taught to know.
No foreign banished wight shall anchor in this port;
Our realm brooks not seditious sects, let them elsewhere resort.
My rusty sword through rest shall first his edge employ
To poll their tops that seek such change or gape for future joy.

7. Written in her French psalter. Four lines in the margin of her own prayer book. Nobody was meant to read it.

No crooked leg, no bleared eye,
No part deformed out of kind,
Nor yet so ugly half can be
As is the inward suspicious mind.

Written by a woman who was spied on from the age of fifteen and who ran the most effective spy network in Europe. She knew exactly what suspicion does to a face from the inside.

8. "When I Was Fair and Young." Attribution is not certain but the tradition is old and the voice is unmistakable. A woman looking back at every man she sent away and admitting that the god of love collected.

When I was fair and young, then favor graced me.
Of many was I sought their mistress for to be.
But I did scorn them all and answered them therefore:
Go, go, go, seek some other where; importune me no more.

How many weeping eyes I made to pine in woe,
How many sighing hearts I have not skill to show,
But I the prouder grew and still this spake therefore:
Go, go, go, seek some other where, importune me no more.

Then spake fair Venus' son, that proud victorious boy,
Saying: You dainty dame, for that you be so coy,
I will so pluck your plumes as you shall say no more:
Go, go, go, seek some other where, importune me no more.

As soon as he had said, such change grew in my breast
That neither night nor day I could take any rest.
Wherefore I did repent that I had said before:
Go, go, go, seek some other where, importune me no more.

9. "On Monsieur's Departure", c.1582. The best poem she wrote and the only place she ever wrote the truth about herself in the first person. She kept it private; it was found in her papers after her death. The first stanza is a machine of contradictions, and the sixth line is the whole diagnosis: the self she performs has replaced the self that feels.

I grieve and dare not show my discontent,
I love and yet am forced to seem to hate,
I do, yet dare not say I ever meant,
I seem stark mute but inwardly do prate.
I am and not, I freeze and yet am burned,
Since from myself another self I turned.

My care is like my shadow in the sun,
Follows me flying, flies when I pursue it,
Stands and lies by me, doth what I have done.
His too familiar care doth make me rue it.
No means I find to rid him from my breast,
Till by the end of things it be supprest.

Some gentler passion slide into my mind,
For I am soft and made of melting snow;
Or be more cruel, love, and so be kind.
Let me or float or sink, be high or low.
Or let me live with some more sweet content,
Or die and so forget what love ere meant.

Or be more cruel, love, and so be kind is a woman asking to be hurt properly rather than held in the middle, because the middle is where she cannot put anything down. Also worth noticing: she says I am soft and made of melting snow exactly once in her recorded life, on a piece of paper she showed to nobody.

10. Speech to the troops at Tilbury, 9 August 1588. The Armada is in the Channel. She has ridden into an armed camp against her council's advice, and she opens by telling the soldiers she was warned not to trust them.

My loving people, we have been persuaded by some, that are careful of our safety, to take heed how we commit ourselves to armed multitudes, for fear of treachery; but I assure you, I do not desire to live to distrust my faithful and loving people. Let tyrants fear. I have always so behaved myself that, under God, I have placed my chiefest strength and safeguard in the loyal hearts and good will of my subjects. And therefore I am come amongst you at this time, not as for my recreation or sport, but being resolved, in the midst and heat of the battle, to live or die amongst you all; to lay down, for my God, and for my kingdom, and for my people, my honour and my blood, even in the dust.

I know I have but the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too, and think foul scorn that Parma or Spain, or any prince of Europe, should dare to invade the borders of my realm: to which, rather than any dishonour should grow by me, I myself will take up arms; I myself will be your general, judge, and rewarder of every one of your virtues in the field.

I know already, by your forwardness, that you have deserved rewards and crowns; and we do assure you, on the word of a prince, they shall be duly paid you… not doubting but by your obedience to my general, by your concord in the camp, and by your valour in the field, we shall shortly have a famous victory over the enemies of my God, of my kingdom, and of my people.

11. To the Polish ambassador, 25 July 1597, extempore in Latin. He expected to deliver a complaint. She was sixty-three and had not used her Latin in public for years. Translation of the Latin as recorded.

O quam decepta fui! Expectavi legationem, mihi vero querelam adduxisti. How I have been deceived! I was expecting a diplomatic mission, but you have brought me a quarrel! By virtue of your testimonials I have received you as an ambassador, but I have found you instead a challenger. Never in my life have I heard such audacity. I marvel, indeed I marvel at so great and such unprecedented impertinence in public…

…even though the King is young and a King not by birth but by election — and newly elected at that — he would show himself as having a very imperfect understanding of the manner in which such matters are handled between Princes… As for yourself, you give me the impression of having studied many books, but not yet of having graduated to the books of Princes, rather remaining ignorant of the dealings between Kings…

For the other matters which are too numerous to be dealt with here and now, you shall wait until you hear what is considered by certain of my counsellors appointed to consider them. Meanwhile farewell, and hold your peace.

She then turned to her court and said, reportedly: God's death, my lords, I have been enforced this day to scour up my old Latin that hath long been rusting.

12. The Golden Speech, 30 November 1601. Her last speech to Parliament, sixteen months before she died. She has just backed down over the monopolies, which is the only real climb-down of her reign, and instead of defending herself she does this.

We have heard your declaration and perceive your care of our estate. I do assure you there is no prince that loves his subjects better, or whose love can countervail our love. There is no jewel, be it of never so rich a price, which I set before this jewel: I mean your love. For I do esteem it more than any treasure or riches; for that we know how to prize, but love and thanks I count invaluable. And, though God hath raised me high, yet this I count the glory of my Crown, that I have reigned with your loves.

Of myself I must say this: I never was any greedy, scraping grasper, nor a strait fast-holding Prince, nor yet a waster. My heart was never set on any worldly goods. What you bestow on me, I will not hoard it up, but receive it to bestow on you again… render unto them I beseech you Mr Speaker, such thanks as you imagine my heart yieldeth, but my tongue cannot express… For had I not received a knowledge from you, I might have fallen into the lapse of an error, only for lack of true information.

…That my grants should be grievous to my people and oppressions to be privileged under colour of our patents, our kingly dignity shall not suffer it. Yea, when I heard it, I could give no rest unto my thoughts until I had reformed it. Shall they, think you, escape unpunished that have oppressed you, and have been respectless of their duty and regardless our honour?… But I perceive they dealt with me like physicians who, ministering a drug, make it more acceptable by giving it a good aromatical savour, or when they give pills do gild them all over.

I have ever used to set the Last Judgement Day before mine eyes and so to rule as I shall be judged to answer before a higher judge… I know the title of a King is a glorious title, but assure yourself that the shining glory of princely authority hath not so dazzled the eyes of our understanding, but that we well know and remember that we also are to yield an account of our actions before the great judge. To be a king and wear a crown is a thing more glorious to them that see it than it is pleasant to them that bear it.

…There will never Queen sit in my seat with more zeal to my country, care to my subjects and that will sooner with willingness venture her life for your good and safety than myself. For it is my desire to live nor reign no longer than my life and reign shall be for your good. And though you have had, and may have, many princes more mighty and wise sitting in this seat, yet you never had nor shall have, any that will be more careful and loving.

And I pray to you Mr Comptroller, Mr Secretary and you of my Council, that before these gentlemen go into their countries, you bring them all to kiss my hand.

13. On fortune. Two lines, and the argument of her entire life against the shutter she scratched at Woodstock forty years earlier.

Never think you fortune can bear the sway
Where virtue's force can cause her to obey.

Sources, all public domain: the Woodstock verses, the French psalter lines, "On fortune", "The Doubt of Future Foes" and "On Monsieur's Departure" as transcribed at tudorhistory.org and the Poetry Foundation; the Tide Letter from the manuscript transcription published by the UK National Archives; the 1559 answer to the Commons from D'Ewes' Journals via the Elizabeth Files; the 1566 response, the Tilbury speech and the Golden Speech from the Internet Modern History Sourcebook texts reproduced by Hanover College; the Polish ambassador speech from the same Sourcebook. Biographical detail cross-checked against the Elizabeth I, Anne Boleyn, Robert Dudley, Thomas Seymour and Golden Speech entries at Wikipedia and the Royal Museums Greenwich and National Archives education pages. "When I Was Fair and Young" is traditionally attributed to her; the attribution is not certain and is flagged above.

Carl Gustav Jung

Swiss psychiatrist · 26 July 1875 – 6 June 1961 · the man who gave us the shadow, the persona, the collective unconscious and the words introvert and extravert — and who got there by spending three years deliberately letting his own mind come apart to see what was underneath

aug 14, 2026▼

childhood & early life

He was born in a lakeside village in Thurgau in July 1875, the first child of his parents to live. Two stillbirths came before him and a brother named Paul who lasted a few days. That is the household he arrived into: a pastor's house with a small graveyard behind it in every sense.

His father Paul was a country clergyman who had lost his faith and could not say so. Carl decided early that his father was reliable and completely powerless, a man who recited answers he no longer believed and got irritated when his son asked follow-up questions. His mother Emilie was the other problem. During the day she was a perfectly ordinary Swiss housewife. At night, by his account, she became someone else entirely, spoke in a different voice, said things that were far too accurate, and told him spirits came to her room. He was three when she was hospitalised for months for something never properly named, and he was sent to an aunt, and he broke out in eczema over his whole body. He called that arrangement the handicap he started off with.

So he grew up believing, quite literally, that a person could contain two people, because he watched it happen at the dinner table. He then found the same split in himself and gave the halves numbers. Number One was a schoolboy in 1880s Basel with homework and bad shoes. Number Two was an old man from the eighteenth century, dignified, unhurried, who had always existed and found Number One's anxieties provincial. He did not experience this as illness. He experienced it as the truth about people that everyone else was politely ignoring.

Two childhood things he never stopped chewing on. First: he carved a tiny man out of the end of a wooden ruler, painted a stone in two halves to keep it company, hid the pencil case in the attic, and for years smuggled up little scrolls written in a private script. Nobody knew. It made him feel safe. Decades later he read about soul-stones kept in caves near Arlesheim and the churinga of central Australia and had the shock of his life, because he had invented the same ritual alone in an attic at ten with no possible way of having heard of it. Every theory he ever wrote grows out of that moment of recognition.

Second: at twelve a boy shoved him over and he cracked his head and briefly blacked out, and a thought arrived fully formed — now you won't have to go to school anymore. After that he fainted every time he approached a schoolbook. Six months off. Doctors muttered about epilepsy. Then he overheard his father telling a visitor he was frightened the boy would never be able to earn a living, and something in him went cold and practical. He walked into his father's study, opened the Latin grammar, fainted three more times over it, and then never fainted again in his life. He said afterwards that this was the moment he learned what a neurosis is. Not from a textbook. From catching himself doing it.

what he did & why he's remembered

He wanted to dig up ruins; the family could only afford the University of Basel, which did not teach archaeology, so he did medicine instead and spent his life excavating people. His father died a year into his degree and left them nearly destitute. Relatives paid for the rest.

His doctoral dissertation, published in 1903, is the strangest start to any famous career in psychology. He sat in on two years of séances held by a fifteen-and-a-half-year-old medium he called Miss S. W. and wrote her up as a case. Miss S. W. was Helene Preiswerk, his own cousin. He described her family's mental history, her looks, her poor schooling and her mother's rough treatment of her, all in flat clinical prose, and then spent a hundred pages taking apart the "spirits" who spoke through her. His conclusion is the interesting part, and it is quoted below: the noble second personality she produced in trance was not a ghost and not a fraud. It was her, twenty years ahead of schedule, building the woman she wanted to become because her actual life offered no way to get there. Helene later found the book. She was recognisable in it to everyone in Basel. It did not go well for her.

Then Zürich, and the Burghölzli asylum under Bleuler, and the piece of hard science that made his name: the word-association experiment. Read a list of words to someone, have them answer with the first word that comes, and time it with a stopwatch. Most answers land in a second or so. Some take four. Some get a laugh, a stammer, a repeat of the question, a forgotten answer. Jung realised the delays were not random and not stupidity, they were the footprints of something in the mind with a charge on it, and he named those clusters complexes. This is the origin of every "complex" you have ever heard of and, indirectly, of the polygraph. He once used the method to work out which hospital employee had committed a theft. A stopwatch and a word list, and he found the thief.

Freud read the association studies and decided this Swiss Protestant with the good academic post was his heir. They met in Vienna in 1907 and talked for thirteen hours straight. Freud called him his crown prince and got him made first president of the International Psychoanalytical Association. Then it fell apart, over one question: is the engine of the psyche sex, or something wider. Jung said wider. Freud would not move. In 1912, at a congress in Munich, Jung was talking about something that touched the conflict and Freud fainted at the table; Jung picked him up and carried him to a couch. In early 1913 Freud wrote proposing they end the private relationship entirely, saying he would lose nothing by it. That was that.

What he built after that break is what he is remembered for. The persona, from the Latin for an actor's mask, the face you assemble to meet the world, which he insisted is not you and is not even really individual. The shadow, everything you had to disown to build that mask, which does not go away and which you will meet again in whoever you cannot stand. The anima and animus, the contrasexual figure inside, which you will helpfully project onto some real human being and then be confused about. The collective unconscious and its archetypes, the claim that the deepest layer of the mind is not personal at all but inherited, the same in every head, which is why a schizophrenic locksmith and an old manuscript produce the same image. Individuation, the lifelong job of becoming the specific person you actually are instead of a well-behaved excerpt of your culture. Synchronicity, meaningful coincidence. And the pair of words that escaped psychology entirely and got into everyone's dating profile: introvert and extravert, coined by him in print, and later stretched by Katharine Briggs and Isabel Myers into the MBTI. Every INFJ result you have ever taken traces back to a Swiss psychiatrist trying to explain why hysterics and schizophrenics fail in opposite directions.

He also did something nobody in his position had done: he insisted the analyst must be analysed first. His argument was that the doctor cures with his personality whether he likes it or not, so an unexamined doctor is a surgeon with dirty hands. That is now standard training everywhere.

And the part that has to be said plainly. In 1933, with the Nazis in power, Jung accepted the presidency of the General Medical Society for Psychotherapy and the editorship of its journal. He restructured it so that Jewish doctors barred from the German society could stay members internationally, and he later got at least one colleague out of the reach of deportation. He also let an editorial run praising Nazi ideology, and in 1934 published an essay of his own contrasting "Jewish" with "Aryan" psychology and calling the Aryan unconscious the one with higher potential. He spent the rest of the decade writing scathingly about German mass psychosis and the war years quietly profiling Nazi leaders for the American OSS as Agent 488, and Allen Dulles said he never heard a syllable from him that was not anti-Nazi. He never squarely apologised for the 1934 essay. Both halves of that are true and neither cancels the other, and a man who wrote a whole psychology about the shadow being the thing you cannot see in yourself is a fair place to test the theory.

family life

Five children with Emma: Agathe in 1904, Gret in 1906, Franz in 1908, Marianne in 1910, Helene in 1914. Not one of them went into his field, which given the household is probably the healthiest data point available.

The family lived in a house he designed himself on the lake at Küsnacht from 1908 until he died there. Emma's father owned the International Watch Company; when he died in 1905 the daughters and their husbands inherited it, and the Jungs stayed shareholders in a very profitable Swiss watch firm for decades. This is the unromantic engine under the whole legend. He could break with Freud, resign his lectureship, refuse patients for years and spend most of a decade painting a manuscript nobody would see, because his wife's family made watches. Freud, reading Jung's dreams in 1906, had already privately called it a marriage for money and predicted it would fail. He was wrong about the second part.

He also built himself a second house, and it says more about him than the first. In 1922, months after his mother's death, he bought land at Bollingen and began putting up a round stone tower with his own hands. No electricity, no telephone, no running water. He chopped wood, cooked, carved inscriptions into the walls, and added a piece every time his life changed shape, four times across thirty years; the last extension went up after Emma died, which he described as an extension of consciousness reached in old age. The tower was connected to the dead, he said, and he never pretended otherwise.

romantic life

He met Emma Rauschenbach in 1896, when she was fourteen and he was twenty, and reportedly announced at the time that she would one day be his wife. They married in February 1903. She had a limited formal education and no obvious route into intellectual life, so she taught herself, worked as his assistant at the Burghölzli, and ended up a practising analyst and author with her own patients and her own lectures. He called her his intellectual editor to the end.

He also slept with a patient. Sabina Spielrein arrived at the Burghölzli at nineteen in a state of severe disturbance; he treated her, she recovered, she became a doctor and one of the more original psychoanalytic thinkers of her generation, and somewhere in the middle of that they had an affair. When it threatened to become public he denied it in writing to her mother and to Freud before eventually admitting it. Spielrein's own work later fed directly into Freud's death-drive theory. She was murdered by an SS death squad in Rostov in 1942 along with her two daughters.

Then Toni Wolff, who came to him as a patient in 1910 at twenty-two and stayed for the rest of her life. During the years when he was deliberately going down into his own unconscious and was genuinely frightened of not coming back, she was the one who went with him and kept him tethered. She became a serious analyst in her own right. And she became a permanent fixture in the household: Sunday lunches at Küsnacht with the wife and the mistress and the five children, an arrangement Emma agreed to rather than chose. He had written to Freud years earlier that he had polygamous components in himself and that the prerequisite for a good marriage was the licence to be unfaithful, which is a sentence with a great deal of theory doing the work of an apology. Both women stayed. Both women worked. He had the two of them for forty years and never once resolved it, and the man who taught the world about holding the tension of opposites was, in his own living room, simply refusing to choose.

Toni died suddenly in March 1953. He was too unwell to go to the funeral and never wrote about her publicly again. Emma died of cancer in November 1955. He carved a stone for her and cut into it she was the foundation of my house, and people in the house heard him saying, over and over, she was a queen.

life until death

The middle of his life is the part that should be famous and mostly is not. After the break with Freud in 1913 he stopped lecturing, stopped writing for publication, and by his own account came very close to going under. He had waking visions of Europe drowning in blood and seriously considered that he was becoming psychotic; then in August 1914 the war started and he decided the visions had not been about him. What he did next was deliberate and, in a doctor of his standing, close to reckless. He began inducing the visions on purpose, sitting down, dropping into them, letting figures appear and then talking to them like people. He called it active imagination. He wrote every session into a set of small black notebooks, and then copied the results into an enormous red leather folio in medieval script with his own painted illuminations, arguing with an old winged man called Philemon who told him that thoughts are not things you make, they are creatures in a forest that you happen to meet.

He worked on that book from 1913 to about 1930 and never published it. His family kept it in a bank vault. It came out in 2009, forty-eight years after he died, and it turns out to contain, in raw form, every single idea he spent the rest of his career explaining in respectable academic prose. He said it himself: everything he did later was only the attempt to work out what had burst upon him in those years.

He came back up and had an enormously productive second half. Psychological Types in 1921. Travel that shook him: East Africa, India, the Pueblo of New Mexico, where an elder told him that white men all look tense and cruel and must be mad because they think with their heads instead of their hearts, and Jung reported the sentence without a defence. Alchemy, which he spent his last twenty-five years on and which everyone assumed was senility until they understood that he was reading the alchemists as men who had projected their own psyches into their flasks and written down what came back. A heart attack in 1944 at sixty-nine, with a near-death experience he described as being suspended high over the earth and desperately not wanting to return. He came back irritated about it and then wrote his most extraordinary work.

His last decade was thinned by loss: Toni, then Emma, then most of his generation. He kept receiving visitors at Küsnacht and kept going to the tower to split wood. He finished his final essay, "Approaching the Unconscious", ten days before he died at home on 6 June 1961, eighty-five years old. He had told the world for sixty years that the second half of life is not a decline but the part where the work actually starts, and he had the unusual decency to demonstrate it.

his works

Nearly everything of Jung's is still in copyright, so what follows is drawn from the three books of his that are public domain in English: his 1902 dissertation and the essays gathered as Collected Papers on Analytical Psychology (trans. Constance Long, 2nd ed. 1917, Project Gutenberg 48225), The Theory of Psychoanalysis (1915, PG 66041), and Psychology of the Unconscious (trans. Beatrice Hinkle, 1916, PG 65903). These are the young and middle Jung, before the vocabulary hardened. Nothing has been reworded; ellipses mark cuts.

1. The girl who dreamed herself into a better woman. The end of the dissertation, on his cousin. This is the seed of everything: the idea that the split-off personality is not a disease but a draft.

Ivenes is just the continuation of the waking self. She contains the entire consciousness of S. W.'s waking state… The characteristics of Ivenes contrast favourably with the patient's ordinary self. She is a calmer, more composed personality; her pleasing modesty and accuracy, her uniform intelligence, her confident way of talking must be regarded as an improvement of the whole being…

The patient pours her own soul into the rôle of the prophetess, thus seeking to create an ideal of virtue and perfection. She anticipates her future. She incarnates in Ivenes what she wishes to be in twenty years—the assured, influential, wise, gracious, pious lady… S. W. builds up a person beyond herself. It cannot be said "she deceives herself" into, but that "she dreams herself" into the higher ideal state.

— On the Psychology and Pathology of So-Called Occult Phenomena, 1902.

And the conclusion he draws from it, which quietly reclassifies a whole category of "madwomen" as people under construction:

We know also that at this period the future character is formed and fixed… It is not therefore unthinkable that these phenomena of double consciousness are nothing but character-formations for the future personality, or their attempts to burst forth. In consequence of special difficulties (unfavourable external conditions, psychopathic disposition of the nervous system, etc.), these new formations, or attempts thereat, become bound up with peculiar disturbances of consciousness. Occasionally the somnambulism, in view of the difficulties that oppose the future character, takes on a marked teleological meaning, for it gives the individual, who might otherwise be defeated, the means of victory. Here I am thinking first of all of Jeanne d'Arc…

— ibid.

2. The persona. The passage that put the word into the language. Note how far he pushes it — not "your mask hides the real you", but "the mask is collective too, and what is genuinely yours is a much smaller and harder thing to find".

The term persona is really an excellent one, for persona was originally the mask which an actor wore, that served to indicate the character in which he appeared… we can only concede individuality to the bounds of the persona, that is to the particular choice of personal elements, and that only to a very limited extent. It is only by virtue of the fact that the persona is a more or less accidental or arbitrary excerpt of the collective psyche that we can lapse into the error of deeming it to be in toto individual, whereas as its name denotes, it is only a mask of the collective psyche; a mask which simulates individuality, making others and oneself believe that one is individual, whilst one is only acting a part through which the collective psyche speaks.

If we analyse the persona we remove the mask and discover that what appeared to be individual is at bottom collective… Finally, to our astonishment, we realise that the persona was only the mask of the collective psyche.

— The Conception of the Unconscious, 1916. trans. Constance Long.

And the warning attached to it, which is the best thing ever written about people who mistake copying someone for having a self:

Upon close consideration it is astonishing to note how much of our so-called individual psychology is really collective; so much that the individual element quite disappears. Individuation, however, is an indispensable psychological requirement. The crushing predominance of what is collective should make us realise what peculiar care and attention must be given to the delicate plant "individuality," if it is to develop.

…we see daily how the mechanism of imitation is used, or rather abused, for the purposes of personal differentiation; some prominent personality, or peculiar trait or activity is simply imitated, which at least brings about an external differentiation from the environment. As a rule this delusive attempt to attain individual differentiation by means of imitation comes to a standstill as mere affectation, the individual remaining on the same plane as before, only a few degrees more sterile than formerly, and under an unconscious compulsory bondage to his environment.

In order to find out what is really individual in us, we should have to give the matter deep thought, and we should certainly become aware how exceedingly difficult such a discovery is.

— ibid.

3. Where introvert and extravert come from. Everybody uses these words and almost nobody knows they were invented to describe the opposite failure modes of two illnesses. Here is the actual sentence in which they enter English.

I propose to use the terms "extroversion" and "introversion" to describe these two opposite directions of the libido… We say that he is extroverted when he gives his fundamental interest to the outer or objective world, and attributes an all-important and essential value to it: he is introverted, on the contrary, when the objective world suffers a sort of depreciation, or want of consideration, for the sake of the exaltation of the individual himself…

It is obvious that these two contrary movements of the libido, as simple psychic mechanisms, may play a part alternately in the same individual, since after all they serve the same purpose by different methods—namely, to minister to his well-being…

The existence of two mental affections so opposite in character… suggests that these two psychological types may exist equally well in normal persons, who may be characterised by the relative predominance of one or other of the two mechanisms… As Binet pointed out so well, the neurotic only accentuates and shews in relief the characteristic traits of his personality.

— A Contribution to the Study of Psychological Types, 1913. This is the paragraph the entire personality-test industry stands on.

4. The primordial images. His break with Freud, in one page. Freud said the unconscious is a cupboard of things you shoved out of sight. Jung said the cupboard has no back wall.

In every individual, in addition to the personal memories, there are also, in Jacob Burckhardt's excellent phrase, the great "primordial images," the inherited potentialities of human imagination… The fact of this inheritance also explains the otherwise incredible phenomenon, that the matter and themes of certain legends are met with all the world over in identical forms. Further, it explains how it is that persons who are mentally deranged are able to produce precisely the same images and associations that are known to us from the study of old manuscripts…

The primordial images are quite the most ancient, universal, and deep thoughts of mankind. They are feeling just as much as thought, and might therefore be termed original thought-feelings.

We have therewith now found the object selected by the libido when it was freed from the personal-infantile form of transference. Namely, that it sinks down into the depths of the unconscious, reviving what has been dormant there from immemorial ages. It has discovered the buried treasure out of which mankind from time to time has drawn, raising thence its gods and demons, and all those finest and most tremendous thoughts without which man would cease to be man.

— The Conception of the Unconscious, 1916.

His illustration of it is a locksmith's apprentice in an asylum who said the world was his picture-book and he turned its pages by looking around, which is Schopenhauer's entire philosophy arriving in a mind that had never heard of Schopenhauer. Jung refuses to call the patient a philosopher and equally refuses to give the philosopher credit for the image:

The primordial image has also sprung up naturally in the philosopher, and is nothing but a part of the universal human heritage in which, theoretically at least, every one has a share. The golden apples come from the same tree whether they are gathered by a locksmith's apprentice or a Schopenhauer.

— ibid.

5. Inflation, or what happens when you learn too much about yourself too fast. Anyone who has ever done six months of therapy or read three psychology books and started diagnosing their family should read this one twice. He is describing a real clinical hazard and he is not being funny.

This condition is often ushered in by peculiar symptoms; for instance, by dreams of flying through space like a comet, of being either the earth, the sun, or a star, or of being either extraordinarily big or small, of having died, etc. Physical sensations also occur, such as sensations of being too large for one's skin, or too fat… This state is characterised psychologically by an extraordinary loss of orientation about one's personality, about what one really is, or else the individual has a positive but mistaken idea of that which he has just become. Intolerance, dogmatism, self-conceit, self-depreciation, contempt and belittling of "not analysed" fellow-beings, and also of their opinions and activities, all very frequently occur.

The wealth of the possibilities of the collective psyche is both confusing and dazzling… It is very hard to hold one's own against such an overwhelming impression. That is why this phase must be reckoned one of the real dangers of analysis, a fact that should not be concealed.

— ibid.

6. Dreams as a bill coming due. Jung's alternative to reading every dream as a hidden wish. A patient dreams of climbing stairs and being handed a child; Jung's reading is not desire but debt.

One only has to hear this material in order to understand at once that the patient's dream is not so much the fulfilment of infantile desires, as it is the expression of biological duties which he has hitherto neglected because of his infantilism. Biological justice, which is inexorable, sometimes compels the human being to atone in his dreams for the duties which he has neglected in real life.

…we can also learn from the example furnished us by this dream, that there can be no fixed and unalterable dream symbols, but at best a frequent repetition of fairly general meanings.

— Psychoanalysis, 1913.

7. The doctor's own hands. From his 1913 exchange of letters with Dr. Loÿ. This is the argument that made training analysis compulsory in every school of therapy that exists, and it is also just a good description of how to be trusted by anyone.

Because I recognise that the patient does attempt to lay hold of the doctor's personality, in spite of all possible rational safeguards, I have formulated the demand that the psychotherapeutist shall be held just as responsible for the cleanness of his own hands as is the surgeon. I hold it to be an absolutely indispensable preliminary that the psychoanalyst should himself first undergo an analysis, for his personality is one of the chief factors in the cure.

Patients read the doctor's character intuitively and they should find in him a human being, with faults indeed, but also a man who has striven at every point to fulfil his own human duties in the fullest sense. I think that this is the first healing factor. Many times I have had the opportunity of seeing that the analyst is successful with his treatment just in so far as he has succeeded in his own moral development.

— On Some Crucial Points in Psychoanalysis, Letter II, 1913.

With the corollary, which is the sharpest sentence in the book:

We must not forget that, as the doctor shows, and must show, a searching interest in the psychology of his patient, so, too, the patient, if he has an active mind, gains some familiarity with the psychology of the doctor and assumes a corresponding attitude towards him. Thus the doctor is blind to the mental attitude of the patient to the exact extent that he does not see himself and his own subconscious problems.

…persons who cannot admit certain morally grave sides to their characters, project their deficiencies upon the doctor by calmly presuming that he is more or less deficient morally, and that for this reason they cannot communicate certain unpleasant things to him.

— Psychoanalysis, 1913.

8. What analysis is actually for. Not relief. Not comfort. A trade.

Analysis helps the neurotic to exchange his unconscious conflict for the real conflict of life.

— Psychoanalysis, 1913 (author's own summary of the chapter).

And on when analysis is finished, which is his answer to everyone who thinks the point is to be fixed:

End of analysis reached when enough psychological insight and mastery of technique is acquired to enable individual to follow his ever-changing life-line… "Life-lines" have a short and ephemeral value… hence the patient must remain in contact with the unconscious.

— from the author's synopsis to The Conception of the Unconscious, 1916.

9. Where his family sits in his theory. He wrote a whole essay on the father, and the summary line reads like a man describing his own childhood with the names removed.

Unconscious tendency to repetition of parental mistakes… Neurosis, a counter-argument against the personality with which the patient is most nearly concerned… Parental power guides the child like a higher controlling fate… the conflict for the development of the individual.

— from the synopses to The Association Method and The Significance of the Father in the Destiny of the Individual, 1909/1913.

Sources, all public domain: C. G. Jung, Collected Papers on Analytical Psychology, trans. Constance E. Long, 2nd edition — Project Gutenberg 48225, which contains the 1902 dissertation, the association-method lectures, the Loÿ letters, the psychological-types paper and "The Conception of the Unconscious". The Theory of Psychoanalysis, 1915 — PG 66041. Psychology of the Unconscious, trans. Beatrice M. Hinkle, 1916 — PG 65903. Biographical detail cross-checked against the Jung and Emma Jung entries at Wikipedia, the Speaking of Jung timeline, the Library of Congress Red Book exhibition, and Sonu Shamdasani's paper on S. W. Passages marked as synopses are the printed chapter summaries in the Long edition rather than body text, and are labelled as such. Memories, Dreams, Reflections, the Red Book and the later Collected Works are still in copyright and are not quoted here.

Clytemnestra

Queen of Argos · Greek myth, dramatised c.458 BC · she waited ten years for the man who cut her daughter's throat for a favourable wind, ran his kingdom while he was gone, and killed him in the bath on the day he came home — then stood over the body and refused to apologise for any of it

aug 13, 2026▼

childhood & early life

She was a Spartan princess, daughter of Tyndareus and Leda, and she had a sister you have heard of. On the night Leda conceived, Zeus came to her as a swan; the tradition splits the four children into two pairs, two of the god and two of the mortal husband, and Clytemnestra always lands on the mortal side. Helen was the divine one, the beautiful one, the one wars get fought over. Clytemnestra was the other one. That arrangement — being the sister who is not the story — is the first fact of her life and she is still arguing with it in Euripides three hundred years later.

Her first marriage is the part most retellings quietly drop, and it is the part that explains everything. She was married to Tantalus, a king of Pisa, and she had a baby with him. Agamemnon wanted her. So Agamemnon killed her husband, took the infant out of her arms, and dashed it on the ground, and then married her over the corpses. Her brothers Castor and Pollux came for him with an army. Her own father talked them down and handed her back to the man who had done it. She stayed married to him for roughly twenty years and bore him four children.

So before the famous story starts, she has already survived a murdered spouse, a murdered child, a forced marriage, and a father who chose the diplomatic solution over his daughter. Nobody in the myth ever treats this as relevant. She raises it exactly once, in Euripides, standing in front of the man himself, and it is quoted in full below.

what she did & why she's remembered

Helen ran off with Paris. Greece mobilised. The fleet sat at Aulis and the wind would not turn, and the prophet Calchas said the goddess wanted Agamemnon's eldest daughter. So Agamemnon sent home a letter saying that Iphigenia was to come to camp because Achilles wanted to marry her. Clytemnestra dressed her girl for a wedding and drove her to the harbour herself.

What happened at the altar is described by Aeschylus with a detail that has never stopped being unbearable: the girl started begging, so they gagged her. Bit her mouth shut like a horse, specifically so that she could not curse the house on her way out. She was lifted over the stone like a kid goat, her saffron robe trailing on the ground, and the last thing she had left was her eyes, which she used. Then the wind changed and a thousand ships sailed for Troy.

Clytemnestra went home and ruled Argos for ten years. This is the part that gets skipped. She was not sitting in a tower weeping; she was governing a kingdom in wartime, and she was good at it. Aeschylus's chorus of old men, who despise her, call her the woman in whose breast beats the heart of a man, which is the highest compliment their vocabulary contains and is not meant as one. She set up a relay of signal fires from Troy to Argos across the whole Aegean, a chain of mountaintop beacons run on a schedule, so that she would know the city had fallen the same night it fell and would have several days' head start on her husband's ship. That is not grief. That is planning.

He came home in a chariot with a captive concubine sitting behind him — Cassandra, princess of Troy, a prophet whom nobody believes, brought into his wife's house as a prize. Clytemnestra came out and gave him a public welcome speech of such sustained, fluent, faultless devotion that the elders praised her for it, and every single line of it is a lie she is enjoying. She had purple cloth spread from his chariot to the door and pushed him, gently and with total control, into walking on it, because a man who tramples wealth in front of his own people looks like a tyrant and she wanted him to look like one before he died. He argued. He lost the argument. He walked on the purple.

Then she ran him a bath, and when he stood up she threw a robe over him with no armholes — a net — and hit him three times with an axe while he was tangled in his own clothes. She killed Cassandra beside him. Then she opened the doors, stood over both bodies where the whole city could see, and delivered the speech she is remembered for: no denial, no plea of madness, no shifting it onto Aegisthus. All is avowed, and as I smote I stand. She tells them the blood hit her face and it felt like rain on a field of grain.

She is remembered because of what she says next. She turns on the elders and asks where their outrage was when he killed the girl. They had nothing to say then. They have a great deal to say now. Twenty-five centuries later that question is still the load-bearing beam of the entire trilogy, and Aeschylus, who is not on her side, was honest enough to write it so well that she wins the exchange.

family life

Four children by Agamemnon: Iphigenia, Electra, Chrysothemis and Orestes. She lost the first to her husband, the second to hatred, the third to irrelevance, and the fourth killed her.

Electra is the wound that stayed open. Her father's daughter, entirely, and she looked at her mother and saw a murderer with a lover and jewellery paid for out of a dead man's estate. Clytemnestra's answer to her, in Euripides, is one of the most exhausted lines in Greek tragedy: I know thy heart, from long ago. Thou hast alway loved him best. 'Tis oft-time so: one is her father's daughter, and one hot to bear her mother's part. I blame thee not. And then, when she thinks nobody is listening: think not I am happy, child. 'Tis all as I have willed it. She got exactly what she planned and she says out loud that it did not help.

Orestes she sent away as a small boy. She says she did it to keep him safe from a mob if Argos turned. He says she sold him. Both may be true; that is how families argue. He came back grown and unrecognisable and killed her, and the tell in Aeschylus is that she does not recognise him either — she hears a stranger's voice in her own hall and calls for a battle-axe, at maybe fifty years old, ready to fight her way out one more time. Only when she sees him does she stop.

The night before he came she dreamed she gave birth to a snake, and swaddled it, and put it to her breast, and it bit her and drew blood mixed into the milk. She woke up screaming and had every lamp in the palace lit, which is the single most human sentence anyone writes about her. Then she sent offerings to her dead husband's grave to buy the dream off. The offerings arrived at the tomb at the same time as her son.

romantic life

Two husbands and a lover, and she chose none of the first two.

Tantalus she seems to have wanted and was widowed from by force. Agamemnon she was taken by. Aegisthus, her cousin by the family's own poisoned blood — son of Thyestes, raised on the far end of the curse, with his own inherited grievance against Agamemnon — she picked.

Homer, who is the oldest source and the most hostile, says it took work. She held out. Agamemnon had left a court poet behind with instructions to keep watch on her, and she listened to him; Aegisthus had to maroon the man on a desert island before she gave in. The Odyssey frames this as a woman corrupted. Read it the other way and it is a woman under surveillance, informed on by a servant, for years, in her own house, while her husband is overseas with other men's daughters.

Euripides lets her say the real thing, and it is not romantic at all. She had not intended to kill him, she says. She could have lived with the daughter, given years. What finished it was that he brought Cassandra into the house: and set her in my room; and in one wall would hold two queens. Then comes the argument no Greek man in that theatre wanted to hear out loud — if a husband strays, why exactly does a wife not get to; and the world calls her cursed while the lords of all the wrong must hear no curse. Aegisthus is her answer to that question more than he is her love. In Aeschylus she calls him her shield and in the same breath calls Agamemnon false, and the whole speech is less about desire than about scorekeeping.

And she is not fooled about him. Aegisthus is a coward — the chorus tells him so to his face, that he stayed home and let a woman do the killing. Cassandra, who can see everything, calls him a lion with no courage lying in a lair. Clytemnestra had the nerve; he had the claim. She knew which of them held the axe.

life until death

She ruled with Aegisthus for seven or eight years. She kept Electra in the house and then, in Euripides's version, married her off to a peasant farmer so that any grandson would be too low-born to matter — a cold, competent, dynastic move, and the farmer turns out to be the most decent man in the play and never touches her. She kept Chrysothemis quiet. She kept the kingdom. She let it be known that Orestes was somewhere far away and not coming.

Then two travellers arrived with a story about a dead prince and an urn of ashes, and she believed it, and Aeschylus gives her a half-line as she takes the news that is impossible to read cleanly — relief and grief in the same breath, because the safest thing that could happen to her was her son dying. The travellers were Orestes and Pylades. He killed Aegisthus first. She heard the scream from another room, worked out instantly what it meant, and called for an axe.

When she saw who it was she pulled open her dress and showed him her breast, and told him he had fallen asleep against it. He hesitated. It is the pivot of the whole trilogy — a man with a god's order in one hand and his mother in front of him — and it takes Pylades, silent for the entire play up to this point, saying three lines about Apollo, to move him. Then mother and son have a short brutal argument, ten lines each way, about who abandoned whom. She loses it on the merits and wins it on the last word: beware thy mother's vengeful hounds from hell. He drove her inside and killed her over Aegisthus's body.

The hounds were real. The Furies came for Orestes within minutes, invisible to everyone but him, and hunted him across Greece until Athens put him on trial — the first murder trial, in the founding myth of the jury. The jury split evenly. Athena cast the deciding vote for acquittal and gave her reason: she has no mother, she was born from her father's head, and she is always for the male. That is the actual verdict. Not that Clytemnestra was wrong, but that killing a husband outranks killing a wife, and killing a mother is a lesser crime than killing a father, because the mother, Apollo argues in court, is only the soil the seed was planted in.

So she gets the last thing the myth had to give her, which is to be right and lose anyway. Even dead she will not shut up — she comes back as a ghost in the third play to wake the sleeping Furies and shout at them for slacking, still furious, still organising. Three thousand years of readers have called her a monster on Homer's word, and every serious writer who has actually looked at her, from Aeschylus to Euripides to the last twenty years of novelists, has come back with the same uncomfortable finding: she did an unforgivable thing for a reason nobody has ever adequately answered.

her works

She wrote nothing; she is a character, not an author. But she has more lines than almost any woman in surviving Greek drama, and they are the works — Aeschylus's Oresteia of 458 BC, Euripides's Electra and Iphigenia at Aulis, and Homer's version, which is the prosecution case. Translations here are all public domain: E. D. A. Morshead's 1881 verse House of Atreus for Aeschylus, Gilbert Murray's 1905 Electra, Theodore Alois Buckley's 1850 prose for Iphigenia at Aulis, Samuel Butler's 1900 prose Odyssey.

1. The watchman, before she appears. The Oresteia opens with a man on a roof who has been lying there for a year waiting for a fire, and the first thing anyone says about Clytemnestra is said behind her back.

I pray the gods to quit me of my toils,
To close the watch I keep, this livelong year;
For as a watch-dog lying, not at rest,
Propped on one arm, upon the palace-roof
Of Atreus' race, too long, too well I know
The starry conclave of the midnight sky…

And now, as ever, am I set to mark
When shall stream up the glow of signal-flame,
The bale-fire bright, and tell its Trojan tale—
Troy town is ta'en: such issue holds in hope
She in whose woman's breast beats heart of man.

Thus upon mine unrestful couch I lie,
Bathed with the dews of night, unvisited
By dreams—ah me!—for in the place of sleep
Stands Fear as my familiar…

Home—but I say no more: upon my tongue
Treads hard the ox o' the adage.
                      Had it voice,
The home itself might soothliest tell its tale;
I, of set will, speak words the wise may learn…

— Agamemnon, opening. trans. E. D. A. Morshead, 1881.

2. The gagging of Iphigenia. The reason for everything. The chorus remembers it and cannot finish.

Lusting for war, the bloody arbiters
Closed heart and ears, and would nor hear nor heed
      The girl-voice plead,
  Pity me, Father! nor her prayers,
      Nor tender, virgin years.

     So, when the chant of sacrifice was done,
     Her father bade the youthful priestly train
Raise her, like some poor kid, above the altar-stone,
     From where amid her robes she lay
        Sunk all in swoon away—
Bade them, as with the bit that mutely tames the steed,
      Her fair lips' speech refrain,
Lest she should speak a curse on Atreus' home and seed,

      So, trailing on the earth her robe of saffron dye,
    With one last piteous dart from her beseeching eye
       Those that should smite she smote—
    Fair, silent, as a pictur'd form, but fain
    To plead, Is all forgot?
…
  And then—but I beheld not, nor can tell,
    What further fate befel…

— Agamemnon. trans. Morshead. Those that should smite she smote is one of the great lines in Greek.

3. The beacon speech. Her first substantial appearance. The old men doubt her, condescend to her, ask if she had a dream or heard a rumour, and she takes them apart one line at a time and then delivers the logistics. This is a woman describing a system she built.

CHORUS: Hath some night-vision won thee to belief?
CLYTEMNESTRA: Out on all presage of a slumb'rous soul!
CHORUS: But wert thou cheered by Rumour's wingless word?
CLYTEMNESTRA: Peace—thou dost chide me as a credulous girl.
CHORUS: Say then, how long ago the city fell?
CLYTEMNESTRA: Even in this night that now brings forth the dawn.
CHORUS: Yet who so swift could speed the message here?

CLYTEMNESTRA:
From Ida's top Hephaestus, lord of fire,
Sent forth his sign; and on, and ever on,
Beacon to beacon sped the courier-flame.
From Ida to the crag, that Hermes loves,
Of Lemnos; thence unto the steep sublime
Of Athos, throne of Zeus, the broad blaze flared.
Thence, raised aloft to shoot across the sea,
The moving light, rejoicing in its strength,
Sped from the pyre of pine, and urged its way,
In golden glory, like some strange new sun,
Onward, and reached Macistus' watching heights.
There, with no dull delay nor heedless sleep,
The watcher sped the tidings on in turn…
And like a long beard streaming in the wind,
Full-fed with fuel, roared and rose the blaze…
And thence leapt light unto Arachne's peak,
The mountain watch that looks upon our town.
Thence to th' Atrides' roof—in lineage fair,
A bright posterity of Ida's fire.
So sped from stage to stage, fulfilled in turn,
Flame after flame, along the course ordained,
And lo! the last to speed upon its way
Sights the end first, and glows unto the goal.
And Troy is ta'en, and by this sign my lord
Tells me the tale, and ye have learned my word.

— Agamemnon. trans. Morshead.

And then, unprompted, she imagines the sack from inside the city, including a warning that if the Greeks desecrate the Trojan temples they will not get home. She is right about that too.

Think you—this very morn—the Greeks in Troy,
And loud therein the voice of utter wail!
Within one cup pour vinegar and oil,
And look! unblent, unreconciled, they war.
So in the twofold issue of the strife
Mingle the victor's shout, the captives' moan.
For all the conquered whom the sword has spared
Cling weeping—some unto a brother slain,
Some childlike to a nursing father's form…

Yet let them reverence well the city's gods,
The lords of Troy, tho' fallen, and her shrines;
So shall the spoilers not in turn be spoiled…
Now, hearing from this woman's mouth of mine,
The tale and eke its warning, pray with me,
Luck sway the scale, with no uncertain poise.
For my fair hopes are changed to fairer joys.

CHORUS: A gracious word thy woman's lips have told,
Worthy a wise man's utterance, O my queen…

— Agamemnon. trans. Morshead.

4. The welcome home. Read this knowing she has an axe. The joke about him being full of holes is genuinely funny and she is doing it in front of the entire court. Then the sudden turn to the purple cloth, and a marital negotiation she wins in nine lines.

Old men of Argos, lieges of our realm,
Shame shall not bid me shrink lest ye should see
The love I bear my lord…

  Had this my husband met so many wounds,
  As by a thousand channels rumour told,
  No network e'er was full of holes as he.
  Had he been slain, as oft as tidings came
  That he was dead, he well might boast him now
  A second Geryon of triple frame…
  And thus distraught by news of wrath and woe,
  Oft for self-slaughter had I slung the noose,
  But others wrenched it from my neck away…
  For me, long since the gushing fount of tears
  Is wept away; no drop is left to shed.
  Dim are the eyes that ever watched till dawn,
  Weeping, the bale-fires, piled for thy return,
  Night after night unkindled. If I slept,
  Each sound—the tiny humming of a gnat,
  Roused me again, again, from fitful dreams
  Wherein I felt thee smitten, saw thee slain,
  Thrice for each moment of mine hour of sleep.

All this I bore, and now, released from woe,
I hail my lord as watch-dog of a fold,
As saving stay-rope of a storm-tossed ship,
As column stout that holds the roof aloft,
As only child unto a sire bereaved,
As land beheld, past hope, by crews forlorn,
As sunshine fair when tempest's wrath is past,
As gushing spring to thirsty wayfarer…

                      Sweet lord, step forth,
Step from thy car, I pray—nay, not on earth
Plant the proud foot, O king, that trod down Troy!
Women! why tarry ye, whose task it is
To spread your monarch's path with tapestry?
Swift, swift, with purple strew his passage fair,
That justice lead him to a home, at last,
He scarcely looked to see.
                           For what remains,
Zeal unsubdued by sleep shall nerve my hand
To work as right and as the gods command.

— Agamemnon. trans. Morshead. That last couplet is a confession said out loud to a room that cannot hear it.
AGAMEMNON: Know, I have said, and will not mar my word.
CLYTEMNESTRA: Was it fear made this meekness to the gods?
AGAMEMNON: If cause be cause, 'tis mine for this resolve.
CLYTEMNESTRA: What, think'st thou, in thy place had Priam done?
AGAMEMNON: He surely would have walked on broidered robes.
CLYTEMNESTRA: Then fear not thou the voice of human blame.
AGAMEMNON: Yet mighty is the murmur of a crowd.
CLYTEMNESTRA: Shrink not from envy, appanage of bliss.
AGAMEMNON: War is not woman's part, nor war of words.
CLYTEMNESTRA: Yet happy victors well may yield therein.
AGAMEMNON: Dost crave for triumph in this petty strife?
CLYTEMNESTRA: Yield; of thy grace permit me to prevail!

— Agamemnon. trans. Morshead. She gets him with vanity, in public, in twelve lines.

5. Cassandra sees it coming. The one person in the play who knows, cursed so that nobody will believe her, standing in the courtyard watching it happen in advance.

O wretch, O purpose fell!
Thou for thy wedded lord
The cleansing wave hast poured—
A treacherous welcome!
                     How the sequel tell?
Too soon 'twill come, too soon, for now, even now,
She smites him, blow on blow!
…
God! a new sight! a net, a snare of hell,
Set by her hand—herself a snare more fell!
  A wedded wife, she slays her lord,
Helped by another hand!
…
  Away, away—keep him away—
  The monarch of the herd, the pasture's pride,
  Far from his mate! In treach'rous wrath,
  Muffling his swarthy horns, with secret scathe
    She gores his fenceless side!
  Hark! in the brimming bath,
  The heavy plash—the dying cry—
Hark—in the laver—hark, he falls by treachery!

— Agamemnon. trans. Morshead.

And her verdict on Clytemnestra, which is also the fullest description of her in the whole play, from the only other woman on stage:

For this, for this, I say there plots revenge
A coward lion, couching in the lair—
Guarding the gate against my master's foot—
My master—mine—I bear the slave's yoke now,
And he, the lord of ships, who trod down Troy,
Knows not the fawning treachery of tongue
Of this thing false and dog-like—how her speech
Glozes and sleeks her purpose, till she win
By ill fate's favour the desired chance,
Moving like Atè to a secret end.
O aweless soul! the woman slays her lord—
Woman? what loathsome monster of the earth
Were fit comparison? The double snake—
Or Scylla, where she dwells, the seaman's bane…
Nay then, believe me not: what skills belief
Or disbelief? Fate works its will—and thou
Wilt see and say in ruth, Her tale was true.

— Agamemnon. trans. Morshead.

6. Standing over the body. The doors open. This is the speech. Note the first line: she is telling them, before anything else, that every word she has said in the play so far was a lie and she is not embarrassed about it.

Ho, ye who heard me speak so long and oft
The glozing word that led me to my will—
Hear how I shrink not to unsay it all!
How else should one who willeth to requite
