They found sand in his hip bag traced to a skate park and, reportedly, to desert soil from the American southwest.

The DNA says his father's line is East Asian and his mother's line traces to somewhere around the Mediterranean or the Caucasus, though that could be a very distant ancestor. And a Philippine detail you will like and also hate: in 2019 investigators noticed the way the knife was wrapped in a handkerchief matched a knotting method used in Ilocos and Isabela, and considered sending officers here to look into it.

None of it matched a single database. Which means the man who did this had never been arrested for anything in his life.

why it matters

Japan used to have a statute of limitations on murder. Fifteen years, and then the state simply stopped being allowed to charge anyone. The families of the Setagaya victims, led largely by Mikio's mother Setsuko and Yasuko's sister, campaigned publicly against it, and in 2010 Japan abolished it for capital crimes. That law exists partly because of these four people.

The case also broke the national story Japan tells about itself, that this is a place where a stranger does not come through your window. Setagaya was the quiet suburb. That is the whole point of Setagaya.

The house stood empty for a quarter of a century because the family fought the demolition order. Teenagers broke in for a dare in 2023. Two men broke in to steal in 2026 and said they had no idea what the place was. The victims' slippers were still boxed up inside.

what stays

Setsuko Miyazawa, Mikio's mother, has spent twenty-five years asking for information. Takeshi Tsuchida, the detective who ran the case, retired and then joined a bereaved families' organisation so he could keep working on it without a badge. Every year the police go back to the site.

It's a case that must be solved.

The thing I cannot get past is the ice cream. Everyone fixates on the violence, but the violence took maybe thirty-five minutes. The other nine hours are the actual horror. He sat in the warm house of the family he had just destroyed and treated it like his own. He bandaged himself with their supplies. He got online. He rested.

People read that as taunting. I do not think it was. I think a person who is taunting cleans up after himself, because he wants the game. This man left his blood, his prints, his clothes, his waste, his smell, and then walked out into the first morning of a new year and simply became nobody. He was not clever. He was not careful. He was just never anyone the system had reason to look at.

Twelve thousand five hundred pieces of evidence and no name attached to any of them. That is the lesson that stays with me, and I am not sure it is a comforting one: knowing everything about someone except who they are turns out to be worth nothing at all.

Njinga Mbande

ngola of ndongo · queen of matamba · the woman who would not be a vassal · c. 1582 – 17 december 1663

aug 11, 2026▼

childhood & early life

Born around 1582 in Kabasa, the capital of Ndongo, in what is now northern Angola. The ruler's title there was ngola, which is where the word Angola comes from. The country is named after the throne her family sat on.

The story her people told about her birth is that she came out feet first with the cord around her neck. Njinga comes from a root meaning to twist or to wrap. A name given for the thing that nearly killed her on the way in.

Her mother Kangela was a concubine, not the chief wife, which mattered later. Her father let her train with the army, which mattered more. She learned weapons, and she learned the thing she turned out to be best at, which was reading a room full of men who had already decided what she was.

what she did & why she's remembered

In 1622 her brother Ngola Mbande, now king and losing badly, sent her to Luanda to negotiate with the Portuguese governor João Correia de Sousa. She was around forty. She arrived draped in Mbundu cloth and jewels and feathers, refusing Portuguese dress entirely.

In the room there was one chair. It was for the governor. She was expected to sit on a mat on the floor, the way the Portuguese made Africans sit.

She gestured to one of her attendants, who knelt on all fours, and she sat on her. Eye level. The whole negotiation happened with the two of them looking straight at each other. When it ended, the governor pointed out that she had left her servant behind. She said it was beneath her to sit in the same chair twice.

That is the story everyone knows. Here is the part they leave out: she won that negotiation. She got the Portuguese to accept Ndongo as a sovereign ally rather than a tributary state. She also had herself baptised as Ana de Sousa, on purpose, as a bargaining chip, with the governor's own relatives standing as godparents. She had been authorised in advance to convert if it bought her anything.

Then they broke the treaty almost immediately, and she spent the next forty years making them regret it.

family life

Her brother took the throne and secured it the usual way, by killing the relatives who could challenge him. Njinga's infant son was among the dead. He let Njinga and her two sisters, Funji and Kambu, live, but he had them sterilised, reportedly with boiling herbs poured onto their bellies.

Read that again. The reason she had no heir was her own brother.

He died in 1624, possibly suicide, possibly poison, and the Portuguese loudly accused her of it. She ruled first as regent for his son, and then the boy died too, reportedly by her hand. I am not going to sand that down. She came out of a family that ate itself and she finished the meal.

Her sisters were captured by the Portuguese in 1629. Funji spent over fifteen years in captivity in Luanda secretly smuggling Portuguese military intelligence out to Njinga. They found her letters in 1647 and drowned her in the river. Kambu was held nearly twenty years, and getting her back was the single hardest term Njinga fought for in the 1656 peace treaty, because Kambu was her successor and she had no one else.

She spent her whole reign trying to get her sisters back. She got one.

romantic life

She married an Imbangala warlord named Kasa, then had him killed, apparently at his own camp on the night of an initiation, once the alliance had done what she needed it to do. She later married a much younger man called Njinga a Mona, whom she had essentially raised as a war captain.

The hostile Capuchin sources also claim she kept a retinue of young men who dressed as women and were called her wives, while she styled herself king rather than queen. Those accounts come from men who wanted her to look monstrous, so hold them loosely. But the part that is not in dispute is that she rejected the word queen. She took the male title. Ngola.

There is no love story here. Every relationship she had was a position on a board.

life until death

Driven out of Ndongo by 1629, she took the kingdom of Matamba by force and ruled from there. She allied with the Dutch West India Company in 1641 when they seized Luanda, and clawed back most of Ndongo before the Portuguese retook the port in 1648.

Then, at around seventy, she changed weapons. She stopped trying to expel the Portuguese and started making it impossible for them to do anything in the interior without going through her. Peace treaty in 1656, her sister returned, her sovereignty formally acknowledged, missionaries welcomed back. She rebuilt churches, took communion, staged her Christianity in public with total commitment and total calculation, and it worked.

She died on 17 December 1663 of a lung infection, at eighty-one, still ruling. Kambu, the sister she bought back, took the throne. Matamba went on being ruled by women long after.

She outlived the empire's patience. That was the strategy.

her words

On why she would not accept vassal status, decades into the war:

There is no reason to do so, because having been born to rule my kingdom, I should not obey or recognize another sovereign.

From a letter to a Portuguese captain, in her own hand, in their language:

Nothing is accomplished by force, and to do so would bring both me and them harm, because everything can be done peacefully and without force.

The woman with the human chair wrote that. The one everyone remembers as the warrior spent most of her forty years negotiating, and the negotiating is what actually worked.

What gets me about her is the seat. Everyone tells it as a clever insult, but it was not a joke, it was a refusal to accept the terms of the room. They built a space where only one person could be a person, and instead of arguing about it she made herself one and got on with the actual business.

She also never got to be soft. Not once in eighty-one years. I do not think that is the lesson, I think that is the cost.

Fu Hao · 婦好

royal consort · high priestess · general of the shang · d. c. 1200 BCE

aug 10, 2026▼

childhood & early life

We don't know where she was born, and that is the first interesting thing about her. The common guess is that she came from outside the Shang core, one of the allied or subject peoples on the frontier, and was married to King Wu Ding as an alliance. He had around sixty wives. She was one of three who mattered.

Everything we know about her comes from two sources: cracked bones, and a hole in the ground.

what she did & why she's remembered

Wu Ding ran a state at Anyang that talked to its dead. The king asked a question, a diviner applied heat to a polished turtle plastron or an ox shoulder blade until it cracked, and the crack was the answer. Then someone carved the question and the outcome into the bone. Tens of thousands survived, and they are the oldest readable Chinese writing.

Fu Hao appears in roughly 170 of them. More than almost anyone.

She led armies, and not symbolically. The inscriptions ask whether she should be ordered against the Tu Fang, the Ba Fang, the Yi, the Qiang. One campaign is recorded with thirteen thousand troops, the largest single force named in the whole oracle bone corpus, and it was hers. Against the Ba Fang she and a general named Zhi Guo ran an ambush, her half setting the trap while the king drove the enemy into it. She was not following the army. She was the pincer.

She also ran rituals, which in a state that governs by divination is not a soft job. She performed the sacrifices, prepared shells herself, and held a title at the top of the religious apparatus. And she held her own estate, paying tribute to the crown from it like any lord.

War, religion, property. She had all three at a time when most people in that kingdom were the thing being sacrificed.

family life

She had at least one child with Wu Ding. One of the eeriest surviving inscriptions is him divining about the birth, over and over, trying to fix the date, worrying. The record of the outcome reads, flatly, that it was not good. It was a girl.

Three thousand two hundred years and the disappointment is still legible. The same court that let her command thirteen thousand men logged the birth of her daughter as a bad result.

romantic life

A political marriage that turned into something else, or at least into something whose shape you can see. They lived apart much of the time because she was on campaign or on her own land. He divined about her health. Her toothache. Whether her childbirth would go well.

After she died he kept talking to her. He asked whether to make offerings to her, whether she was well in the place she was now. Then he did something strange: a series of posthumous spirit marriages, offering her to three of his powerful dead ancestors in turn, so a long-gone king would protect her in the afterlife. A widower arranging his wife's remarriage to dead men.

That is either the most tender or the most possessive thing in the whole record and I can't decide which.

life until death

She died before he did, probably in her thirties, cause unknown. He buried her not in the royal cemetery across the river with the kings but close to the palace, close to the living. Which is exactly why she is the only Shang royal tomb ever found unlooted. Everyone who came to rob the dynasty went to the obvious place.

In 1976 an archaeologist named Zheng Zhenxiang was surveying at Yinxu and kept pushing to dig a spot her colleagues thought unpromising. She was right. Under a house foundation was a shaft holding nearly two thousand objects in seven layers: 468 bronzes, more than 750 jades, some of them already antiques when they were buried because Fu Hao collected old things, thousands of cowrie shells, ivory cups inlaid with turquoise. Four enormous bronze battle axes, one around nine kilos, carved with tigers flanking a human head.

Also sixteen people and six dogs, killed and buried with her, because this was the Shang and that was the price of a queen's funeral. No version of her is clean.

A woman found her. That detail matters more than it should.

her works

She left no writing of her own. What she left is other people's anxiety about her, carved into bone:

Shall we order Fu Hao to follow Zhi Guo and attack the Ba Fang?
In the coming ten days there will be no disaster for Fu Hao.
Fu Hao's childbearing will not be good. It was a girl.
Should Fu Hao be married to Ancestor Yi?

The whole record of her is questions asked about her by men who needed to know what she would do. And the answers came out of fire.

Amanirenas

kandake of kush · qore · the one-eyed queen who fought rome to a draw · c. 60/50 – c. 10 BCE

aug 9, 2026▼

childhood & early life

Born somewhere between 60 and 50 BCE in the Kingdom of Kush, in what is now Sudan, upriver from Egypt past the cataracts. Her capital was Meroë, a city of iron smelting and pyramids, steeper and narrower than the Egyptian ones, hundreds of them, still standing in the desert today with almost nobody looking at them.

We know nothing about her childhood. Not one line. That isn't neglect on her part, it's a language problem: Meroitic is written in an alphabet we can read out loud and a vocabulary we still can't translate. We can sound out her inscriptions and not understand them. So her own record of herself is sitting in museums, physically intact, and mute.

What she grew up inside was a culture where women ruled openly. Kandake, the title Greeks garbled into "Candace" and mistook for a personal name, meant something like great royal woman. Kush produced a whole line of them. She also carried the title qore, ruler, which is the part that matters: not queen consort, not regent for a boy. Sovereign.

what she did & why she's remembered

Rome took Egypt in 30 BCE. Cleopatra was dead, Augustus owned the Nile, and the new administration started pushing taxation south into Nubia. Kush was next on the map and everybody knew it.

In 25 BCE the prefect Aelius Gallus took the bulk of the Roman army off to Arabia on a disastrous expedition. Amanirenas had been watching. She went north the moment the garrisons thinned and took Syene, Elephantine and Philae, the whole southern frontier, freed and enslaved as armies did, and pulled down the imperial statues.

One of those statues was a bronze Augustus, larger than life, the idealised Greek-style face Rome shipped to every corner of the world so the conquered would know what their owner looked like. She had the head cut off and carried nine hundred kilometres south to Meroë. Then she had it buried face down under the threshold steps of a temple to Victory, so that every single person entering the shrine, for as long as the shrine stood, would walk on the emperor's face without even thinking about it.

That is not vandalism. That is a woman who understood exactly how Roman power worked and chose to attack the image rather than pretend the image didn't matter.

family life

Her name appears on stelae beside two others: Teriteqas and Akinidad. Scholars read Teriteqas as her husband and predecessor, Akinidad as her son and co-ruler, though the Meroitic makes even that a careful guess rather than a fact.

Teriteqas died early in the war, possibly in the fighting itself. The command fell to her and Akinidad together, mother and son running a war against the largest military machine on earth. On the Hamadab Stela the two of them stand side by side before Amun and Mut, with bound prisoners under their feet, forty five lines of text underneath explaining what they did, and not one of those lines can be read.

Akinidad died too, during the war. Within a few years she lost her husband and her son to the same enemy and kept fighting anyway. Her successor was Amanishakheto, another woman, another kandake, and the line held.

romantic life

Nothing survives except the marriage, and the marriage survives only as a name carved next to hers. No love poetry, no gossip, no Roman slander about her private life, which is unusual, because Rome slandered every foreign queen it met. Cleopatra got a whole propaganda campaign. Amanirenas got one physical description and it was about her face.

Strabo, writing from Roman reports, called her "a masculine sort of woman, and blind in one eye." That's it. That's the entire surviving portrait of her body by an outsider. A woman who beat them to a negotiated peace, and the detail they kept was that she wasn't pretty and wasn't whole.

life until death

Rome answered with Gaius Petronius, who came south with fewer than ten thousand infantry and eight hundred cavalry against a Kushite force Strabo puts at thirty thousand. The Kushites carried oxhide shields, axes, pikes. Rome had the legion. The numbers didn't save them; Petronius drove them back, took Pselchis and Premnis, and then burned Napata, the old royal and religious heart of Kush, and sold its people.

She had tried to negotiate before that, offering to give back the prisoners and the statues. Petronius ignored her and razed the city anyway. So she came back a second time with thousands of men to retake Premnis, and he outmarched her and got there first, and fortified it, and she couldn't break it.

Here is the turn. Beaten in the field, she sent envoys again, and instead of dealing with the prefect in Egypt she went over his head. Her ambassadors were escorted to Samos, where Augustus was wintering on his way to Syria, and they negotiated with the emperor himself in 21 BCE.

Augustus gave them everything they asked for. The Romans pulled back out of the Thirty-Mile Strip including Primis. The frontier moved north to Hiere Sycaminos. And Kush paid no tribute. Not reduced tribute, none. The empire that taxed the known world walked away from a defeated enemy having collected nothing.

The peace held for roughly three hundred years. Rome never went south again. She died around 10 BCE, probably buried at Jebel Barkal, possibly in the pyramid catalogued as Bar. 4, which was later blown apart by a treasure hunter.

her works & what stays

She left two objects and one silence. The Hamadab Stela, her own account of the war, unreadable. And the head.

"Among these fugitives were the generals of Queen Candace … a masculine sort of woman, and blind in one eye."
— strabo, geography 17.1.54
"Just outside the doorway of this chamber, and buried in a clean pocket of sand, there was a Roman bronze portrait head of heroic size."
— john garstang's excavation report, meroë, december 1910

The sand under the step is why the Meroë Head is the best preserved bronze Augustus in existence. The calcite and glass eyes are still in the sockets, and on nearly every other surviving statue of him those are long gone. She meant it as an insult and accidentally made it the finest portrait of him we have. It sits in the British Museum now, taken from Sudan in 1911, which is its own second story.

My aside: what gets me isn't the war, it's the order of operations. She lost. Her husband dead, her son dead, Napata burned, her army broken twice. And from inside that she still worked out that the prefect was never going to give her anything and the emperor might, and she sent people across the sea to the one man who could overrule him, and she came home with no tribute and a border moved backward. Losing the fight and still setting the terms is a completely different skill from winning, and almost nobody has it. Also: she buried the face of the most powerful man alive under a doorstep so that ordinary people would step on him for centuries without ceremony. Two thousand years later we dug him up and put him in a glass case in London, at eye level, lit beautifully. Sometimes I think she'd find that funnier than we do.

Giulia Tofana

poisoner · apothecary · the widow-maker of rome · d. 1651

aug 8, 2026▼

childhood & early life

Almost nothing survives, which is the first honest thing to say about her. No birth record, no baptism, no portrait painted from life. Probably Palermo, probably the first decades of the 1600s, probably poor, in a Sicily ruled by Spanish viceroys where a woman's legal existence ran through her father and then her husband and nowhere else.

The one thread historians pull on is a name. On 12 July 1633 a poisoner called Teofania di Adamo was executed in Palermo, either drawn and quartered in a way contemporaries described as excruciating even by the standards of the time, or sewn alive into a canvas sack and thrown from the roof of the bishop's palace into the street while the city watched. Sicilian custom let children of parents with unusual first names take those names as surnames. Tofana. Teofania. The 19th century archivist Salvatore Salomone-Marino thought that made Giulia her daughter. It is a guess, a good one, and it has never been proven.

If it's true, then her education was watching her mother die in public for selling women a way out.

what she did & why she's remembered

She turns up in Rome in the 1640s, arriving from Palermo with a much younger woman named Girolama Spara, reportedly after a poisoning in Sicily went wrong. What she built there was not a murder spree. It was a small business, staffed entirely by women, with a supply chain.

Six of them. Tofana at the head, Spara moving through aristocratic houses as a cunning woman selling charms and cures, two makers of the product, Giovanna De Grandis and Maria Spinola nicknamed Grifola, and two dispensers, Laura Crispolti and Graziosa Farina, working the poorer parishes. Their arsenic came through a priest, Father Girolamo of Sant'Agnese in Agone, whose brother was an apothecary with loose standards.

The genius was the packaging. They bottled the stuff as Manna of St Nicholas, a devotional healing oil supposed to sweat miraculously from the saint's bones in Bari, sold everywhere in pretty glass flasks. A woman could keep it on her dressing table in plain sight, next to the perfume, in a Catholic city, and no husband alive would think to ask.

Four to six drops was said to be enough. It went in over weeks: first a man is a little out of sorts, then weak, then bedridden, then dead of what everyone agrees was a wasting illness. He had time to make a will. He had time to confess and receive last rites, which mattered enormously, because it meant the wife had not damned him, only removed him. She could grieve properly at the funeral and inherit properly afterward.

Her clientele were wives. In a world with no divorce, where a bad marriage was a life sentence and a beating was a domestic matter, she was the only exit that existed. Ademollo, working from the Roman court records, notes that Spara sometimes gave the poison away free to poor women whose husbands were especially brutal. Six hundred deaths is the number always quoted. It comes from an 18th century letter about a completely different woman in Naples and there is no evidence for it whatsoever.

family life

A dead mother on a scaffold, maybe. A daughter, maybe: Girolama Spara is usually called hers, though the only firm link is that they travelled together and Spara inherited everything. De Grandis confessed under interrogation that Tofana had taught her how to make the poison, which is the closest thing to a documented relationship in the whole story. Teacher and apprentice.

So her family, functionally, was the gang. Sicilians and Romans, makers and sellers, bound by a secret that would hang all of them. It held for a decade, which is longer than most marriages in this story lasted.

romantic life

Blank. Not one lover, not one husband named in any source. The woman who made her living off other people's marriages left no record of ever being inside one.

The romance in the case belongs to a client. In June 1657 Francesco Cesi, Duke of Ceri, died suddenly. His wife Maria Aldobrandini had been married to him at thirteen, to a man thirty years older, and was twenty two when he died, by then hopelessly in love with a charming Rosicrucian poet named Francesco Santinelli who was writing her verse. De Grandis testified that Father Girolamo came to her on the duchess's behalf, worried the poison might make him vomit and give her away, and that the priest reassured her the duke's food passed through so many hands nobody would look at them. De Grandis went to see the body lying in open casket at Santa Maria sopra Minerva and knew at a glance. Aldobrandini's own family then locked her up to stop her marrying Santinelli. She was never charged. The pope personally ordered her name kept out of the trial. She lived until 1703.

life until death

Giulia Tofana died around 1651, in her own bed, unsuspected. That is the part nobody dramatises and it is the most remarkable thing about her. No trial, no scaffold, no crowd. She got away with it and then she just stopped existing.

The gang unravelled eight years later without her. One version says a woman confessed the plot to her priest and the church traded her immunity for the whole story. The other says De Grandis, who worked the poor clients, had been picked up three times already, and on the fourth she was carrying a sample and claimed it was a cosmetic for removing facial blemishes. The authorities let her walk, then imported a Florentine woman, signora Loreti, installed her in a grand house as the fictional "Marchesa Romanini," and sent her in with a sad story about her marriage and a great deal of money. The moment the bottle changed hands, two officers and a notary came out from behind a curtain. They tested the liquid on stray animals. It worked.

On 6 July 1659, Girolama Spara, Giovanna De Grandis, Maria Spinola, Laura Crispolti and Graziosa Farina were hanged together in the Campo de' Fiori before an enormous crowd. Forty six of their customers were immured for life, walled into prison rather than quietly retired to convents, because they were poor. Father Girolamo was never questioned, never tried, and vanishes from the record entirely.

what she left

Not writing. A word. Aqua Tofana entered European vocabulary as the name for the perfect undetectable poison and stayed there for a hundred and fifty years, which is how a Sicilian woman with no birth record ended up in the mouth of a dying composer in Vienna.

"I feel definitely that I will not last much longer; I am sure that I have been poisoned. I cannot rid myself of this idea. Someone has given me aqua tofana and calculated the precise time of my death."
— mozart, autumn 1791, while writing the requiem
"There was not a lady in Naples who had not some of it lying openly on her toilette among her perfumes. She alone knows the phial, and can distinguish it."
— the abbé galiani, a century later

Mike Dash, who went through the sources properly, thinks the potion was probably just ordinary arsenic and the legend of its supernatural subtlety was the sound of a ruling class discovering it could be reached by the poor. Every account written by men reduces these women to hags and their customers to faithless Jezebels. Nobody thought to ask why the demand was there.

My aside: I don't want to make her a folk hero, she sold death for money and some of those men were only inconvenient, not cruel, and forty six women went into a wall for life while a duchess who almost certainly did it died free at seventy. That's the actual moral of the case, and it isn't about poison. But the thing I can't stop turning over is the bottle. She understood that the safest place to hide something is inside the exact object nobody is allowed to question. A holy relic on the dressing table, in daylight, for years. She hid a weapon inside the one thing the system insisted was sacred, and the system never once looked at it.

Qiu Jin · 秋瑰

poet · swordswoman · bomb maker · woman knight of mirror lake · 1875–1907

aug 7, 2026▼

childhood & early life

Born 8 November 1875 in Fuzhou, raised mostly in the family's ancestral home in Shaoxing, Zhejiang. Wealthy household: her father a government official, her mother from a literati family, her grandfather responsible for city defense in Xiamen. Zhejiang was known for educating its daughters, so she got what almost no girl of her era got, a real classical education.

Her feet were bound anyway. That's the detail that explains her whole life. The same family that taught her poetry, horse riding and swordwork also broke the bones in her feet, because that was the price of being marriageable. She grew up reading about Hua Mulan and other martial heroines while walking on ruined feet, and she never stopped noticing the contradiction.

what she did & why she's remembered

In 1903 she pawned her jewelry and sailed to Tokyo alone to study, self-funded, not sponsored by the Qing. She went to a Japanese language school, then Shimoda Utako's Girls' Practical School. She unbound her feet. She wore Western men's suits, drank, learned martial arts, and learned to make bombs. She called herself Jianhu Nuxia, the Woman Knight of Mirror Lake, deliberately claiming a title that had only ever belonged to men.

She edited a vernacular journal so ordinary women could actually read it, and published A Respectful Proclamation to China's Two Hundred Million Women Comrades, arguing against foot binding and forced marriage from direct experience. Back in China in 1906 she co-founded China Women's News with the poet Xu Zihua. Two issues, then the authorities shut it down.

At a heated meeting of Zhejiang students in Tokyo, arguing over whether to go home and fight or stay and prepare, she drove a dagger into the podium and said: if I go back, surrender to the Manchus and betray the Han people, stab me with this. She joined the Guangfuhui, then Sun Yat-sen's Tongmenghui, and was put in charge of Zhejiang. The only woman at that level in the movement.

In 1907 she became head of the Datong School in Shaoxing. Officially a teachers' college. Actually a recruitment and training center for an armed uprising.

family life

Married in 1896 at twenty one, late for the time, to Wang Tingjun, youngest son of a rich Hunan merchant. Her father arranged it. She described him as newly rich, unscrupulous, uneducated, a man interested only in enjoying himself. She had a son, Yuande, in 1897 and a daughter, Guifeng, in 1901, and only then were her in-laws satisfied with her.

She was profoundly lonely inside that marriage, and it's where the poems started, because there was no one in the house to say any of it to.

Then she left. Sold her jewelry through her friend Wu Zhiyin, left her husband, left both children, and got on a ship. She never framed it as sacrifice or as guilt-free liberation. It sits in the poems as a wound she chose.

romantic life

Essentially nothing on record after the marriage, and that seems to be the truth rather than a gap in the sources. The great loves of her adult life were friendships: Wu Zhiying and Xu Zihua, both writers, both sworn sisters to her in the formal sense, a bond with obligations attached.

Those two are the reason we have her. After the execution Wu wrote three essays attacking the Qing officials and defending her name in public, at real risk. Then the two of them buried her by West Lake in Hangzhou, near the old heroes, which is where she'd said she wanted to be. The state ordered the tomb destroyed. Her brother got the body out in time. Wu took the memorial stele into her own house and sold rubbings of it to keep the name circulating.

life until death

The uprising was set for 19 July 1907. The plans leaked and early unrest put the army on alert. Her cousin and co-founder Xu Xilin, meant to create a diversion in Anhui, salvaged what he could by shooting the Anhui governor dead on 6 July. He was captured and executed almost immediately. Troops turned toward Shaoxing.

Friends warned her. She had time. She stayed at the school. Arrested 13 July, tortured, and she admitted nothing, so the court convicted her using her own poems as evidence. Beheaded publicly on 15 July 1907 in Shanyin, her home village, at thirty one. Her body was left lying in the market square in the summer heat as a warning.

Lu Xun, who was from Shaoxing too, was harsh about it later. He thought the adulation she'd received in Japan made her reckless, said she was "clapped to death." Nobody has ever fully explained why she didn't run.

her works

Classical shi and ci poetry, essays, a journal, and an unfinished ballad novel, Stones of the Jingwei Bird, about five wealthy women who run from their arranged marriages to study and join the revolution. Named after the bird in myth that drowned and came back to fill in the sea one pebble at a time.

"Don't speak of how women can't become heroes:
alone, I rode the winds eastward, for ten thousand leagues."
— a reply verse in matching rhyme, trans. yilin wang
"I pawned my jewels to sail across the open seas,
parting from my children as I left the border at Jade Gate.
Unbinding my feet to pour out a millennium's poisons,
I arouse the spirit of women, hundreds of flowers, abloom.
Oh, this poor handkerchief made of merfolk-woven silk,
half stained with blood and half soaked in tears."
— reflections, written during travels in japan
"秋風秋雨愁玧人
Autumn wind, autumn rain — they fill the heart with sorrow."
— her death poem. her name means autumn gem

My aside: two things stay with me. First, that her poems were used as the evidence to kill her, which is the most literal proof imaginable that writing counted as a weapon. Second, that she'd already told everyone she wasn't going to run, years earlier, with a dagger in a podium in Tokyo. When the soldiers came she just did the thing she'd said. There's a version of courage that isn't bravery in the moment, it's refusing to renegotiate with yourself later. I don't think it was worth her life. I also don't think she'd take the question seriously.

Julie d'Aubigny · La Maupin

opera singer · duelist · convent arsonist · twice pardoned by louis xiv · 1673–1707

aug 6, 2026▼

childhood & early life

Born in Paris in 1673 to Gaston d'Aubigny, secretary to the Comte d'Armagnac, who was Master of the Horse for Louis XIV. That job meant her father trained the court's pages: fencing, riding, reading, dancing, how to behave in front of a king. He had one daughter and no interest in raising her separately from the boys, so Julie learned everything they learned, in their clothes, with a real blade in her hand. She was nine when they moved into Versailles.

By fourteen she was the Comte d'Armagnac's mistress, which at Versailles was less a scandal than a career step, and entirely his choice not hers. To keep it tidy he married her off in 1687 to a quiet minor official, the Sieur de Maupin, then had the new husband posted to a tax job in the provinces. Some accounts say Maupin left the morning after the wedding. She kept his name and almost nothing else of him, and she was famous under it for the rest of her life.

what she did & why she's remembered

Two things at once, which is the whole point of her. She was a genuinely great singer, a contralto in an era when France did not really use contraltos, and she was a genuinely dangerous swordfighter, in an era when duelling was illegal and women did not do it at all.

Still in her teens she ran off with a fencing master called Sérannes, who was wanted for killing a man in an illegal duel. They fled south and funded themselves by giving fencing exhibitions in taverns and singing for coins. She fought men for money before she was seventeen. When drinkers refused to believe a woman was under the shirt, she reportedly opened it and settled the argument.

Then Avignon. She fell in love with a young woman whose family shipped the girl to a convent to end it. Julie entered the same convent as a postulant to reach her. According to the accounts, when a nun died she moved the body into her lover's bed, set the place on fire, and walked out into the confusion with the girl. They lasted a few months. Julie was tried in absentia for arson, kidnapping and body snatching, sentenced to death by fire, and the sentence was written for a man, because the court had no idea the accused was a woman.

She went back to Paris, got the Comte to beg the King for a pardon, got it, and debuted at the Paris Opéra in December 1690 as Pallas Athena in Lully's Cadmus et Hermione. Seventeen years old, walking onstage as the goddess of strategic war, weeks after being condemned to burn.

The famous night came at a court ball. She arrived in men's clothes, kissed a young woman on the dance floor, and three noblemen challenged her over it. She told each of them she'd meet him outside. She went out and fought all three, and beat all three, then came back in and finished the evening. Duelling in Paris carried a death penalty. She was pardoned again, this time through the King's brother, and the argument that saved her was reportedly that the edict said men. Twice the law couldn't hold her because it hadn't imagined her.

family life

Thin, and that's the sad part. Her father died around 1687 and she seems to have had no one after that. No children on record. The husband reappeared around 1701 and made no difference to anything she did; they simply existed near each other. Her real household was the Opéra: the old singer Bouvard who vouched for her, the star Marie Le Rochois who she came up under, and a strange assortment of men she'd wounded and then nursed back to health, at least one of whom, the Comte d'Albert, stayed a friend for life.

She also once beat a fellow singer, Dumesny, in the street after he insulted the women of the company, took his snuffbox and his watch, and let him tell everyone he'd been jumped by robbers until she produced the watch in front of him.

romantic life

Constant, public, men and women, and mostly short. The count who bought her a husband. The fugitive fencing master. The girl in the convent. Thevénard the singer, who got her the audition. Various noblemen, at least one acquired by stabbing him first.

And then, near the end, the Marquise de Florensac, called the most beautiful woman in France. They lived together roughly two years and one contemporary described them as dwelling in an affection they believed to be perfect. Florensac died suddenly of fever in 1705.

That's the thing about her record. She survived a death sentence, three swords in one night, and a decade of the most vicious gossip in Europe. What ended her was ordinary grief.

life until death

Between 1690 and 1694 she sang in nearly every major Paris Opéra production, then spent time in Brussels performing at the Opéra du Quai au Foin, then came back and performed for the court at Versailles. Composers began writing parts for her voice, most notably Campra, whose Tancrède in 1702 gave her the title role: a warrior, written low, written for her specifically. She was around thirty and at the top of it.

After Florensac died she left the stage entirely and entered a convent, the same kind of building she'd once burned down to get someone out of. She died in 1707, thirty-three or thirty-four. One nineteenth-century biographer wrote that she was destroyed by "an inclination to do evil in the sight of her God and a fixed intention not to," and claimed her body was thrown on a rubbish heap. No grave. No stone.

Worth saying plainly: the wildest stories, the corpse and the fire, the three duels, come mainly from later biographers, especially Letainturier-Fradin's 1904 book, and from the gossip of her own century. What is documented beyond argument is the career: the roles, the dates, the pardons, the fact that she was employed at the top of French opera while being openly everything she was.

her works & what was said

She left no writing. A singer's work dies with the room. What survives is a handful of roles and other people's sentences about her.

"She had the most beautiful voice in the world."
— contemporary audience account, paris opéra
"They dwelt in such affection they believed to be perfect."
— on her and the marquise de florensac
"Roles: Pallas Athena in Cadmus et Hermione (1690) · Clorinde and the title role in Campra's Tancrède (1702) · the woman who brought the contralto voice into French opera."

Théophile Gautier wrote a novel about her in 1835, Mademoiselle de Maupin, and turned her into a romance. It became one of the most censored books of the century, and it is barely about her. She keeps getting rewritten into something more comfortable, which tells you how uncomfortable the real one was.

My aside: what gets me isn't the swords. It's that she was never punished by the thing that should have punished her. The court kept pardoning her because she was useful, entertaining, and connected, and she used that gap for everything it was worth. She wasn't free, she was tolerated, and she pushed until tolerated looked like free. Then the one thing no pardon covers happened, and she put herself in a convent and stopped. Every fight in her life she won by attacking. Loss doesn't have a body you can run through.

Christine de Pizan

1364–c.1430 · Venetian-born French poet, historian, polemicist · widowed at twenty-five with three children and a household to feed, she became the first woman in Europe to make a living entirely from writing — and then used it to pick a public fight with the most beloved book of her century

aug 12, 2026▼

childhood & early life

She was born Cristina da Pizzano in Venice in September 1364, into the most useful accident of birth a clever girl could have had in the fourteenth century: her father was a physician and astrologer, and he was good enough at it to get headhunted. Tommaso di Benvenuto da Pizzano had two offers on the table, one from the King of Hungary and one from Charles V of France. He took France. Christine was five when her mother put her on the road to Paris to join him.

What she walked into was the best-funded reading room in Europe. Charles V was building the royal library in a tower of the Louvre, panelled in rare wood, hung with some thirty small chandeliers and one big silver lamp that was kept burning day and night so that work never had to stop for darkness. Twelve hundred manuscripts. Translators on staff, turning Greek, Latin and Arabic into French so students could actually use the collection. That tower is the seed the Bibliothèque Nationale grew out of, and a foreign astrologer's daughter had the run of it.

Her father encouraged her to learn, which was not the default setting. Her mother, by Christine's own later account, thought the girl should be doing needlework like everybody else, and the compromise reached in that house is basically the reason we have any of this. She read constantly. She married at fifteen, in 1379, to Étienne du Castel, a notary and secretary to the king, a Picard about ten years older whom she had known since she was small. By every line she ever wrote about him, she loved him, and she was happy, and she assumed it would keep.

Then the wheel turned. Charles V died in 1380, and the household's protector was gone. Her father lost his position, his pension shrank, and he died around 1388. The next year, in 1389, Étienne rode to Beauvais on the king's business, caught plague, and died there at thirty-four. Christine was twenty-five. She had three children, a widowed mother and a niece in the house, no income, and a pile of unpaid royal salary she was legally owed and could not get anyone to hand over. The lawsuits went on for years. She lost most of them.

what she did & why she's remembered

She did the thing nobody in her position did. A well-born widow with debts had three respectable options in 1390 — remarry, take vows, or move in with relatives and get quiet. Christine looked at the three of them and started selling poems instead.

She began with love ballades, because that was the market. Nobles wanted verse and would pay for it, and she was extremely good and extremely fast — hundreds of poems inside a decade, some in her own voice, many written to order for men who wanted to sound heartbroken at somebody. She was blunt about the difference: often, she says, she was making merry on the page and would rather have been weeping. Then she used the money and the access to educate herself properly, on history, philosophy, Aristotle, Dante, and moved into prose, where the real money and the real arguments were.

And she ran it like a business, which is the part usually left out of the romantic version. She did not simply hand manuscripts to a patron and hope. She oversaw the copying, employed scribes and illuminators, supervised the miniatures, and assembled bespoke presentation volumes for specific rich people — the huge collected manuscript she put together for Queen Isabeau is still in the British Library. She was author, editor, production manager and account handler of her own small press, three hundred years before an author could expect royalties. Henry IV of England tried to poach her for his court. So did the Duke of Milan. She thanked them beautifully and refused, twice, because France was at war and she was not going to go work for the other side.

Then in 1399 she picked the fight. The most fashionable book in France was the Roman de la Rose, and the section of it written by Jean de Meun was, underneath the allegory, several thousand lines instructing men that women are deceitful, that their refusals are theatre, and that persistence is the correct technique. Christine wrote L'Epistre au Dieu d'Amours — a formal complaint to the God of Love, filed on behalf of women of all ranks — and then kept going into a documented, circulated, years-long literary war, the querelle de la Rose, against senior royal secretaries who were absolutely not used to being answered back. Her flattest and best reply to the charge that all the books condemn women: the books were not written by women. And to the argument that women are naturally weak and easily fooled, she asks why, in that case, the great Jean de Meun needed to fill a hundred pages with tricks and stratagems, since one does not lay siege to a place that isn't defended.

Out of that came Le Livre de la Cité des Dames in 1405, her masterpiece: a city built stone by stone out of the lives of real and legendary women, designed as a fortress for the reputation of the whole sex. In it she argues that God made the soul, and made it as good in a woman as in a man; that intelligence is not sexed; that girls taught the same subjects as boys learn them just as well; and, in a passage that lands strangely hard for 1405, that a woman without means should think hard before marrying a second time, because plenty of wives get a beating for supper when the husband comes home from enjoying himself. She wrote a treatise on warfare so competent that Caxton printed it in English in 1489 by order of Henry VII, and it was still being cited as an authority under Henry VIII. She is, on the record, the first woman in Europe to have supported a family entirely by her pen.

family life

Her father was her first patron and her first ally, the one who decided she should be taught. Her mother wanted a normal daughter. Christine records the disagreement without bitterness and it is clear which parent she was arguing with for the rest of her life; a fair amount of the Cité des Dames is a grown woman still answering that objection.

She and Étienne had three children in ten years. A daughter, born around 1381, who eventually took vows at the royal convent of Poissy. A son who died as a baby. And Jean, born about 1385, whose childhood is its own strange story: the Earl of Salisbury, visiting the French court, was so taken with the boy that he took him back to England to be brought up in his own household — and then Salisbury was killed in the rebellion against Henry IV. Jean ended up in the hands of the English king, who offered Christine a position at his court in exchange, essentially, for coming to get her son. She spent three years negotiating him home rather than take the job. He came back to France, worked as a secretary like his father, and predeceased her.

And she carried everyone. After 1389 the household was Christine, her mother, her niece and the children, and the only earner was her. She writes about that in the most unromantic terms available — the debts, the creditors, the court appearances, the humiliation of arguing for money that was legally hers and being made to wait years for it by men who found the whole thing faintly amusing. The famous line about herself from this period is that she had to become a man: je devins vrai homme. She did not mean it happily. She meant that the work, the fighting and the providing had all landed on her, and she had done them, and she wanted that noticed.

romantic life

One marriage, ten years, and then forty years of writing about love for money while refusing to have any.

The marriage was arranged, in the sense that her father chose Étienne, and it was also a love match, which she seems to have understood was luck rather than merit. She wrote a poem about their wedding night that has no medieval business existing — not allegory, not courtly convention, just a fifteen-year-old girl reporting that the man did not touch her, that he kissed her a hundred times before morning, and that he told her God had made him for her. It is quoted in full below. Read it and then remember she was writing it as a widow.

She never remarried. She was twenty-five, well connected, and it would have solved the money immediately, which is exactly the reason it is worth noticing that she didn't. Instead she turned the grief into product: the Cent Ballades open with a run of widow poems that are among the most exposed things in medieval French, and then slide, without comment, into commissioned love lyrics for other people's affairs. She tells you outright in the prologue that she is doing this. That double register — performing feeling professionally while the real one sits underneath, unavailable — is the most modern thing about her.

Her actual position on romance, once she stopped writing to order, is unsentimental to the point of cold. In The Book of the Duke of True Lovers she builds a lush, beautiful courtly love story about a young prince and a married lady — the tournaments, the coded letters, the go-betweens — and then drops a letter into the middle of it, from an older woman, the Lady of La Tour, which quietly takes the whole genre apart. The letter tells the lady that the servants have already noticed she has started laughing more, withdrawing more, and whispering with a favoured few, and that this is how everyone knows. That the fantasy of a love that is pure because nothing physical happens is exactly that, a fantasy. That she has watched noble women lose everything on suspicion alone, with nothing ever proved. Christine wrote the seduction and then wrote the invoice, and left both in the same book.

life until death

The second half of her life is a country coming apart while she writes memos nobody reads. Charles VI went mad in recurring fits, and while the king was absent from his own mind the Dukes of Orléans and Burgundy fought over the regency until it became civil war. Christine wrote to Queen Isabeau begging her to intervene. She wrote treatises on the duties of princes to the people. She wrote, in Le Livre de la Paix, an argument for a strong middle class as the thing that holds a kingdom's two extremes together, which was not a commonplace idea in 1413. Orléans was assassinated in the street. Then in 1415 came Agincourt, and the French nobility was cut down in an afternoon.

In 1418, with Paris fallen to the Burgundians and massacres in the streets, she went into the abbey at Poissy where her daughter was a nun, and stopped publishing. Eleven years of silence from the most prolific writer in France. We do not know what she was doing in there beyond one devotional book about human life as a prison.

Then in 1429 a teenage girl from Domrémy broke the siege of Orléans and walked the disinherited dauphin to his coronation at Reims, and Christine came out of the abbey at sixty-four to write one last poem. The Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc, finished on 31 July 1429, eleven days after the coronation, is the only work about Joan of Arc written in French during Joan's own lifetime, and the only one by a woman. It opens with her announcing, after eleven years of weeping in a walled abbey, that she is going to start laughing. The two of them never met.

She died around 1430, at Poissy, aged about sixty-six. The date is not recorded, and there is no tomb. Almost certainly she died before Joan was burned at Rouen in May 1431, which is the single mercy in the whole arrangement: the last thing she wrote was a woman winning. Then she disappeared for four hundred years. The nineteenth century mostly remembered her as a curiosity, and it took until the 1980s and Earl Jeffrey Richards's translation of the Cité des Dames for the argument she actually made to get read again on its own terms. She has been dead six centuries and the fight she picked is still on the schedule.

her works

Christine wrote in Middle French and most of her verse has never had a good public-domain English translation, so this section mixes two things, and says which is which. Where an out-of-copyright translation exists — Laurence Binyon and Eric Maclagan's 1908 versions of the ballads, Alice Kemp-Welch's prose, Constance Fletcher's Joan of Arc verses — it is used and credited. Where none exists, the Middle French is given from Maurice Roy's edition of the Œuvres poétiques with a plain literal English rendering underneath, marked as such. Nothing has been prettied up.

1. “Seulete suy.” Her most famous poem, and the one she is still in the anthologies for. Twenty-five lines, and the word seulete — alone, in a small and diminutive form, all alone, little and alone — opens twenty-two of them. It is a ballade, so it is built to a strict form, which is the point: she took the most controlled shape available to her and used it to say one word over and over until the form itself starts to sound like a symptom.

Seulete suy et seulete vueil estre,
Seulete m'a mon doulz ami laissiée,
Seulete suy, sanz compaignon ne maistre,
Seulete suy, dolente et courrouciée,
Seulete suy en langour mesaisiée,
Seulete suy plus que nulle esgarée,
Seulete suy sanz ami demourée.
Alone am I, and alone I want to be,
alone my sweet love has left me,
alone am I, without companion or master,
alone am I, grieving and full of anger,
alone am I, sick and languishing,
alone am I, more lost than anyone,
alone am I, left without my love.

Alone am I at the door or at the window,
alone am I, hidden away in a corner,
alone am I, feeding myself on tears,
alone am I, whether grieving or quiet,
alone am I, and nothing suits me so well,
alone am I, shut inside my room,
alone am I, left without my love.

Alone am I everywhere and in every place.
Alone am I whether I walk or sit,
alone am I more than any other thing on earth,
alone am I, abandoned by every one,
alone am I, brought hard and low,
alone am I, and often all in tears,
alone am I, left without my love.

Prince, now my sorrow has begun:
alone am I, threatened by every grief,
alone am I, stained darker than mulberry,
alone am I, left without my love.

— Cent Ballades XI. Literal rendering; French from Roy's edition.

2. “Doulce chose est que mariage.” The wedding-night poem. She is writing in the present tense of a marriage that was already over when she wrote it, which is either a professional exercise or the most self-inflicted thing in her collected works. Note what she picks out as evidence that he was good: that on the first night he did her no oultrage, asked for nothing, and kissed her a hundred times.

Doulce chose est que mariage,
Je le puis bien par moy prouver,
Voire a qui mary bon et sage
A, comme Dieu m'a fait trouver…
A sweet thing is marriage,
I can prove it well enough by myself,
truly, for anyone who has a good and wise husband
such as God granted me to find.
Praised be He, who I pray will keep him
safe for me; for his great goodness
I can prove by the fact of it,
and certainly the sweet man loves me well.

The very first night of the marriage
I could already prove
his great goodness, for he did me no
outrage that should have hurt me;
but, before it was time to get up,
a hundred times he kissed me, so I hold,
and asked for nothing coarser than that,
and certainly the sweet man loves me well.

And he said, in such gentle language,
“God has brought me to you,
sweet friend, and I believe
he raised me up for your sake.”
And so he went on dreaming out loud
all night long in just that way,
never straying from it,
and certainly the sweet man loves me well.

— Cent Ballades XXVI. Literal rendering; French from Roy's edition.

3. Two widow rondeaux. The first is dated 1396, which makes it seven years after Étienne died — she puts the arithmetic in the poem herself. The second is the one that starts with what she is wearing.

Like the turtledove without her mate I am all alone,
and like a sheep gone astray without a shepherd;
for by death I was parted, long since,
from my sweet mate, whom I miss at every hour.
It is seven years since I lost him, poor thing that I am —
better for me if I had been buried then!
Like the turtledove without her mate I am all alone.
For ever since, in grief and in want
and in very hard trouble I have stayed,
nor have I any hope, as long as I last,
of any solace that could put me back into joy;
like the turtledove without her mate I am all alone.

— Rondeaux I (1396). Literal rendering.
I am a widow, alone, and dressed in black,
my sad face plainly covered over;
in great anger and in a mourning manner
I carry the very bitter grief that is killing me.
And it is only right that I be beaten down,
full of weeping and saying little;
I am a widow, alone, and dressed in black.
Since I lost the one through whom the pain
keeps being called back to me, which drives me out of my senses,
all my good days and all my joy are gone,
my fortune struck down into a hard state;
I am a widow, alone, and dressed in black.

— Rondeaux III. Literal rendering.

4. “What use is it then to complain.” The shortest of the grief poems and the one with the hardest edge, because it is a woman interrogating her own mourning and concluding that it is useless and that she is going to keep doing it anyway.

What use is it, then, to complain,
    or to lament,
about the pain I carry,
when nothing can make it less?
    Rather it grows greater,
and will, until death.
Pain comes at me so hard
    that I cannot hold in
my great distress;
what use is it, then, to complain?
Since the one I loved without pretending
    death chose to take,
and in that it wronged me;
that put out my joy,
    nor since then have I reached
any pleasure at all;
what use is it, then, to complain?

— Rondeaux II. Literal rendering.

5. On Fortune. Fortune is her lifelong subject — she wrote an enormous book called La Mutation de Fortune about it — and her position is not the pious one. She says flatly that Fortune is not a blindfolded goddess spinning a wheel; it is something rooted in us. But in the ballades she is still furious with it.

What good does it do me, then, to knead and to bake,
to pull, to brew, to take on labour,
since Fortune is against me?

Long ago she pulled me out of joy,
and since then has not finished harming me;
she is still so angry with me
that she takes me constantly from bad to worse.
Whatever I build, she tears up.
And what profit could I possibly draw,
since Fortune is against me?

Her wild influence
I thought I could always beat
by doing well and holding out a long time,
expecting to see some hour of light
for me, the one bad luck chases.
But none of it is worth anything, I can get nowhere,
since Fortune is against me.

— Cent Ballades X. Literal rendering. Anyone who has ever taken on a second job knows the kneading-and-baking line.
Whoever trusts too much in Fortune's great gifts
is, in truth, deceived by them;
for she is more inconstant than the moon.
Plenty of the greatest have found this out,
and even those she has raised up high
she throws down fast, and it is seen often enough
that her joys are nothing but plain wind.

— Cent Ballades XII. Literal rendering.

6. From The Book of the Duke of True Lovers (1405). The courtly machinery, working at full power. These are the ballads a young prince sends to a married woman, in Laurence Binyon's 1908 translation, which keeps the original metres. Christine is writing a man writing to a woman — a woman ventriloquising the exact style of pleading she elsewhere warns women to distrust.

Sweet Lady, fair and gentle without peer,
Have mercy on me, who all thy words obey
Body and soul do I abandon here
Unto thy will, and humbly thus I pray:
  Come quickly nigh,
Have pity, and cure my sickness when I cry:
Oh, I beseech thee, graciously attend
And so consent to take me for thy friend.

To thee I give myself, O flower most dear.
For mercy I beseech, and wilt thou slay?
I charge thee by that Lord whom we revere
To lift this wrong that crushes me away.
  No help have I
From any other: leave me not to die!
See, faithfully I serve thee to the end,
And so consent to take me for thy friend.

Seest thou not how I shed full many a tear:
And if thy help for longer shall delay
I am but shent, what need to speak more clear?
Ah, love me, Love so holds me in his sway!
  Then hither hie,
Be merciful, for near to death I lie:
'Tis truth, thou knowest, I have no hope to mend,
And so consent to take me for thy friend.

Lady, I thank thee, and all my duty send,
And so consent to take me for thy friend.

— trans. Laurence Binyon & Eric Maclagan, 1908.

And here is the technically astonishing one. Every line begins by picking up the last word of the line before it — a form called rime annexée. She is showing off, and she has earned it.

In this sad world have pity, my lady dear,
Dear to me more than any other there:
Their pride you know not; let not gracious cheer
Cheer me at so great cost, oh white and fair!
Fare I thus ill, yet canst thou bid me see
Seasons of solace that may comfort me.

If for unfitness I be slighted here,
Here am I dead, and arrows of despair
Spare not to pierce my heart, and life grows drear,
Drear as my brooding on the doom I bear.
Bear witness, Love withholds in obduracy
Seasons of solace that might comfort me.

O loveliest one and sweetest, without peer,
Peerless in honour, of all bounties heir,
Ere I thy servant pine in sorry fear
Fear not a kind and gentle guise to wear.
Where shall I find, 'mid this deep dolorous sea,
Seasons of solace that may comfort me?

Dear Lady, grant in gracious courtesy
Seasons of solace that may comfort me.

— trans. Binyon & Maclagan, 1908.

7. The letter that ruins the love story. From the same book. The lady, unhappy in her marriage and falling into the affair, writes to her old governess asking her to come and be a confidante. This is the reply she gets, in Kemp-Welch's 1908 translation. It is the coldest and most useful thing Christine ever wrote about being watched.

My Lady, I have heard certain rumours touching your conduct which grieve me from the bottom of my heart because of the fear I have of the ruin of your good name…

And although the foregoing conditions, and all other usages befitting a noble princess, were aforetime observed by you, you now act quite otherwise, it is said, for you amuse yourself much more, and have become more communicative and mirthful than was your wont, and it is when the outward signs are changed, that one usually judges the disposition to be altered, and now you desire to be alone, and withdrawn from others save one or two of your waiting-women, and some of your dependants, with whom, even in the presence of others, you consult privately, and titter, and talk secretly, as if you well understood one another, and naught but the company of such pleases you, and the others can in nowise serve you to your liking, the which things and doings arouse envy in your other servants, and cause them to think that your heart is enamoured of some one.

Ah, my very sweet Lady, for God's sake remember who you are… and do not put trust in the vain fancy which many young women have, who permit themselves to believe that there is no wrong in loving with tender passion provided this is not accompanied by any wrongful act… and that it makes life more pleasurable, and that one thus makes a man gallant and renowned for aye. Ah, my dear Lady, it is quite the reverse… take warning from such noble ladies as you have seen in your time (and such there are), who, through being merely suspected of such love, have, without the truth ever becoming known, on this account lost both…

— the Lady of La Tour to her former charge, trans. Alice Kemp-Welch, 1908.

8. The Order of the Rose. In 1402 she wrote up an actual scene — an assembly at the Duke of Orléans's house where a company of men swore an oath to defend the reputation of women. She was given custody of the charter. This is the vow, in her Middle French:

A bonne amour je fais veu et promesse
Et à la fleur qui est rose clamée,
A la vaillant de Loyauté deesse,
Par qui nous est ceste chose informée,
Qu'à tous jours mais la bonne renommée
Je garderay de dame en toute chose
Ne par moy ja femme n'yert diffamée:
Et pour ce prens je L'Ordre de la Rose.
To good love I make this vow and promise,
and to the flower that is called the rose,
and to the valiant goddess Loyalty,
by whom this thing is made known to us:
that from this day forward I will guard
the good name of women in all things,
and no woman shall ever be slandered by me.
And for this I take the Order of the Rose.

— Le Dit de la Rose, ll. 197–204. Literal rendering.

9. Two lines she wrote for her son. Her advice on the Roman de la Rose, compressed into a couplet, in the middle of a book of moral proverbs written to a boy.

Se bien veulx et chastement vivre,
De la Rose ne lis le livre.

If you want to live well and cleanly,
do not read the book of the Rose.

And her single flattest sentence in the whole querelle, on why the literary record is so uniformly against women, as reported by Kemp-Welch: to the charge that books are full of the condemnation of women, she replies with the simple remark that books were not written by women.

10. Le Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc, 31 July 1429. Sixty-four years old, eleven years silent, writing about a nineteen-year-old girl in armour. The opening stanza first, from the Middle French:

Je, Christine, qui ay plouré
XI ans en abbaye close,
Où j'ay tousjours puis demouré…
Ore à prime me prens à rire;

I, Christine, who have wept
eleven years in a closed abbey,
where I have stayed ever since
Charles — and this is a strange thing! —
the king's son, if I dare say it,
fled straight out of Paris
because of the treason shut up inside it:
now, for the first time, I begin to laugh.

— stanza I. Literal rendering.

And four verses in Constance Fletcher's 1913 English, which is the last public-domain verse translation of her that exists, and gets the joy of it:

O Thou! ordainèd Maid of very God!
Joanna! born in Fortune's golden hour,
On thee the Holy Spirit pours His Flood
And His high grace is given thee for dower.
Now all great gifts are thine:—O blessed be He
That lent thee life!—how word my grateful prayer?
—No prayer of thine was spoken fruitlessly,
O Maid of God! O Joan! O Virgin rare!

Mark me this portent! strange beyond all telling!
How this despoilèd Kingdom stricken lay,
And no man raised his hand to guard his dwelling,
Until a Woman came to show the way.
Until a Woman (since no man dare try)
Rallied the land and bade the traitors fly.
Honour to Womankind! It needs must be
That God loves Woman, since He fashioned Thee!

O strange! This little maid sixteen years old
On whom no harness weigheth overmuch.
So strong the little hands! enduring hold
She seemeth fed by that same armour's touch,
Nurtured on iron—as before her vanish
The enemies of her triumphal day;
And this by many men is witnessèd;
Yea, many eyes be witness of that fray!

Castles and towns, she wins them back for France,
And France is free again, and this her doing!
Never was power given as to her lance!
A thousand swords could do no more pursuing.
Of all staunch men and true she is the Chief,
Captain and Leader, for that she alone
Is braver than Achilles the brave Greek.
All praise be given to God who leadeth Joan!

— trans. Constance Fletcher (“George Fleming”), in Alice Kemp-Welch, Of Six Mediæval Women, 1913.

Honour to Womankind! It needs must be / That God loves Woman, since He fashioned Thee. That is the last surviving thing Christine de Pizan wrote. She had spent forty years arguing that women were worth the ink, mostly against men who found the argument funny, and then a farm girl with a sword walked into the middle of her retirement and proved it in public. She got to see it. She did not live to see it undone.

Sources: Œuvres poétiques de Christine de Pisan, ed. Maurice Roy (Société des anciens textes français, 1886–96), vols. I–II, for all Middle French; The Book of the Duke of True Lovers, trans. Alice Kemp-Welch, ballads by Laurence Binyon and Eric R. D. Maclagan (Chatto & Windus, 1908); Alice Kemp-Welch, Of Six Mediæval Women (Macmillan, 1913), chapter on Christine, including Constance Fletcher's verses from the Ditié. Biographical dates checked against Britannica and current scholarship; the literal English renderings of the French are mine and make no claim to be poetry.

Virginia Woolf

1882–1941 · English novelist, essayist, printer · she was never allowed to go to school, so she read her father's entire library instead, then rebuilt the English sentence so it could finally hold what a mind actually does in a day

aug 12, 2026▼

childhood & early life

She was born Adeline Virginia Stephen on 25 January 1882 at 22 Hyde Park Gate, South Kensington, into a house with eight children in it and not one of the girls at school. Her father, Sir Leslie Stephen, was a critic, a mountaineer and the founding editor of the Dictionary of National Biography — a man who had catalogued the lives of thousands of eminent Englishmen and could not imagine sending his daughter to be educated. Her mother, Julia, was a famous beauty who had modelled for the photographer Julia Margaret Cameron, her aunt, and who spent her life nursing other people. Both parents had been widowed. Julia brought three Duckworth children into the marriage, Leslie brought a daughter, and together they had four more: Vanessa, Thoby, Virginia, Adrian.

Virginia's education was piecemeal, done at the kitchen table by her parents and later by tutors in Greek and Latin. What saved her was that her father, having decided she could not be schooled, also decided she could read anything. She said so plainly years later: “Even today there may be parents who would doubt the wisdom of allowing a girl of fifteen the free run of a large and quite unexpurgated library. But my father allowed it. There were certain facts – very briefly, very shyly he referred to them. Yet 'Read what you like', he said, and all his books … were to be had without asking.” The result was a woman better read than any of the Cambridge men she would spend her life talking to, and permanently, structurally furious that she had not been allowed to sit in their rooms.

She started writing early and never really stopped: letters at five, a family newspaper called the Hyde Park Gate News from the age of ten, and a diary from 1897 that she kept for twelve years. Every summer until she was thirteen the family took Talland House at St Ives, with a view across Porthminster Bay to the Godrevy Lighthouse. That house is the engine room of her whole imagination. She would spend the rest of her life writing books that are, one way or another, attempts to get back into it.

Then everything collapsed in a decade. Her mother died in May 1895, when Virginia was thirteen, and the breakdown that followed was the first of many. Her half-sister Stella, who stepped into the mothering role, married in April 1897 and was dead by July. Her father died in February 1904 and she went into a crisis that included at least one attempt on her own life. She later summarised the years 1897 to 1904 in four words: the seven unhappy years. In an essay written in 1939 she also disclosed, for the first time, that she had been sexually abused as a child by her half-brother Gerald Duckworth, with further improprieties from George during the years he was supposedly escorting her and Vanessa into society. She was blunt about that society too: “a very competent, perfectly complacent, ruthless machine. A girl had no chance against its fangs. No other desires — say to paint, or to write — could be taken seriously.”

what she did & why she's remembered

After their father's death the Stephen children sold the South Kensington house and moved to Bloomsbury, which was cheaper and, to their relations, faintly disgraceful. Thoby's Cambridge friends started coming round on Thursday evenings — Lytton Strachey, Clive Bell, Maynard Keynes, Leonard Woolf — and the Bloomsbury Group was simply that: a set of people who talked to each other for thirty years without pretending to be respectable. In 1906 the siblings travelled to Greece and Turkey; Thoby caught typhoid and died at twenty-six. Two days later Vanessa accepted Clive Bell's proposal. That is the tempo of Woolf's life. Loss, then someone getting married, then work.

She married Leonard Woolf in August 1912 and published her first novel, The Voyage Out, in 1915. In 1917 the two of them bought a small hand printing press and set it up in the dining room at Hogarth House, partly as occupational therapy for her nerves. The Hogarth Press ended up publishing T. S. Eliot, Katherine Mansfield, the first English translations of Freud, and every book Woolf wrote after 1917. That last part matters more than it sounds: she is one of the very few major novelists in English who never had to submit a manuscript to a man for approval. She could write anything, and she did.

What she actually invented is hard to overstate and easy to miss, because everyone steals it now. The Victorian novel told you what a character did and then what it meant. Woolf threw out the scaffolding and wrote consciousness directly — a mind moving sideways through a single day, hauling in memory, weather, other people's faces, a bus, a regret from twenty years ago, all in one unbroken sentence held together by semicolons. Mrs Dalloway (1925) is one June day in London. To the Lighthouse (1927) is two days ten years apart, with the entire decade between them — a war, three deaths — disposed of in a middle section narrated by an empty house. Orlando (1928) is a mock-biography of a poet who lives four hundred years and changes sex halfway through without particularly minding.

And then A Room of One's Own (1929), built from two talks she gave to women students at Cambridge, which is the most durable argument about women and work ever written, mostly because it refuses to be inspirational. Her thesis is money and a door that locks. Not genius, not encouragement, not believing in yourself. Five hundred a year and a lock. She followed it in 1938 with Three Guineas, which connects the tyranny of the Victorian father directly to European fascism and which people liked considerably less.

family life

The Stephen household was a blended one and a crowded one: George, Stella and Gerald Duckworth from her mother's first marriage; Laura Stephen from her father's, a girl considered defective who was eventually put in an institution and effectively erased from the family; and the four full siblings. Virginia was the seventh child of the house. She adored her mother and lost her at thirteen, and spent thirty years being haunted by her until she wrote To the Lighthouse and found, to her surprise, that the haunting stopped. Mrs Ramsay in that book is Julia Stephen, down to the way she made people fall in love at dinner.

Her sister Vanessa was the great constant — painter, mother, rival, the one person she never stopped writing to. Thoby's death at twenty-six in 1906 is the wound she kept reopening on the page; he is Jacob in Jacob's Room and Percival in The Waves, both of them young men who are only ever described from the outside by people who loved them and then lose them.

She had no children. Woolf wanted them; Leonard, after consulting doctors and watching her breakdowns, decided she was not strong enough and refused. Whether he was protecting her or managing her is one of the permanent arguments about their marriage, and she never fully stopped grieving it. Vanessa's children were the ones she wrote silly letters to, and Vanessa's fertility was a thing she could look at all her life from just outside the window.

romantic life

Leonard Woolf first saw the Stephen sisters in Thoby's rooms at Cambridge and remembered them in “white dresses and large hats, with parasols in their hands, their beauty literally took one's breath away.” He then went off to run a colonial district in Ceylon for seven years, came home on leave in 1911 after Lytton Strachey wrote to him about Virginia, and never went back. He proposed in January 1912. She said no, kept seeing him, and on 29 May told him she loved him. They married that August. He resigned his career for her.

The marriage was not sexually successful and both of them knew it early. What it was instead was a working partnership of unusual completeness: a press they ran together, a house in Sussex, and a man who spent nearly thirty years watching for the signs of an oncoming collapse and enforcing milk and rest and no visitors. There is a version of this story where Leonard is a jailer. There is another where he is the reason she got twenty-nine more years and eight more books. Both versions have evidence.

The love affair of her life was with Vita Sackville-West: aristocrat, novelist, gardener, married to a diplomat, considerably more experienced and considerably less clever. They met in December 1922 and the affair ran through the mid-twenties. Vita's husband knew. Leonard knew. The letters are extraordinary because the roles keep swapping — the famous stylist insisting she is not making phrases, the glamorous one admitting she has no defences left.

I am reduced to a thing that wants Virginia. I composed a beautiful letter to you in the sleepless nightmare hours of the night, and it has all gone: I just miss you, in a quite simple desperate human way … Damn you, spoilt creature; I shan't make you love me any the more by giving myself away like this — But oh my dear, I can't be clever and stand-offish with you: I love you too much for that.
— Vita Sackville-West to Virginia Woolf, from Milan, 21 January 1926
