Every one of them has some interesting point, and she is acquainted with ancient literature also, but she is not like a true artist who is filled with the genuine spirit of poetry. Yet I think even she cannot presume to pass judgment on the poems of others.

… Those who compose poems whose loins are all but broken, yet who are infinitely self-exalted and vain, deserve our contempt and pity.

LADY SEISHONAGON. A very proud person. She values herself highly, and scatters her Chinese writings all about. Yet should we study her closely, we should find that she is still imperfect. She tries to be exceptional, but naturally persons of that sort give offence. She is piling up trouble for her future. One who is too richly gifted, who indulges too much in emotion, even when she ought to be reserved, and cannot turn aside from anything she is interested in, in spite of herself will lose self-control. How can such a vain and reckless person end her days happily!

"She scatters her Chinese writings all about." From the woman secretly teaching Chinese poetry at dawn. The charge is not that Sei knows Chinese. It is that she lets people see her know it.

Then, without warning, the diary turns inward and she writes the loneliest paragraphs in Heian literature.

Having no excellence within myself, I have passed my days without making any special impression on any one. Especially the fact that I have no man who will look out for my future makes me comfortless. I do not wish to bury myself in dreariness. Is it because of my worldly mind that I feel lonely? On moonlight nights in autumn, when I am hopelessly sad, I often go out on the balcony and gaze dreamily at the moon. It makes me think of days gone by. People say that it is dangerous to look at the moon in solitude, but something impels me, and sitting a little withdrawn I muse there. In the wind-cooled evening I play on the koto, though others may not care to hear it. I fear that my playing betrays the sorrow which becomes more intense, and I become disgusted with myself—so foolish and miserable am I.

My room is ugly, blackened by smoke. I play on a thirteen or six-stringed koto, but I neglect to take away the bridges even in rainy weather, and I lean it up against the wall between the cabinet and the door jamb. On either side of the koto stands a lute. A pair of big bookcases have in them all the books they can hold. In one of them are placed old poems and romances. They are the homes of worms which come frightening us when we turn the pages, so none ever wish to read them. As to the other cabinet, since the person who placed his own books [there] no hand has touched it.

"Since the person who placed his own books there, no hand has touched it." Her husband, dead eight years, is in that sentence and is never named. She wrote a book about a man's whole erotic career and could not write the words my husband's shelf.

Two passages on being read by other people. The first is the gap between her reputation and her face; the second is her rule for conversation, which is the single most INFJ sentence written before the twentieth century.

Pretty and coy, shrinking from sight, unsociable, proud, fond of romance, vain and poetic, looking down upon others with a jealous eye—such is the opinion of those who do not know me, but after seeing me they say, "You are wonderfully gentle to meet with; I cannot identify you with that imagined one."

I see that I have been slighted, hated, and looked down upon as an old gossip, and I must bear it, for it is my destiny to be solitary. The Queen said once, "You were ever mindful not to show your soul, but I have become more intimate with you than others."

… after all, when I was among the ladies of the Court I did not say what I wanted to say either, for it is useless to talk with those who do not understand one and troublesome to talk with those who criticize from a feeling of superiority. Especially one-sided persons are troublesome. Few are accomplished in many arts and most cling narrowly to their own opinion.

… Moreover, in this muddy world it is best to let alone the persons who hate us. If we compare one who tries to excel in hatred saying extraordinary words and watching [their effect] ill-humouredly face to face, with one who coldly hides her heart with a tranquil manner, we can see which is superior.

The night at the door. Michinaga knocks; she lies still in the dark and does not answer; in the morning the poem arrives. A kuina, water-rail, is a bird famous for a knocking call, and it is also the standard poetic euphemism for a man at a woman's door at night. Her reply uses his own bird against him.

One night I slept in a room near the corridor. Some one came knocking at the door. I was afraid and passed the night without making a sound. The next morning the following poem was sent me [from the Prime Minister]:

All the night through, knocking louder than a water-rail,
I stood in vain at the door of hinoki wood
weary and lamenting.

I wrote back:

A cause of deep regret, indeed,
Had the door opened at the knocking of the water-rail!

No. Politely, in metre, to the most powerful man in Japan, with the deniability of a joke. And then she copied the exchange into her own diary so that it would survive.

Court life in one scene. A drunken banquet, ministers making holes in the screens, and a novelist trying to physically hide from her own reputation.

The Minister of the Right came dancing wildly and made a hole in the kichō behind which ladies were sitting. They laughed, saying, "He has long passed the age for that." He did not notice, but made a great many unbecoming jokes, taking away ladies' fans. … The First Officer of the Light Bodyguard said, "I think Lady Murasaki must be somewhere here!" I listened, thinking, "How can she be here in a place where there is no such graceful person as Prince Genji?" … It was an awful night of carousal, so after the ceremony I signalled to Lady Saisho and we hid ourselves, but there came noisily the Prime Minister's sons and Lieutenant-General Saisho, so, although we two had remained hidden behind the screen, even this was taken away and we were captives. "Compose a poem each, and you shall be excused," said the Lord Prime Minister.

A man shouts her character's name across a party as a pickup line. She thinks a witheringly good comeback and says nothing. Then she is dragged out from behind a screen and made to perform a poem on demand at midnight. Freelancing has not changed.

Two on friendship, which she took more seriously than romance. She is at her parents' house, missing Lady Dainagon, with whom she shared a room at court; the reply came back the same day.

I long for Lady Dainagon with whom I spent every night before the Queen, when we told each other all our heart's secrets—is it also my worldly heart that longs for a companion other than Buddha?

Like two wild ducks
Floating with unrestful slumber,
Yet even those nights I would recall—
Feathers wet and cold—
But colder tears!

Lady Dainagon returned this answer:

Midnight sleep was broken
But no friend to brush away the cold tears!
I envy the Oshidori which has ever its mate by its side.

And then the fragment that is not a diary entry at all. It looks like the covering letter she sent with the manuscript to a friend, and it is the closest she ever comes to asking for something.

I wish I could make known everything to you, good and bad, things of the world, and those relating to my life—all that I could not write in my letters. You could not expect such writing as this from your friend? You feel weary of life; please look into my heart, also weary. Please write to me—even a little—whatever comes into your mind. It would be very unfortunate if my writings were scattered about and made known to others. I have written many things of this sort, but recently I have torn up all my old writings, burying some, and making dolls' houses of the rest. Since that time I have received no letters and am determined to write no more on fresh paper, so thrifty have I become! I think I am not in the wrong. After reading, please return quickly. As I could not revise all there may be some defects; read—overlooking them.

She burned and buried her old papers and pasted the rest into dolls' houses for her daughter. Then she asked one person to write back, said please don't show anyone, said please send it back, and apologised for not proofreading. A thousand years later it is on a private dashboard on the other side of the planet. She would be appalled.

Now Genji. Suematsu's 1882 English is stiff and Victorian, but the architecture survives. This is the first paragraph of the first novel, and notice that it opens not with a hero but with office politics and a woman being bullied to death.

In the reign of a certain Emperor, whose name is unknown to us, there was, among the Niogo and Koyi of the Imperial Court, one who, though she was not of high birth, enjoyed the full tide of Royal favor. Hence her superiors, each one of whom had always been thinking—"I shall be the one," gazed upon her disdainfully with malignant eyes, and her equals and inferiors were more indignant still.

Such being the state of affairs, the anxiety which she had to endure was great and constant, and this was probably the reason why her health was at last so much affected…

Genji's mother dies a few pages in. The Emperor has just extracted a promise that neither of them will go first.

Distracted by his vain endeavors to devise means to aid her, the Emperor … went to her apartment and cried despairingly: "Did not we vow that we would neither of us be either before or after the other even in travelling the last long journey of life? And can you find it in your heart to leave me now?" Sadly and tenderly looking up, she thus replied, with almost failing breath:—

"Since my departure for this dark journey,
Makes you so sad and lonely,
Fain would I stay though weak and weary,
And live for your sake only!"

"Had I but known this before—"

She appeared to have much more to say, but was too weak to continue.

"Had I but known this before" and then nothing. She cuts the sentence off mid-clause because the woman ran out of air. That is a novelist's instinct, and it is the year 1002.

Later, the grieving Emperor sends a messenger to the dead woman's mother with a poem about their orphaned son. The imagery is a fawn asleep under bush clover on a windy autumn plain, which is also the palace, which is also him.

"I thought that time only would assuage my grief; but time only brings before me more vividly my recollection of the lost one. Yet, it is inevitable. How is my boy? Of him, too, I am always thinking. Time once was when we both hoped to bring him up together. May he still be to you a memento of his mother!"

"The sound of the wind is dull and drear
Across Miyagi's dewy lea,
And makes me mourn for the motherless deer
That sleeps beneath the Hagi tree."

And the scene that founded a genre: the rainy night, chapter two, where four young men shut in by the weather sort women into categories and rate them. She wrote the whole thing as a set piece of male self-satisfaction, and then spends the next fifty chapters demonstrating that every rule they invent is wrong.

"I have only just now discovered," continued he, "how difficult it is to meet with a fair creature, of whom one can say, 'This is, indeed, the one; here is, at last, perfection.' There are, indeed, many who fascinate; many who are ready with their pens, and who, when occasion may require, are quick at repartee. But how often such girls as these are conceited about their own accomplishments, and endeavor unduly to disparage those of others! There are again some who are special pets of their parents, and most jealously watched over at home. Often, no doubt, they are pretty, often graceful; and frequently they will apply themselves with effect to music and to poetry, in which they may even attain to special excellence. But then, their friends will keep their drawbacks in the dark, and eulogize their merits to the utmost. If we were to give full credence to this exaggerated praise, we could not but fail in every single instance to be more or less disappointed."

… "In my opinion, the most and the least favored are in the same proportion. I mean, they are both not many. Their birth, also, divides them into three classes. Those, however, who are especially well born, are often too jealously guarded, and are, for the most part, kept secluded from the outside gaze, which frequently tends to make their deportment shy and timid. It is those of the middle class, who are much more frequently seen by us, who afford us most chance of studying their character."

A woman of exactly that middle class, sitting in a room being studied, wrote this transcript of men deciding what she is. Then she gave every one of those categorised women an interior life and let them ruin the men who catalogued them.

Last, the two poems in the Hundred Poets, in MacCauley's 1917 version. Hers, number 57, is about running into someone she knew long ago and losing them again before she could be sure it was them. The headnote says a childhood friend, glimpsed and gone in the same instant.

Meeting in the way—,
While I can not clearly know
If 'tis friend or not;—
Lo! the midnight moon, ah me!
In a cloud has disappeared.
— Murasaki Shikibu, no. 57

And her daughter's, number 58, which is an answer to a man who accused her of being unfaithful. Mount Arima's winds through the bamboo of Ina is a proverb for gossip and inconstancy.

If Mount Arima
Sends his rustling winds across
Ina's bamboo-plains;—
Well! in truth, 'tis as you say;
Yet how can I e'er forget?
— Daini no Sanmi, no. 58, her daughter

The mother's poem is about someone vanishing before she could hold them. The daughter's is about refusing to be talked out of what she feels. Two women, one household, filed next to each other for a thousand years, and neither of their real names survives.

Marcus Aurelius

Rome, 121–180 AD · emperor, Stoic, the most powerful man alive writing a private notebook telling himself to get out of bed

aug 6, 2026▼

childhood & early life

He was born in Rome on 26 April 121, into a family with money and a name, and his father died when he was about three. That is the first fact and it quietly explains a lot of the rest. He was raised by his grandfather and by his mother, Domitia Lucilla, who had inherited an enormous brick and tile works and was, in practical terms, an industrialist. The boy grew up in a house full of tutors and around a woman who ran a business.

He was a serious child in an obvious way. Somewhere around twelve he took up philosophy properly, started sleeping on the floor on a plank with a skin over it, in the Greek manner, and his mother had to beg him to use a bed. Hadrian noticed him early and called him Verissimus, a pun on his family name Verus, meaning "most truthful", which is either affectionate or slightly mocking depending on how you read emperors. In 138 Hadrian arranged the succession so that Antoninus Pius adopted Marcus. He was sixteen or seventeen and had just been handed the largest empire on earth as a homework assignment.

There is a story, from the Historia Augusta, about the night he was told. He was distressed rather than delighted, and when his household asked him why he was sad about being adopted into the imperial family, he listed for them all the evils that sovereignty carries with it. He was a teenager. He had already done the maths.

what he did & why he's remembered

He ruled from 161 to 180 and it was, by any external measure, a bad nineteen years to be in charge. He insisted from day one on sharing power with his adoptive brother Lucius Verus, which had never been done, apparently because he thought it was fair. Then the Parthian war. Then the returning armies brought back what we now call the Antonine Plague, almost certainly smallpox, which burned through the empire for fifteen years and may have killed millions. Then the Danube frontier collapsed and Germanic and Sarmatian peoples poured across into Italy for the first time in centuries. Then, in 175, one of his own generals, Avidius Cassius, declared himself emperor in the East.

Look at what he actually did with each of those. When the treasury was empty and he refused to raise emergency taxes on the provinces, he held a two-month public auction in the Forum of Trajan and sold the palace: gold and crystal goblets, jewels out of Hadrian's cabinet, paintings by great artists, and his wife's silk gold-embroidered robes. Afterwards he told the buyers that anyone who wanted to return what they had bought and get their money back could, and he made it awkward for nobody.

When Cassius was killed by his own soldiers and the head was brought to Marcus, he refused to look at it and ordered it buried. He then asked the Senate, in writing, to execute nobody: not Cassius's family, not the senators involved. Cassius's children kept over half their father's estate and were allowed to travel where they liked. Marcus said he grieved that he had not managed to finish his reign without a single senator's blood.

And he is remembered for none of that. He is remembered because in a tent on the Danube, in the middle of the plague years, he kept a private notebook in Greek arguing with himself. It has no title in the manuscript tradition beyond Ta eis heauton, "to himself". It was never meant to be read by you. That is precisely why it works: there is no audience to perform for, so he does not perform. The most powerful human being alive is writing notes to remind himself that fame is noise, that his position is a costume, and that he has to stop being irritated by his colleagues.

family life

He married his cousin Faustina the Younger, daughter of Antoninus Pius, in 145. Over the next twenty-three years she bore at least thirteen children, including two sets of twins. Roughly six lived to be adults. He buried something like eight of his own children.

The one that gets to me is Verus Caesar, aged seven, dead from an operation on a tumour behind his ear in 169. Marcus was at Praeneste, about to leave for the German war. The record says he mourned for five days, and that even during those five days he answered questions on state business when they were put to him. The games of Jupiter were running and he would not have them stopped for public mourning, so all he did was order statues for his dead son and have the boy's name written into the hymn the Salian priests sang. That is a father managing a schedule around his own child's death because thousands of people are waiting on him. Whether you read that as monstrous discipline or as the only way he could stay upright, it is the same five days.

The twins Commodus and Titus Aurelius Fulvus Antoninus were born in 161. The second one died at four. The first one survived, and Rome would have been better off the other way round. Marcus knew. Two days before his death he told his friends he thought about his son roughly what Philip had thought about Alexander, and said it grieved him to leave a son behind at all.

The other family, the one he chose, was his teachers. Book One of the Meditations is nothing but a list of people and exactly what he took from each of them, and it reads like a man doing an inventory of everything in him that came from somebody else. His letters to his Latin tutor Fronto, which survive because a monk scraped a manuscript to reuse the parchment and somebody read the underwriting in 1815, are absurdly warm. He signs off to a middle-aged rhetoric teacher with "my love, my delight".

romantic life

Thirty years with one woman, and Rome spent most of them gossiping about her. Faustina was accused of sleeping with gladiators, sailors, pantomime actors, and half the Senate. The story went around that Commodus came out the way he did because he was really a gladiator's son. It was also said she backed Avidius Cassius's coup because she thought her husband was dying and wanted a strong man in place.

Marcus's response to all of it was to promote the men she was rumoured to be sleeping with, defend her in letters, and, when someone told him he should divorce her if not kill her, reply: "If we send our wife away, we must also return her dowry." Her dowry was the empire. It is the driest possible way to end a conversation.

She died suddenly in 175, in a village in the foothills of the Taurus mountains, having followed him on campaign for years; the soldiers called her Mother of the Camp. He asked the Senate to make her a goddess, delivered the eulogy himself, founded a charity for orphan girls in her name, turned the village where she died into a city, and built her a temple there. And in the private notebook that nobody was supposed to read, where he had no reason at all to lie, he thanked the gods for a wife who was "so obedient, and so affectionate, and so simple." Simple, in his vocabulary, is high praise. It means unpretending, without an angle.

After she died a noblewoman named Fabia manoeuvred to marry him. He took a concubine instead, the daughter of one of his wife's stewards, on the stated grounds that he did not want to put a stepmother over that many children.

life until death

He spent the last decade of his life in military camps on the Danube, in a climate he hated, with a stomach that barely worked, dosed on theriac, sleeping badly, running an empire by dictation. He was close to annexing Marcomannia and Sarmatia as provinces. One more year would probably have done it.

He died on 17 March 180, at 58, either at Vindobona (Vienna) or Sirmium; the sources disagree. The account in the Historia Augusta is unusually plain. He got sick, called Commodus in and begged him not to abandon what was left of the war. Commodus said what he wanted was to not get sick. Marcus let him go, asking only that he wait a few days. Then, being ready to die, Marcus stopped eating and drinking, which sped things up. On the sixth day he called his friends in and, with what the text calls derision for all human affairs, said: "Why do you weep for me, instead of thinking about the pestilence and about death which is the common lot of us all?" As they were leaving he groaned and said, "If you now grant me leave to go, I bid you farewell and pass on before." Asked to whom he entrusted his son, he said: "To you, if he prove worthy, and to the immortal gods."

On the seventh day he was too tired for anyone. He allowed Commodus in and then sent him straight out again, afraid the boy would catch it. Cassius Dio adds one detail: a tribune came for the night's watchword, and the dying emperor said "Go to the rising sun; I am setting." Then he covered his head as if to sleep and died in the night.

The Senate and the people, sitting together, which was not done, hailed him as a gracious god. For generations afterwards Romans kept small statues of him among their household gods, next to the family spirits, which is a strange and touching thing to do with an emperor. And then Commodus took over, fought a thousand gladiatorial bouts in the arena, was strangled in his bath by his wrestling partner in 192, and the empire fell into a civil war it took a century to finish having. Marcus was the last of the so-called Five Good Emperors and the one who broke the pattern by having a biological son to hand it to. He saw it coming and did it anyway, which is the one place where his judgement, or his nerve, plainly failed.

his works

Everything below is George Long's 1862 translation of the Meditations, out of copyright, plus two letters in C. R. Haines's 1919 Loeb translation. Long's "thou" is old-fashioned but he keeps the shape of the Greek, which matters, because the whole book is written in the second person. Marcus is talking to himself the entire time. Read it as somebody's private argument with their own morning.

Start with the most famous thing in it. Book Two, section one. This is the first substantive line of the book, written by the emperor of Rome, about having to go to work.

Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil. But I who have seen the nature of the good that it is beautiful, and of the bad that it is ugly, and the nature of him who does wrong, that it is akin to me; not only of the same blood or seed, but that it participates in the same intelligence and the same portion of the divinity, I can neither be injured by any of them, for no one can fix on me what is ugly, nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him. For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. To act against one another, then, is contrary to nature; and it is acting against one another to be vexed and to turn away.

He is not saying be nice. He is saying: pre-load the difficulty, so that when it arrives it costs you nothing. And notice the tell in "I can neither be injured by any of them" - that is a man who is, in fact, injured by them, writing the sentence down again in the hope it takes.

Then Book Five, section one, which is the single least imperial thing ever written by an emperor.

In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present, — I am rising to the work of a human being. Why then am I dissatisfied if I am going to do the things for which I exist and for which I was brought into the world? Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm? — But this is more pleasant. — Dost thou exist then to take thy pleasure, and not at all for action or exertion? Dost thou not see the little plants, the little birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees working together to put in order their several parts of the universe? And art thou unwilling to do the work of a human being, and dost thou not make haste to do that which is according to thy nature? But it is necessary to take rest also. — It is necessary. However, Nature has fixed bounds to this too.

He argues with himself in dialogue. He puts the lazy voice in the text, gives it the good line ("but this is more pleasant"), and then answers it. Eighteen centuries later this is still the best written account of not wanting to get up.

Book Four, section three. This one is for people who keep thinking that the answer is a different location.

Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself. For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul, particularly when he has within him such thoughts that by looking into them he is immediately in perfect tranquillity; and I affirm that tranquillity is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind. Constantly then give to thyself this retreat, and renew thyself; and let thy principles be brief and fundamental.

Book Two, section seventeen, written at Carnuntum, in camp, during the plague. The note "This in Carnuntum" sits at the end of the book in the manuscript like a location stamp on a photograph.

Of human life the time is a point, and the substance is in a flux, and the perception dull, and the composition of the whole body subject to putrefaction, and the soul a whirl, and fortune hard to divine, and fame a thing devoid of judgment. And, to say all in a word, everything which belongs to the body is a stream, and what belongs to the soul is a dream and vapour, and life is a warfare and a stranger's sojourn, and after fame is oblivion. What then is that which is able to conduct a man? One thing, and only one, philosophy. But this consists in keeping the daemon within a man free from violence and unharmed, superior to pains and pleasures, doing nothing without a purpose, nor yet falsely and with hypocrisy, not feeling the need of another man's doing or not doing anything; and besides, accepting all that happens, and all that is allotted, as coming from thence, wherever it is, from whence he himself came.

Book Six, section thirty. He is warning himself, by name, about the specific occupational hazard of his own job.

Take care that thou art not made into a Caesar, that thou art not dyed with this dye; for such things happen. Keep thyself then simple, good, pure, serious, free from affectation, a friend of justice, a worshipper of the gods, kind, affectionate, strenuous in all proper acts. Strive to continue to be such as philosophy wished to make thee. Reverence the gods, and help men. Short is life. There is only one fruit of this terrene life — a pious disposition and social acts.

"Take care that thou art not made into a Caesar." He is Caesar. He means the personality, not the office. He is afraid of turning into the thing he already is.

A run of short ones, because the short ones are where he stops being tactful with himself:

No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such. (x. 16)

Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good. (iv. 17)

Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away. (iv. 7)

The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong-doer. (vi. 6)

When a man has done thee any wrong, immediately consider with what opinion about good or evil he has done wrong. For when thou hast seen this, thou wilt pity him, and wilt neither wonder nor be angry. (vii. 26)

Think not so much of what thou hast not as of what thou hast: but of the things which thou hast select the best, and then reflect how eagerly they would have been sought, if thou hadst them not. (vii. 27)

Consider thyself to be dead, and to have completed thy life up to the present time; and live according to nature the remainder which is allowed thee. (vii. 56)

Loss is nothing else than change. (ix. 35)

Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it. (iv. 49)

Soon, very soon, thou wilt be ashes, or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; but name is sound and echo. (v. 33)

A spider is proud when it has caught a fly, and another when he has caught a poor hare, and another when he has taken a little fish in a net, and another when he has taken wild boars, and another when he has taken bears, and another when he has taken Sarmatians. Are not these robbers, if thou examinest their opinions? (x. 10)

That last one is him. He had just taken Sarmatians. He put himself in the list of spiders.

Book Six, section forty-seven, on the levelling effect of the plague years, and Book Four's answer to it:

Hippocrates, after curing many diseases, himself fell sick and died. The Chaldaei foretold the deaths of many, and then fate caught them too. Alexander and Pompeius, and Caius Caesar, after so often completely destroying whole cities, and in battle cutting to pieces many ten thousands of cavalry and infantry, themselves too at last departed from life. Heraclitus, after so many speculations on the conflagration of the universe, was filled with water internally and died smeared all over with mud. And lice destroyed Democritus; and other lice killed Socrates. What means all this? Thou hast embarked, thou hast made the voyage, thou art come to shore; get out.

… always observe how ephemeral and worthless human things are, and what was yesterday a little mucus, to-morrow will be a mummy or ashes. Pass then through this little space of time conformably to nature, and end thy journey in content, as an olive falls off when it is ripe, blessing nature who produced it, and thanking the tree on which it grew.

And this, from Book Four, is the closest the book comes to a prayer:

Everything harmonizes with me, which is harmonious to thee, O Universe. Nothing for me is too early nor too late, which is in due time for thee. Everything is fruit to me which thy seasons bring, O Nature: from thee are all things, in thee are all things, to thee all things return.

The very last thing in the Meditations. Book Twelve, section thirty-six. He is dying, and he tells himself he is an actor being let off stage early, and that this is fine.

Man, thou hast been a citizen in this great state; what difference does it make to thee whether for five years or three? for that which is conformable to the laws is just for all. Where is the hardship then, if no tyrant nor yet an unjust judge sends thee away from the state, but nature, who brought thee into it? the same as if a praetor who has employed an actor dismisses him from the stage. — "But I have not finished the five acts, but only three of them." — Thou sayest well, but in life the three acts are the whole drama; for what shall be a complete drama is determined by him who was once the cause of its composition, and now of its dissolution: but thou art the cause of neither. Depart then satisfied, for he also who releases thee is satisfied.

"In life the three acts are the whole drama." He is arguing himself out of wanting more time, and the book simply stops there. No conclusion, no signature. It ends because he did.

Now the letters, which are a completely different man. This one is Marcus at about twenty-two, writing to Fronto from the country during the grape harvest, giving an hour-by-hour account of an ordinary day because he misses him. Haines's translation.

Hail, my sweetest of masters.

We are well. I slept somewhat late owing to my slight cold, which seems now to have subsided. So from five a.m. till nine I spent the time partly in reading some of Cato's Agriculture and partly in writing not quite such wretched stuff, by heavens, as yesterday. Then, after paying my respects to my father, I relieved my throat, I will not say by gargling — though the word gargarisso is, I believe, found in Novius and elsewhere — but by swallowing honey water as far as the gullet and ejecting it again. After easing my throat I went off to my father and attended him at a sacrifice. Then we went to luncheon. What do you think I ate? A wee bit of bread, though I saw others devouring beans, onions, and herrings full of roe. We then worked hard at grape-gathering, and had a good sweat, and were merry and, as the poet says, still left some clusters hanging high as gleanings of the vintage. After six o'clock we came home.

I did but little work and that to no purpose. Then I had a long chat with my little mother as she sat on the bed. My talk was this: What do you think my Fronto is now doing? Then she: And what do you think my Gratia is doing? Then I: And what do you think our little sparrow, the wee Gratia, is doing? Whilst we were chattering in this way and disputing which of us two loved the one or other of you two the better, the gong sounded, an intimation that my father had gone to his bath. So we had supper after we had bathed in the oil-press room; I do not mean bathed in the oil-press room, but when we had bathed, had supper there, and we enjoyed hearing the yokels chaffing one another. After coming back, before I turn over and snore, I get my task done and give my dearest of masters an account of the day's doings, and if I could miss him more, I would not grudge wasting away a little more.

Farewell, my Fronto, wherever you are, most honey-sweet, my love, my delight. How is it between you and me? I love you and you are away.

"I love you and you are away." The Latin is amo absentem, two words. That is the boy who grew into the man who wrote that fame is sound and echo. It is worth holding both.

And one from twenty-odd years later, in 165. Fronto, now old and ill, has lost his grandson; he had already buried five children, each one an only child at the time, "so I always lost children without any left to console me, and with my grief fresh upon me I begat others." Marcus, emperor, mid-plague, mid-war, writes back this. It is very short, and the last line is the reason I am showing it to you.

To my master, greeting.

I have just heard of your misfortune. Suffering anguish as I do when a single joint of yours aches, my master, what pain do you think I feel when it is your heart that aches? Under the shock of the news I could think of nothing else than to ask you to keep safe for me the sweetest of masters, in whom I find a greater solace for this life than you can find for your sorrow from any source.

I have not written with my own hand because after my bath in the evening even my hand was shaky. Farewell, my most delightful of masters.

He does not offer philosophy. He does not tell a grieving old man that loss is nothing else than change, which is a thing he genuinely believed and had written down in his own notebook. He says: stay alive, I need you. And then he apologises for the handwriting.

Cassandra of Troy

Greek myth · princess of Troy, priestess of Apollo · the one who was right every single time and was called mad for it

aug 5, 2026▼

childhood & early life

She was born into the largest and most doomed household in Greek literature. Her father was Priam, king of Troy, who by some counts fathered fifty sons and a great many daughters. Her mother was Hecuba, who would end the war as a slave and, in one version, as a dog. Her brothers were Hector and Paris, which is to say the best man in the story and the one who broke the world. Homer calls Cassandra the most beautiful of Priam's daughters, and that is the last easy sentence anyone gets to write about her.

She had a twin, Helenus, and the twinning is the cruellest structural joke in the myth. In the oldest version of the gift, Priam and Hecuba left the two infants overnight in the temple of Apollo at Thymbra, and in the morning found sacred serpents licking the children's ears clean, so that both could hear the future. Same night, same temple, same snakes, same power. Helenus grew up to be a respected seer whose advice generals took. Cassandra grew up to be a woman nobody believed. The difference between them is not talent. It is who gets listened to.

The better known version is uglier and more specific. Apollo wanted her, offered prophecy as the price of her body, and she took the gift and then refused him. He could not take a god's gift back, so he adjusted the terms instead. She would see everything, exactly, always, and no one would ever believe a word. It is a punishment engineered with real understanding of what would hurt. Not blindness. Sight, plus permanent isolation inside it.

what she did & why she's remembered

She warned them. That is the entire résumé, and it is enough to have kept her alive in the language for three thousand years. She told Troy that Paris would burn the city and that the infant should not be spared. She told them the Greek ship coming for Helen was the end of them. She told them, at the very end, that the wooden horse was full of men and that they should not bring it inside the walls. Every warning was correct. Every warning was ignored. The city held out ten years and then destroyed itself in a single night by carrying the weapon through its own gates while dancing.

Notice what the curse actually does. It does not make her wrong, and it does not make her quiet. She keeps saying the true thing to people who have decided in advance that she is hysterical, and the more urgent she sounds the more she confirms their diagnosis. In Aeschylus the chorus of Argive elders listens to her describe a murder that is happening on the other side of the door, agrees she is impressive, and concludes that seercraft is only a weaving of words, a craft of woe, to make mankind afraid. They are polite. They are sympathetic. They do nothing. That is the modern part of the story and the reason her name became a clinical term. The Cassandra complex is the documented pattern of the credible warning that is dismissed because of who is giving it.

The night Troy fell, she ran to the temple of Athena and took hold of the goddess's statue, which under every law of the ancient world made her untouchable. Ajax the Lesser dragged her off it and raped her, pulling the image of the goddess over in the struggle. Odysseus argued that the Greeks should stone him for it. They did not. Athena did the accounting herself and wrecked the fleet on the way home, and Ajax drowned boasting.

Here is the detail I cannot get past. The Locrians, Ajax's own people, were told by the oracle at Delphi to send two well-born girls every year to serve in Athena's temple at Ilion, and to keep sending them for a thousand years. The girls arrived to a show of force, could be stoned if caught, served until they died, and were replaced. An inscription found in Locris in the nineteenth century shows they were still doing it in the third century BC. One man assaulted one woman at an altar and an entire people paid in daughters for six hundred years. It is the only case I know of where a myth left a paper trail.

family life

Father, Priam, murdered at his own altar during the sack while Hecuba watched. Mother, Hecuba, enslaved to Odysseus. Twin brother, Helenus, who survived the war comfortably, married Hector's widow Andromache, and ended up ruling in Epirus, because his identical gift came without the tax. Brothers Hector and Paris and Troilus and Deiphobus, all dead. Sisters Polyxena, sacrificed on Achilles's grave, and Laodice, swallowed by the earth. Cassandra outlived nearly all of them and was made to watch.

There is one small moment in the Iliad that shows you who she was before the catastrophe swallowed her whole. Priam has gone alone into the Greek camp to beg Achilles for Hector's body, and is bringing him home at dawn. Cassandra is the first person awake, standing on the tower, and she sees it. Pope's version: Cassandra first beholds, from Ilion's spire, the sad procession of her hoary sire. She calls the whole city out to meet him. It is the one time everybody listens to her, and it is because the terrible thing has already happened. That is the curse in one image. They believe her the moment the news is no longer useful.

She had children, in the later tradition. Twin boys by Agamemnon, Teledamus and Pelops, born or conceived in captivity, and killed by Aegisthus after their parents were dead so that no branch of that line survived. Nobody wrote them a play.

romantic life

There is no romance here, and it is worth saying that plainly rather than dressing it up. There is a god who bargained for her body, a soldier who took it by force in a temple, and a king who shipped her home as property. The pattern of her life is men deciding what happens to her and then being surprised she is not grateful.

Aeschylus lets her tell the Apollo story herself, in the middle of the Agamemnon, in seven lines of stichomythia so compressed they read like someone being interrogated. An elder asks whether the god desired her. She says there was a time she thought it shameful to speak of. He says shame is for the mighty, not the weak, which is one of the more brutal throwaway lines in Greek drama. She says: we wrestled, and his breath to me was sweet. He asks, in the flat bureaucratic way of men in choruses, whether they came to the getting of children, as is meet. And she says: I swore to Loxias, and I swore a lie. Then, four words later, after that sin, no man believed me more.

The Trojan Women gives her one stranger note. Agamemnon, the most powerful king in Greece, is genuinely obsessed with her, and the herald Talthybius finds this humiliating to watch and says so. Cassandra's response is to put on her wedding wreaths and dance, singing a bridal hymn, because she has already seen what happens in Argos and she knows she is going to be the instrument that brings the house of Atreus down. She calls herself the bride of desire while carrying a torch to her own murder. That is not madness. That is a woman turning the only event available to her into a weapon, in public, and being called mad because the alternative is admitting she can see.

life until death

She was awarded to Agamemnon in the division of the spoils and taken by ship to Argos. She knew the whole itinerary before it began. She knew Clytemnestra had spent ten years waiting with an axe and a lover, that the king would be cut down in his bath in a net of rich cloth, and that she herself would be killed beside him. She said all of it, out loud, in the street, to a chorus of old men who found her moving and did not move.

The most extraordinary thing Aeschylus does is give her a choice, sort of, and make her take the worse one deliberately. She sits silent on the chariot while Clytemnestra orders her inside, silent through the threats, silent until the queen gives up and goes back in. Then she speaks, tears off her prophetic robes and staff, stamps on them, and walks through the door herself. The chorus leader asks why she is walking to slaughter with clear eyes like a god-blinded beast, and she says the day is come, small profit now to fly. What she asks for is not rescue. It is one clean stroke.

She did not get it. In the Odyssey, Agamemnon's ghost tells Odysseus in the underworld that he lay dying with a sword in him and heard Priam's daughter Cassandra scream as Clytemnestra killed her close beside him. He raised his hands to stop it and could not. That is the oldest surviving account of her death, and in it she is a sound offstage in another man's story about his own bad luck.

Her prophecy came true. Orestes came back and killed his mother, the house of Atreus tore itself apart exactly as she described, and every person who dismissed her was proven wrong on schedule. Being right cost her everything and saved nothing, and Aeschylus refuses to pretend otherwise. What she leaves behind is a question that has outlasted the play: what do you do with knowledge nobody will accept from you. Her answer, in the end, was to say it anyway, on the record, and walk in.

their works

Cassandra wrote nothing; she is a character, and the words are Aeschylus's and Euripides's. Everything below is Gilbert Murray's verse translation, the same translator as the Medea entry, all out of copyright. Start with the Agamemnon, 458 BC. She has been standing silent on a chariot for the entire play. Clytemnestra has just failed to get her indoors and gone back inside in disgust. Then, finally, this.

Apollo, Apollo! Light of the Ways of Men!
Mine enemy!
Hast lighted me to darkness yet again?

Apollo, Apollo! Light of all that is!
Mine enemy!
Where hast thou led me? … Ha! What house is this?

Her first coherent words in the play are the name of the god who ruined her, twice, with "mine enemy" as the refrain. Then she starts reading the building. She has never been to Argos in her life.

Nay, nay. This is the house that God hateth.
There be many things that know its secret; sore
And evil things; murders and strangling death.
'Tis here they slaughter men…A splashing floor.

The witnesses … I follow where they lead.
The crying … of little children … near the gate:
Crying for wounds that bleed:
And the smell of the baked meats their father ate.

She is picking up the Thyestean feast, a generation-old atrocity in that family, off the walls. The elder's answer to this is the single most infuriating line in the play: Word of thy mystic power had reached our ear long since. Howbeit we need no prophets here.

She keeps going, and it gets more specific, and they keep not moving.

CASSANDRA. O Woman, thou! The lord who lay with thee!
Wilt lave with water, and then … How speak the end?
It comes so quick. A hand … another hand …
That reach, reach gropingly….

LEADER. I see not yet. These riddles, pierced with blind
Gleams of foreboding, but bemuse my mind.

CASSANDRA. Ah, ah! What is it? There; it is coming clear.
A net … some net of Hell.
Nay, she that lies with him … is she the snare?
And half of his blood upon it. It holds well….

CASSANDRA. Ah, look! Look! Keep his mate from the Wild Bull!
A tangle of raiment, see;
A black horn, and a blow, and he falleth, full
In the marble amid the water. I counsel ye.
I speak plain … Blood in the bath and treachery!

"I speak plain." She does. Murder weapon, location, method, perpetrator. And the chorus replies that they are no great interpreter of oracles but this seems to spell some mischief, and then wonders aloud whether prophecy is anything more than a weaving of words to make mankind afraid.

Then she stops chanting, pulls herself together, and speaks to them like an adult, which is the moment the scene breaks your heart.

'Fore God, mine oracle shall no more hide
With veils his visage, like a new-wed bride!
A shining wind out of this dark shall blow,
Piercing the dawn, growing as great waves grow,
To burst in the heart of sunrise … stronger far
Than this poor pain of mine. I will not mar
With mists my wisdom.
Be near me as I go,
Tracking the evil things of long ago,
And bear me witness.

… Hath it missed or struck, mine arrow? Am I a poor
Dreamer, that begs and babbles at the door?
Give first thine oath in witness, that I know
Of this great dome the sins wrought long ago.

She is asking them to go on the record that she was right about the past, so that they will take her seriously about the future. She is building a case. It does not work, and she knows it will not work, and she does it anyway.

Then the Apollo exchange. Seven lines, and it is the only time in surviving Greek tragedy that she gets to say what happened to her.

CASSANDRA. The Seer Apollo made me too to see.

ELDER (in a low voice). Was the God's heart pierced with desire for thee?

CASSANDRA. Time was, I held it shame hereof to speak.

ELDER. Ah, shame is for the mighty, not the weak.

CASSANDRA. We wrestled, and his breath to me was sweet.

ELDER. Ye came to the getting of children, as is meet?

CASSANDRA. I swore to Loxias, and I swore a lie.

ELDER. Already thine the gift of prophecy?

CASSANDRA. Already I showed my people all their path.

ELDER. And Loxias did not smite thee in his wrath?

CASSANDRA. After that sin … no man believed me more.

ELDER. Nay, then, to us thy wisdom seemeth sure.

Read that last line again. He hears the whole story and concludes, sincerely, that her wisdom seems sure to him. And then he does nothing, and lets the king walk in, and stands outside the door listening to him die. Belief without action turns out to be its own version of the curse.

Now she names Clytemnestra directly, and the imagery is all teeth.

Mine, mine! The yoke is nailed about my neck….
Oh, lord of ships and trampler on the wreck
Of Ilion, knows he not this she-wolf's tongue,
Which licks and fawns, and laughs with ear up-sprung,
To bite in the end like secret death?—And can
The woman? Slay a strong and armèd man? …
What fangèd reptile like to her doth creep?
… God! And she shouted in his face her joy,
Like men in battle when the foe doth break.
And feigns thanksgiving for his safety's sake!
What if no man believe me? 'Tis all one.
The thing which must be shall be; aye, and soon
Thou too shalt sorrow for these things, and here
Standing confess me all too true a seer.

"What if no man believe me? 'Tis all one." That is the whole psychology of her in nine words. She has stopped needing the audience. The truth is going to be true regardless of the reception, so she says it for the record and lets time do the arguing.

Then the last vision hits, and she tears off the robes.

God, she will kill me! Like to them that brew
Poison, I see her mingle for me too
A separate vial in her wrath, and swear,
Whetting her blade for him, that I must share
His death … because, because he hath dragged me here!
Oh, why these mockers at my throat? This gear
Of wreathèd bands, this staff of prophecy?
I mean to kill you first, before I die.
Begone!

Down to perdition! … Lie ye so?
So I requite you! Now make rich in woe
Some other Bird of Evil, me no more!

Ah, see! It is Apollo's self, hath tore
His crown from me! Who watched me long ago
In this same prophet's robe, by friend, by foe,
All with one voice, all blinded, mocked to scorn:
"A thing of dreams," "a beggar-maid outworn,"
Poor, starving and reviled, I endured all…

A thing of dreams. A beggar-maid outworn. Those are the names they called the correct one.

And then she walks in. This is her last speech, and the last four lines of it are, to my mind, the finest thing in the play.

Why should I grieve? Why pity these men's doom?
I who have seen the City of Ilion
Pass as she passed; and they who cast her down
Have thus their end, as God gives judgement sure….
I go to drink my cup. I will endure
To die. O Gates, Death-Gates, all hail to you!
Only, pray God the blow be stricken true!
Pray God, unagonized, with blood that flows
Quick unto friendly death, these eyes may close!

…

One word, one dirge-song would I utter yet
O'er mine own corpse. To this last shining Sun
I pray that, when the Avenger's work is done,
His enemies may remember this thing too,
This little thing, the woman slave they slew!

O world of men, farewell! A painted show
Is all thy glory; and when life is low
The touch of a wet sponge out-blotteth all.
Oh, sadder this than any proud man's fall!

A wet sponge across a painted board. Everything a man builds, wiped with one pass of a damp rag, and she says the erasure is sadder than the fall. Written in 458 BC by a man who fought at Marathon.

Twenty-three years later, Euripides put her in The Trojan Women (415 BC), in the smoking ruins, being handed over as a concubine. She comes out of the tent in white with a torch, singing her own wedding song, and her mother thinks the tent is on fire.

Lift, lift it high:
Give it to mine hand!
Lo, I bear a flame
Unto God! I praise his name.
I light with a burning brand
This sanctuary.
Blessèd is he that shall wed,
And blessèd, blessèd am I
In Argos: a bride to lie
With a king in a king's bed.

Hail, O Hymen red,
O Torch that makest one!
Weepest thou, Mother mine own?
Surely thy cheek is pale
With tears, tears that wail
For a land and a father dead.
But I go garlanded:
I am the Bride of Desire:
Therefore my torch is borne—
Lo, the lifting of morn,
Lo, the leaping of fire!

Then she drops the singing voice and tells her mother exactly what the wedding is for.

O Mother, fill mine hair with happy flowers,
And speed me forth. Yea, if my spirit cowers,
Drive me with wrath! So liveth Loxias,
A bloodier bride than ever Helen was
Go I to Agamemnon, Lord most high
Of Hellas! … I shall kill him, mother; I
Shall kill him, and lay waste his house with fire
As he laid ours. My brethren and my sire
Shall win again …

A bloodier bride than ever Helen was. She has worked out that the only power left to a woman with no army and no city is to be the thing that gets carried inside the enemy's walls. She is making herself the horse.

And then, in the middle of the wreckage of her own home, she delivers a cold cost-benefit analysis proving the losers had the better war. This was staged in Athens the year after the Athenians massacred the men of Melos and enslaved the women. Nobody in that theatre could have missed it.

Nay, I will show thee. Even now this town
Is happier than the Greeks. …
One love, one woman's beauty, o'er the track
Of hunted Helen, made their myriads fall.
And this their King so wise, who ruleth all,
What wrought he? Cast out Love that Hate might feed:
Gave to his brother his own child, his seed
Of gladness, that a woman fled, and fain
To fly for ever, should be turned again!

So the days waned, and armies on the shore
Of Simois stood and strove and died. Wherefore?
No man had moved their landmarks; none had shook
Their wallèd towns.—And they whom Ares took,
Had never seen their children: no wife came
With gentle arms to shroud the limbs of them
For burial, in a strange and angry earth
Laid dead. And there at home, the same long dearth:
Women that lonely died, and aged men
Waiting for sons that ne'er should turn again,
Nor know their graves, nor pour drink-offerings,
To still the unslakèd dust. These be the things
The conquering Greek hath won!

But we—what pride,
What praise of men were sweeter?—fighting died
To save our people. And when war was red
Around us, friends upbore the gentle dead
Home, and dear women's hands about them wound
White shrouds, and here they sleep in the old ground
Belovèd. …

Would ye be wise, ye Cities, fly from war!
Yet if war come, there is a crown in death
For her that striveth well and perisheth
Unstained: to die in evil were the stain!

"Gave to his brother his own child" is Iphigenia, sacrificed at Aulis to get a wind. Cassandra is standing in the ashes of her city naming the exact debt that is going to kill Agamemnon, and the herald's response is that Apollo must have made her mad. It is a perfectly lucid speech. Being lucid has never once helped her.

She tears off the wreaths and goes to the ship.

O, ye wreaths!
Ye garlands of my God, whose love yet breathes
About me; shapes of joyance mystical;
Begone! I have forgot the festival,
Forgot the joy. Begone! I tear ye, so,
From off me! … Out on the swift winds they go.
With flesh still clean I give them back to thee,
Still white, O God, O light that leadest me!

Where lies the galley? Whither shall I tread?
See that your watch be set, your sail be spread.
The wind comes quick! … Three Powers—mark me, thou!—
There be in Hell, and one walks with thee now!

Mother, farewell, and weep not! O my sweet
City, my earth-clad brethren, and thou great
Sire that begat us; but a space, ye Dead,
And I am with you: yea, with crownèd head
I come, and shining from the fires that feed
On these that slay us now, and all their seed!

"Three Powers there be in Hell, and one walks with thee now." She tells the herald to his face that she is one of the Furies and he writes it off as raving. She was right about that too.

And for the oldest version of her ending, Homer, Odyssey XI, Butler's prose. Agamemnon's ghost in the underworld, explaining how he died. Cassandra gets one clause.

I heard Priam's daughter Cassandra scream as Clytemnestra killed her close beside me. I lay dying upon the earth with the sword in my body, and raised my hands to kill the slut of a murderess, but she slipped away from me; she would not even close my lips nor my eyes when I was dying…

Three thousand years of literature and the first time we hear about her death, it is a sound in the background of a man complaining about his wife. Aeschylus gave her back two hundred lines and the best writing in the play. That is what art is for.

Medea of Colchis

Greek myth · princess, priestess of Hecate, granddaughter of the Sun · the most dangerous woman in the ancient imagination

aug 4, 2026▼

childhood & early life

She was born at the far edge of the known world, in Colchis, on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, in a kingdom the Greeks could barely place on a map. Her father was Aeëtes, a hard and suspicious king. Her grandfather was Helios, the Sun himself, which meant that whatever she did, the entire sky was related to her. Her aunt was Circe. The bloodline is not decoration; it is the whole point. Medea grows up knowing she is descended from the thing that sees everything and is never held accountable.

She was raised a priestess of Hecate, goddess of witchcraft, crossroads and the dead, which in practice meant she knew plants. Not folklore plants. She knew what killed, what preserved, what burned through skin, what put a serpent to sleep. In Apollonius's telling she is very young when the Argo arrives, still a girl in her father's house, and the first thing she experiences is not power but panic. Hera and Aphrodite arrange for her to fall in love with the visiting foreigner because the gods need a Greek hero to survive an impossible task, and the cheapest way to arrange that is to make a teenage girl betray her entire family.

So the origin of Medea is this: a clever, isolated, dangerously capable girl in a remote court, aimed like a weapon at her own household by powers that never asked her.

what she did & why she's remembered

Jason came for the Golden Fleece. Aeëtes set him tasks designed to kill him: yoke fire-breathing bronze-hoofed bulls, plough a field, sow dragon's teeth, fight the armed men who sprout from them. Medea gave him a drug that made his skin proof against fire and iron for a day, told him to throw a rock among the sown warriors so they would kill each other, and then drugged the sleepless serpent guarding the fleece herself. Jason's entire legend is, on inspection, her work with his name on it.

Then she fled with him, and to slow her father's pursuit she killed her own brother Absyrtus. In the older versions she scattered the pieces of his body into the sea so Aeëtes would have to stop and gather them. This is the first unforgivable thing, and it happens before she is twenty, for a man she has known for days.

Back in Greece she kept working for him. Jason's uncle Pelias had stolen the throne and would not give it back, so Medea demonstrated her rejuvenation magic on an old ram, cut up and boiled back to a lamb, and then persuaded Pelias's daughters to do the same to their father. They chopped up their own father on her instructions. He did not come back. She murdered a king using his loving daughters as the knife, and Jason got nothing for it except exile, because civilised Greek states do not reward that.

She is remembered, though, for Corinth. In 431 BC Euripides put her on stage as an exiled foreign wife being discarded for a younger, better-connected bride, and gave her the most coherent argument for revenge ever written. The play came third out of three that year. It has since outlived nearly everything that beat it.

One thing worth knowing: the child-killing is probably Euripides's invention. Older sources say the Corinthians killed her children, seven boys and seven girls, at the temple of Hera, and then blamed her. There is an ancient rumour, preserved in the scholia and attributed to Parmeniscus, that the Corinthians paid Euripides five talents to move the murder onto the mother. Which is either the oldest recorded PR settlement in history or a very good joke about how stories about women get edited.

family life

Father: Aeëtes, king of Colchis, son of the Sun, a man who kept his household by fear and lost it in one night. Mother: usually Idyia, an Oceanid. Sister: Chalciope. Brother: Absyrtus, dead by her hand. Aunt: Circe, who in Apollonius performs the purification rite for the murder and then, once she understands what her niece has done, will not have her in the house. Even the witch of Aeaea drew a line.

Her own children in Euripides are two unnamed boys, which is a deliberate choice. They speak four lines from behind a door while they are being killed, and otherwise they are silent, held, kissed, wept over. Later she has a son called Medus by Aegeus of Athens, and in some versions Medus becomes the ancestor of the Medes, which is how the Greeks explained an entire eastern people as the descendants of a woman they had exiled.

The core family fact about Medea is that she has no family left to be rescued by. She says it plainly to Jason, and it is the coldest arithmetic in the play. Her father, betrayed. Her brother, dead. The daughters of Pelias, ruined. Every bridge burned for one man, and every one of them burned by her own hand, which is exactly why the betrayal lands the way it does.

romantic life

One love, total, and it destroys the world. Apollonius writes the falling-in-love as a wound, an arrow burning under the heart, a girl lying awake all night arguing with herself and rehearsing what she will say. She swears oaths with Jason, hand in hand, calling the gods to witness. The oath matters. Greek marriage between a Greek and a barbarian was not legally a marriage, and Medea's whole legal standing rests on a promise Jason can simply decide not to remember.

Years later in Corinth he marries Creon's daughter and explains, at length, calmly, that this is for the good of the household. He is not raving. That is the horror of him. He gives a reasonable, upwardly mobile speech about security and future half-brothers for their sons and tells her she has been well compensated because she got to live in Greece and be famous. He even tells her that Aphrodite, not she, saved him, so her service does not really count. Euripides's Jason is not a villain in the mustache sense. He is a careerist who has stopped noticing that other people are real.

Her answer is the most quoted lines in the play: strip a woman of her right in a man's love and there is no bloodier spirit between heaven and hell. And the second most telling moment is when Jason, at the very end, mourns his ship. Argo, my own, my swift and beautiful. He never once says he loved her.

Afterwards she does marry again. Aegeus, king of Athens, childless and desperate, who in the play swears her an oath of sanctuary in exchange for a cure for his childlessness. She lives in Athens as queen and later tries to poison his son Theseus, is found out, and is exiled again. She keeps choosing men who need something from her, and then discovering that need is not the same thing as loyalty.

life until death

She does not die. That is the strangest thing about her, and the reason the play refuses to give anyone relief. A Greek tragedy is supposed to end with the transgressor broken. Instead Medea appears above the roof in a chariot drawn by winged serpents, sent by her grandfather the Sun, holding the bodies of her children so that Jason cannot even bury them. The murderer leaves in the machine normally reserved for gods. Gilbert Murray's line for it is exact: in this play Medea herself is the deity in the machine.

After Corinth: Athens, marriage to Aegeus, the son Medus, the failed poisoning of Theseus, exile again. Then she goes east with her son, and the myth loses interest in her, which is its own kind of ending. Some later authors say she was taken to the Elysian Fields and married Achilles there, immortal, which is the mythographers' way of admitting they could not kill her off.

Jason gets the punishment instead. Old, friendless, unmarriageable, oath-breaker, wandering back to the beached hull of the Argo to sleep under his one true love, and a rotten timber falls and kills him. The hero dies of his own boat.

What survives is the argument. Euripides refused to make the oppressed virtuous. He shows you exactly how a person is wronged into becoming the worst version of herself, lets you agree with every step of her reasoning, and then makes you watch where the reasoning goes. That is the whole engine of the thing, and it is why she reads less like a myth than like a case study.

their works

Medea left no writings; she is a character, and her words are Euripides's, first performed in 431 BC. Everything below is from Gilbert Murray's verse translation of Medea, which is out of copyright and still the most bruising English version. Start with the nurse, who opens the play by wishing the ship had never been built, and who knows exactly what is coming because she knows the woman.

Methinks she hath a dread, not joy, to see
Her children near. 'Tis this that maketh me
Most tremble, lest she do I know not what.
Her heart is no light thing, and useth not
To brook much wrong. I know that woman, aye,
And dread her! Will she creep alone to die
Bleeding in that old room, where still is laid
Lord Jason's bed? She hath for that a blade
Made keen. Or slay the bridegroom and the king,
And win herself God knows what direr thing?
'Tis a fell spirit. Few, I ween, shall stir
Her hate unscathed, or lightly humble her.

Then Medea comes out of the house and addresses the women of Corinth. This is the speech that people were still arguing about two and a half thousand years later, because a man wrote it in a city where women could not vote, own property meaningfully, or leave.

Of all things upon earth that bleed and grow,
A herb most bruised is woman. We must pay
Our store of gold, hoarded for that one day,
To buy us some man's love; and lo, they bring
A master of our flesh! There comes the sting
Of the whole shame. And then the jeopardy,
For good or ill, what shall that master be;
Reject she cannot: and if he but stays
His suit, 'tis shame on all that woman's days.
So thrown amid new laws, new places, why,
'Tis magic she must have, or prophecy—
Home never taught her that—how best to guide
Toward peace this thing that sleepeth at her side.

Her lord, if he be wearied of the face
Withindoors, gets him forth; some merrier place
Will ease his heart: but she waits on, her whole
Vision enchainèd on a single soul.
And then, forsooth, 'tis they that face the call
Of war, while we sit sheltered, hid from all
Peril!—False mocking! Sooner would I stand
Three times to face their battles, shield in hand,
Than bear one child.

Three times in the shield wall rather than once in childbirth. Written by a man in 431 BC and still the most efficient demolition of "but women are protected" ever put on a stage.

She finishes with the warning, and the chorus of Corinthian women agrees to keep her secret, which is its own small mutiny.

Oh, in all things but this,
I know how full of fears a woman is,
And faint at need, and shrinking from the light
Of battle: but once spoil her of her right
In man's love, and there moves, I warn thee well,
No bloodier spirit between heaven and hell.

Creon, the king, comes to exile her, and gives the single most honest reason a man in Greek tragedy ever gives for being afraid of a woman. He is not afraid she is wicked. He is afraid she is smart and quiet.

CREON. Thy words be gentle: but I fear me yet
Lest even now there creep some wickedness
Deep hid within thee. And for that the less
I trust thee now than ere these words began.
A woman quick of wrath, aye, or a man,
Is easier watching than the cold and still.

And Medea, earlier in the same scene, on what it costs to be visibly intelligent in a place that did not ask you to be.

Come unto fools with knowledge of new things,
They deem it vanity, not knowledge. Aye,
And men that erst for wisdom were held high,
Feel thee a thorn to fret them, privily
Held higher than they. So hath it been with me.
A wise-woman I am; and for that sin
To divers ill names men would pen me in;
A seed of strife; an eastern dreamer; one
Of brand not theirs; one hard to play upon . . .

"One hard to play upon." She lists the slurs used on her and the last one is a compliment she is not allowed to have.

The moment Creon leaves, she drops the mask, and the shift in register is genuinely frightening. She was kneeling and grovelling ten lines ago.

Dost dream I would have grovelled to this man,
Save that I won mine end, and shaped my plan
For merry deeds? My lips had never deigned
Speak word with him: my flesh been never stained
With touching. . . . Fool, Oh, triple fool! It lay
So plain for him to kill my whole essay
By exile swift: and, lo, he sets me free
This one long day. . . .

Shall I burn
Their house with fire? Or stealing past unseen
To Jason's bed—I have a blade made keen
For that—stab, breast to breast, that wedded pair?
Good, but for one thing. When I am taken there,
And killed, they will laugh loud who hate me. . . .
Nay,
I love the old way best, the simple way
Of poison, where we too are strong as men.

"Where we too are strong as men." She is not choosing poison because it is feminine. She is choosing it because it is the one weapon that does not care how big your arms are.

Now Jason, defending himself. Read it slowly. It is a performance review.

Howbeit, in my deliverance, thou hast got
Far more than given. A good Greek land hath been
Thy lasting home, not barbary. Thou hast seen
Our ordered life, and justice, and the long
Still grasp of law not changing with the strong
Man's pleasure. Then, all Hellas far and near
Hath learned thy wisdom, and in every ear
Thy fame is. Had thy days run by unseen
On that last edge of the world, where then had been
The story of great Medea?

. . . Would to God
We mortals by some other seed could raise
Our fruits, and no blind women block our ways!
Then had there been no curse to wreck mankind.

He tells the woman who saved his life that she came out ahead on the deal because she got exposure. Then he wishes women did not have to exist. And her reply, four words long, is the whole play in miniature: Thine old barbarian bride, the dog out of the east who loved thee sore, she grew grey-haired, she served thy pride no more.

The chorus, watching, sings the strangest song in Greek tragedy. It is a feminist manifesto sung by a group of ordinary Corinthian housewives who are about to become accessories to a triple murder.

Back streams the wave on the ever running river:
Life, life is changed and the laws of it o'ertrod.
Man shall be the slave, the affrighted, the low-liver!
Man hath forgotten God.
And woman, yea, woman, shall be terrible in story:
The tales too, meseemeth, shall be other than of yore.
For a fear there is that cometh out of Woman and a glory,
And the hard hating voices shall encompass her no more!

The old bards shall cease, and their memory that lingers
Of frail brides and faithless, shall be shrivelled as with fire.
For they loved us not, nor knew us: and our lips were dumb, our fingers
Could wake not the secret of the lyre.

Then the long scene where she calls the children out to say goodbye while pretending to make peace. This is the passage that made the play unbearable to Athens, and it is written as an argument she is having with herself, in real time, losing and winning and losing again.

My babes, my own,
Why gaze ye so?—What is it that ye see?—
And laugh with that last laughter? . . . Woe is me,
What shall I do?
Women, my strength is gone,
Gone like a dream, since once I looked upon
Those shining faces. . . . I can do it not.
Good-bye to all the thoughts that burned so hot
Aforetime! I will take and hide them far,
Far, from men's eyes. Why should I seek a war
So blind: by these babes' wounds to sting again
Their father's heart, and win myself a pain
Twice deeper? Never, never! I forget
Henceforward all I laboured for.

And yet,
What is it with me? Would I be a thing
Mocked at, and leave mine enemies to sting
Unsmitten? It must be. O coward heart,
Ever to harbour such soft words!

She calls mercy cowardice. That is the hinge of the entire tragedy, and it is a sentence you can hear people say today about forgiving anyone.

Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye,
And royal mien, and bright brave faces clear,
May you be blessèd, but not here! What here
Was yours, your father stole. . . . Ah God, the glow
Of cheek on cheek, the tender touch; and Oh,
Sweet scent of childhood. . . . Go! Go! . . . Am I blind? . . .
Mine eyes can see not, when I look to find
Their places. I am broken by the wings
Of evil. . . . Yea, I know to what bad things
I go, but louder than all thought doth cry
Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.

"I know to what bad things I go." No self-deception, no madness defence, no god possessing her. She sees it clearly and does it anyway, and Euripides makes that the definition of the worst human suffering there is.

The messenger's account of the princess dying in the poisoned crown and robe is one of the great horror set pieces of antiquity, and it starts with something crueller than the poison: a girl admiring herself in a mirror.

When once she saw the raiment, she could still
Her joy no more, but gave him all his will. . . .
She drew
The flowerèd garments forth, and sate her down
To her arraying: bound the golden crown
Through her long curls, and in a mirror fair
Arranged their separate clusters, smiling there
At the dead self that faced her.

. . . The carcanet of gold
That gripped her brow was molten in a dire
And wondrous river of devouring fire.
And those fine robes, the gift thy children gave—
God's mercy!—everywhere did lap and lave
The delicate flesh; till up she sprang, and fled,
A fiery pillar, shaking locks and head
This way and that, seeking to cast the crown
Somewhere away. But like a thing nailed down
The burning gold held fast the anadem. . . .
And touch
The dead we durst not. We had seen too much.

Smiling at the dead self that faced her. Four words of foreshadowing hidden inside a girl liking her own reflection.

And when the messenger tells her, her response is two lines, and they are ice.

MEDEA. I have words also that could answer well
Thy word. But take thine ease, good friend, and tell,
How died they? Hath it been a very foul
Death, prithee? That were comfort to my soul.

Finally the roof. Jason batters at the door with soldiers, and she is already above him, out of reach, in the sun-chariot, with the bodies.

MEDEA. What make ye at my gates? Why batter ye
With brazen bars, seeking the dead and me
Who slew them? Peace! . . . And thou, if aught of mine
Thou needest, speak, though never touch of thine
Shall scathe me more. Out of his firmament
My fathers' father, the high Sun, hath sent
This, that shall save me from mine enemies' rage.
MEDEA. An easy answer had I to this swell
Of speech, but Zeus our father knoweth well,
All I for thee have wrought, and thou for me.
So let it rest. This thing was not to be,
That thou shouldst live a merry life, my bed
Forgotten and my heart uncomforted,
Thou nor thy princess. . . .
Call me what thing thou please,
Tigress or Skylla from the Tuscan seas:
My claws have gripped thine heart, and all things shine.

JASON. Thou too hast grief. Thy pain is fierce as mine.

MEDEA. I love the pain, so thou shalt laugh no more.

"My claws have gripped thine heart, and all things shine." She has destroyed herself completely and describes it as light. That is the most honest line ever written about revenge, and the reason nobody has improved on this play in two and a half thousand years of trying.

Emily Brontë

English novelist and poet, author of Wuthering Heights, published as Ellis Bell · 1818-1848

aug 3, 2026▼

childhood & early life

Emily Jane Brontë was born on July 30, 1818, in Thornton, Yorkshire, the fifth of six children of Patrick Brontë, an Irish curate who had changed his name from Brunty, and Maria Branwell, a Cornishwoman who had six children in nine years and then died of cancer in September 1821, a few months after the family moved to the parsonage at Haworth. Emily was three. The parsonage sat at the top of a steep village street with the graveyard pressed right up against the house, and the moors beginning where the graves stopped.

In 1824 the four eldest girls were sent to the Clergy Daughters' School at Cowan Bridge, a cheap, cold, badly fed institution. Maria and Elizabeth, the two oldest, came home in 1825 and died of tuberculosis within six weeks of each other. Emily was six years old and had now buried a mother and two sisters. What was left was four children in a house of stone: Charlotte, Branwell, Emily, Anne.

So they built other worlds. A box of twelve wooden soldiers Patrick brought home in 1826 turned into an entire invented empire, written in handmade books an inch high in script so small it needed a magnifying glass, partly so adults could not read it. Charlotte and Branwell took Angria.
